# A METHOD FOR FINDING CURVED LINES ENJOYING THE PROPERTY OF A MAXIMUM OR MINIMUM.

---

## CHAPTER ONE.

->*Concerning the method of maxima and minima applied to finding curved lines in general.*<-

### DEFINITION I.

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'M' featuring a landscape with a river or sea and rugged mountains in the background.</image-desc>The **Method** of maxima and minima <note>The study of finding the largest or smallest possible values of a mathematical function.</note> applied to curved lines is the method of finding curved lines that possess some proposed property of a maximum or a minimum.

### COROLLARY I.

<margin>2.</margin> Therefore, by means of this method, those curved lines are discovered in which some proposed quantity attains either the maximum or the minimum value.

<summary>This is the opening page of Euler's landmark 1744 treatise, defining the scope of the "calculus of variations" as a method for identifying curves that optimize a specific geometric or physical property.</summary>
<keywords>calculus of variations, maxima and minima, curved lines, geometry, optimization, Leonhard Euler</keywords>

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

### COROLLARY II.

3. However, since the same curve can be made similar to itself in infinite ways, the problem would be highly indeterminate, and thus impossible to solve, unless some restriction is applied. For whatever curve might be presented as possessing a property of a maximum or minimum, another curve—either similar or dissimilar to it—could always be shown that would contain that same property to a greater or lesser degree.

### COROLLARY III.

4. Therefore, since an adequate knowledge of curves requires that they be related to some axis given by position, and to any portions of it which are called <term>abscissas</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate (x-axis) in a coordinate system.</note>: the first and most important restriction must be sought from the quantity of the abscissa.

### COROLLARY IV.

5. Problems belonging to this method ought to be proposed in such a way that we seek curved lines related to an axis given by position, which, among all other curves corresponding to the same abscissa, are endowed with the property of a maximum or minimum.

## SCHOLION <note>A scholarly explanatory note or commentary on a mathematical text.</note>.

6. This method of maxima and minima, therefore, differs greatly from the one we have explained elsewhere. In that other method, for a given and determined curved line, we determined the location where a certain proposed variable quantity belonging to the curve becomes a maximum or minimum. Here, however, the curved line itself is sought, in which a certain proposed quantity becomes a maximum or minimum. This method began to be cultivated in the previous century, soon after the discovery of the <term>Analysis of Infinites</term> <note>original: "Analysis infinitorum"; this refers to the early development of calculus.</note>, by the celebrated Bernoulli brothers, and from that time it has received the greatest advancements. Indeed, the first problem of this kind to be treated pertained to Mechanics, and in it was sought the curved line upon which a falling heavy body descends most quickly; to which the name *brachystochrone* curve, or *Line of swiftest descent*, was given. In this problem

<summary>The author defines the necessity of using a fixed axis (abscissa) to constrain problems where the shape of a curve itself is the unknown variable. He distinguishes this new method from standard calculus and credits the Bernoulli brothers with its origin via the brachystochrone problem.</summary>
<keywords>calculus of variations, maxima and minima, abscissa, Bernoulli brothers, brachystochrone, analysis of infinites, mechanics</keywords>

# APPLIED TO THE FINDING OF CURVES.
->A 2<-
<meta>catchword: perverse</meta>

It is now manifest that, without an added condition, this could not even retain the name of a "question": for it is clear that the shorter the line chosen and the closer it approaches a vertical position, the shorter the time of descent upon it will be. For this reason, one cannot seek in an absolute sense the line upon which a falling heavy body glides most quickly or in the shortest time; rather, the quantity of the <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate (x-axis) in a coordinate system.</note> to which the curve to be found corresponds must be defined at the same time. Thus, among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa taken on an axis given in position, one would seek that curve upon which a heavy body would glide down most swiftly.

Nor, indeed, was that condition sufficient in this Problem to make it determined: but it was necessary to add this further condition, that the curve to be found must pass through two given points. This Problem had to be constrained by these conditions so that it might become determined—namely, to determine, among all curved lines passing through two given points, that one upon which a descending body completes the arc corresponding to the given abscissa in the shortest time.

Meanwhile, it should be noted here that the condition of passing through two points is not absolutely necessary <insert>in the statement</insert>, but in this Problem, it is brought in by the solution itself. For in the solution of this Problem, one arrives immediately at a <term>differential equation</term><note>An equation involving derivatives, describing how one quantity changes in relation to another.</note> of the second degree, which, when integrated twice, receives two <term>arbitrary constants</term><note>Values that can be any number, usually denoted as C, which appear during the process of integration.</note>. To determine these, one needs two points through which the curve is led, or other similar properties. And this same condition, as if of its own accord, attaches itself to all Problems of this kind whose solution leads immediately to a differential equation of the second degree. 

However, in Problems which are resolved by a differential equation of the fourth or higher order, not even two points are sufficient to determine the curve, but as many points are needed as the degrees the differentials obtain. On the contrary, if the solution leads immediately to an algebraic equation, then the Problem will be perfectly determined without a condition of this kind, provided the length of the abscissa is defined. But all these things will be perceived more clearly when we arrive at the solutions of the Problems below: and there we shall explain these observations more fully. For here at the beginning, it seemed best only to mention these things so that

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

let us remove perverse ideas regarding the determination of problems of this kind.

### DEFINITION II.

7. The absolute method of maxima and minima teaches how to determine, among absolutely all curves related to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate (x-axis) in a coordinate system.</note>, that one in which a certain proposed variable quantity obtains the maximum or minimum value.

### COROLLARY.

8. Therefore, in problems pertaining to this method, the axis is given by position; and, among all curves which can be related to this axis and its determined portion, that one is determined in which a certain variable quantity becomes maximum or minimum.

### SCHOLION <note>A scholarly explanatory note or commentary.</note>.

9. We do not add here, in general, any other condition for the determination of the maximum or minimum besides the quantity of the abscissa. For problems are given which are perfectly determined in this way, as will appear more distinctly below. For even if problems of this kind occur, for the determination of which two or more points can additionally be prescribed through which the sought curve must pass, nevertheless this will finally be perceived from the solution of each problem itself. For if one arrives at an equation of this kind for the sought curve, in which new constant quantities have entered through integration <note>The mathematical process of finding the integral; here referring to the constants of integration that arise when solving differential equations.</note> which were not present in the question itself, then the solution must be deemed ambiguous and vague; because it encompasses within itself innumerable curved lines which can arise from the determination of those constant and arbitrary quantities. In these cases, therefore, it must be concluded that the problem, by its nature, is not entirely determined: but for its full determination, besides the quantity of the abscissa, as many new conditions must be added as are necessary to reduce those arbitrary constants to determined values. For conditions of this kind, the points through which the sought curves <note>original: "quæsitæ"</note> pass are most conveniently assumed.

->APPLIED TO FINDING CURVES.<-

the sought <note>original: "Quæsitæ"</note> curve must pass through; indeed, as many points as there are arbitrary quantities <note>Variables that can take any value until fixed by specific conditions, similar to the constant '+ C' in modern integration.</note> in the discovered equation will make that equation determined. In place of points, however, to perfectly determine the sought curve, one may also employ just as many tangents which touch the sought curve; and, if the contact must occur at a given point on the tangent, this condition will be equivalent to two points. Furthermore, any other conditions whatsoever can be substituted in place of points, provided they are of such a nature that the arbitrary quantities contained in the discovered equation may be determined through them. Nor is it necessary to bring the solution to a conclusion before this judgment is undertaken; rather, certain criteria will be provided below, by the help of which one can immediately distinguish—from that variable quantity which must be a maximum or minimum—which new constants will enter into the equation for the curve that were not contained in the original question. Moreover, these arbitrary constants arise from the degree of the differentials <note>The 'order' of the derivatives in the equation; for example, a second-degree (second-order) differential equation requires two conditions to solve.</note> to which the equation for the sought curve rises; for as many degrees as the differential equation for the sought curve produces, that many arbitrary quantities must be considered to potentially exist within it. Hence, just as many conditions will be needed to determine the curve. This same thing also occurs in the solution of all problems when a differential equation of either the first or a higher degree is found; so that, for our present purpose, no peculiar difficulty should be thought to reside here.

### DEFINITION III.

10. The **relative method of maxima and minima** teaches how to determine the curve which enjoys the property of being a maximum or minimum, not from among absolutely all curves responding to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate or x-axis.</note>, but only from among those which share a certain prescribed common property.

### COROLLARY I.

11. To solve problems of this kind, therefore, first, from absolutely all curves responding to the same abscissa, those are

...must be set apart <note>original: "segregandæ"</note>, into which the same prescribed property fits; and then finally, from these set-apart curves, the one which is sought must be defined.

### COROLLARY II.

12. Although by such a condition the number of all curves related to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal 'x' coordinate on a graph.</note> is greatly restricted, it will nonetheless still remain infinite. Indeed, even if not just one, but several properties are prescribed which all the curves—from which the sought one is to be determined—must possess, the number of curves will still remain infinite.

### COROLLARY III.

13. Therefore, the more properties are proposed that must be common to those curves from which the sought one is to be defined, the more the number of curves among which the choice of the sought one must be made will be restricted, even if it remains infinite.

### SCHOLION I.

14. From this class, in which we establish the **relative** Method of Maxima and Minima, at the beginning of this century, that famous *Isoperimetric Problem* <note>original: "Problema Isoperimetricum"</note> was first brought forward by *Jakob* BERNOULLI. In this problem, a curve endowed with a property of the maximum or minimum was sought, not among all curves related to the same abscissa, but only among those which were of the same length; for this reason, those curves from which the sought one had to be extracted were called *isoperimetric* <note>original: "isoperimetræ"; from the Greek for "having the same perimeter" or boundary length.</note>. Thus, if among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa and equal in length, one seeks the one which encloses the greatest area with the abscissa and the ordinate <note>original: "applicata"; the vertical 'y' coordinate on a graph.</note>, the circular line is found to satisfy the requirement. This was, in fact, already known and demonstrated by geometers long before this method was invented. But in this case again, from the very nature of the problems, new conditions are added, just as in those which pertain to the **absolute** Method of Maxima and Minima;

<summary>This page introduces the concept of 'relative' maxima and minima, where the optimal curve must be chosen from a group that shares a specific property, such as equal length. It highlights Jakob Bernoulli’s Isoperimetric Problem as a foundational example of this method.</summary>
<keywords>Jakob Bernoulli, Isoperimetric Problem, Relative Maxima and Minima, abscissa, ordinate, geometry, calculus of variations, curve determination</keywords>

...which are to be evaluated from the arbitrary constants that the solution introduces. Thus, in the solution of the Problem where a curve is sought which, among all curves of the same length <note>original: "ejusdem longitudinis"</note>, encloses the greatest area with the abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate (x) on a graph, representing the distance along the base line</term>, two new constants enter; because of this, to make the Problem **determinate** <note>In mathematics, a problem is "determinate" when it has a specific, unique solution rather than an infinite number of possibilities.</note>, it must be proposed in such a way that among all curves of the same length—which not only correspond to the same abscissa, but also pass through two given points—the one that yields the maximum area for the given abscissa is sought. And in a similar way, it can happen that four points, and sometimes even more, must be assumed at will so that the Problem becomes determinate; the judgment of this matter must be sought from the very nature of the Problems. Just as, however, in the **isoperimetric problem** <term>isoperimetric: from the Greek for "having the same perimeter"; a problem where you compare shapes that all have the same boundary length</term>, all curves from which the solution must be determined are assumed to be of the same length; so, in place of this property, any other property can be proposed which must be common to all of them. Thus, curves endowed with a property of maximum or minimum have been sought among only those curves related to the same abscissa which, when all are rotated around that abscissa, generate equal surface areas; and in a similar way, any other properties can be proposed. Furthermore, not just one, but several such properties can be prescribed, which must be common to all the curves among which the one containing some maximum or minimum is to be defined. For example, if a curve endowed with some property of maximum or minimum were sought among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa which were all equal to each other in length as well as enclosing equal areas.

## S C H O L I O N  I I.

15. Because of this distinction between the **absolute** and **relative** Method of maxima and minima, our treatment will be divided into two parts. First, we shall present the method for determining the curve endowed with a maximum or minimum property among all possible curves corresponding to the same abscissa. Then, we shall proceed to those types of Problems in which the curve of maximum or minimum pro- <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "property" (original: "proprietate").</note>

...property <note>The sentence begins mid-thought from the previous page: "...any other property [endowed with a maximum or minimum] is sought..."</note> is sought among all curves that have one or more proposed properties in common; and from the number of these properties, a further subdivision of this treatise will arise. In the meantime, however, there will be no need to go further into this subdivision; since a method will soon be found for easily resolving problems, no matter how many properties have been proposed. For the solutions of problems that at first glance appear most intricate will, beyond expectation, become quite easy to handle and can be completed with a light calculation.

## HYPOTHESIS I.

16. *In this treatise, we shall perpetually designate the **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate (x) on a graph</term>, to which we relate all curves, by the letter* x, *and the **ordinate** <term>ordinate: the vertical coordinate (y) on a graph; the original Latin term is "applicata"</term> *by the letter* y. *Then indeed, assuming equal elements of the abscissa <note>This means treating the change in x (dx) as a constant value.</note>, it will always be:* dy = pdx; dp = qdx; dq = rdx; dr = sdx; *etc.*

### COROLL. I.

17. By these substitutions, therefore, all **differentials** <term>differentials: infinitely small changes in a variable, used here to build up higher-order derivatives like acceleration or curvature</term> of y of whatever degree will be removed from the expressions, and no other differentials will be left besides the differential dx. Although in this way all differentials, except dx, are removed only in appearance and not in reality; nevertheless, these substitutions will provide us with immense assistance in the present undertaking.

### COROLL. II.

18. Furthermore, by substitutions of this kind, the assumption of a constant differential is entirely removed from the calculation: for whatever other differential is assumed to be constant, the same formula must always emerge after these substitutions. In the meantime, however, because of the method to be employed below, it will be necessary to assume the differential dx as a constant.

### COROLLARY III.

19. However, to make it more clearly evident how the **differentials** <term>differentials: the infinitesimal changes in a value, which in modern calculus are represented as derivatives like dy/dx</term> of each degree of $y$ vanish <note>original: "evanescant"; in this context, it means they are eliminated or replaced by simpler variables through substitution</note> through these substitutions, it will be helpful to add the following table.

| | | |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $dy$ | $= p dx$ | |
| $ddy$ | $= dp dx$ | $= q dx^2$ |
| $d^3 y$ | $= dq dx^2$ | $= r dx^3$ |
| $d^4 y$ | $= dr dx^3$ | $= s dx^4$ |
| $d^5 y$ | $= ds dx^4$ | $= t dx^5$ |
| &c. | &c. | &c. |

### COROLLARY IV.

20. But if the **arc of the curve** <note>original: "arcus curvae"; this refers to the actual length along the curved path rather than a straight line</note> corresponding to the abscissa $x$ should also occur, along with its differentials of any degree; all these can be expressed through these letters in such a way that no other differentials besides $dx$ are present. For if we set the arc $= w$, it will be:

-> $w = \int \sqrt{(dx^2 + dy^2)} = \int dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$ <-
-> $dw = dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$ <-
-> $ddw = \frac{p q dx^2}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$ <-
-> $d^3 w = \frac{p r dx^3}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}} + \frac{q q dx^3}{(1 + pp)^{3:2}}$ <-
-> &c. <-

### COROLLARY V.

21. In a similar way, from these [substitutions], the **radius of curvature** <term>radius of curvature: the radius of a circle that perfectly fits the curve's bend at a specific point; Euler uses the Latin "radius osculi" (kissing radius)</term> or the radius of the curve's bending at any location can be expressed through quantities that appear, at least in form, to be finite. For since, assuming the element $dx$ is constant, the length of the radius of curvature $= \frac{— d w^3}{dx ddy}$ <note>Euler uses a negative sign here to indicate the direction of the radius relative to the curve's concavity</note>; it will become $= \frac{— (1 + pp)^{3:2}}{q}$.

### COROLLARY VI.

22. Furthermore, from these same substitutions, it will be as follows:

->**Subtangent** <term>subtangent: the segment on the x-axis between the x-coordinate of a point and the point where the tangent line intersects the x-axis</term> $= \frac{y dx}{dy} = \frac{y}{p}$<-
->**Subnormal** <term>subnormal: the segment on the x-axis between the x-coordinate of a point and the point where the normal line (perpendicular to the tangent) intersects the x-axis</term> $= \frac{y dy}{dx} = py$<-
->**Tangent** <term>tangent: here referring to the length of the segment of the tangent line from the point on the curve to the x-axis</term> $= \frac{y dw}{dy} = \frac{y \sqrt{(1 + pp)}}{p}$<-
->**Normal** <term>normal: the length of the segment of the line perpendicular to the curve from the point on the curve to the x-axis</term> $= \frac{y dw}{dx} = y \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$<-

And, in a similar way, all finite quantities pertaining to the curve—unless they involve **integrals** <note>original: "integralia"; Euler distinguishes between properties that can be calculated at a single point (finite) and those requiring the sum of parts along the curve (integrals)</note>—can be expressed through finite quantities of this kind in such a way that no differentials seem to be present any longer.

### DEFINITION IV.

23. The ***Formula of the Maximum or Minimum***, for any problem, shall be for us that quantity which must obtain the maximum or minimum value in the sought-after curve.

### COROLLARY I.

24. Since in all problems to which this method is adapted, a curve is sought which—either among all possible curves, or only among countless curves determined in a specific way—enjoys the property of being a maximum or minimum; this very property, which must be the maximum or minimum in the sought-after curve, will be a quantity, and it will be expressed by the ***Formula***, which we here call the ***Formula of the maximum or minimum***.

## COROLLARY II.

25. ## COROLLARY III.

26. Therefore, the Formula of the maximum or minimum will be a variable quantity depending on the length of whatever abscissa it corresponds to. And in any Problem, that curve will be sought for which, at the definite abscissa, that Formula of the maximum or minimum obtains the maximum or minimum value.

## COROLLARY IV.

27. Nor indeed can the Formula of the maximum or minimum depend on the abscissa alone: for if this were the case, it would obtain the same value for all curves corresponding to the same abscissa, and therefore all would satisfy the condition equally.

## COROLLARY V.

28. For this reason, the Formula of the maximum or minimum—besides the abscissa common to all curves coming under consideration—must depend specifically on each particular curve; so that there is only one curve for which it can take on a maximum or minimum value.

In this very broad question, we have, first, an **abscissa** of a determined length $AZ$; next, a curve must be sought, either from among absolutely all curves related to this same abscissa, or only from among the countless curves that share one or more properties. This depends on whether the question is adapted to the **absolute** or **relative** method of maximums and minimums <note>Euler is distinguishing between "absolute" problems (finding a curve with no constraints) and "relative" problems (finding a curve from a set that shares a specific property, like having the same total length).</note>. Now, it appears immediately that this formula $W$ must be constructed in such a way that it can be applied to all curves that can be imagined. First, it must depend on the quantity of the definite **abscissa** $AZ$, so that the value of $W$ changes as the value of $AZ$ changes. Secondly, it must also depend in a specific way on the nature of whatever curve is being considered; for if it were not so, it would result in the same value for all curves, and there would be no problem to solve. Therefore, the quantity $W$ must include within itself not only the **abscissa**, but also quantities pertaining to the curve itself. Since every curve is determined by the relationship between the **abscissa** and the **ordinate** <term>ordinate: the vertical distance or height of a point on the curve, usually denoted as y. Latin: applicata</term>, the quantity $W$ must be composed of the **abscissa** and the **ordinate**, and the quantities that depend on them. That is, if the indefinite **abscissa** is called $x$ and the corresponding indefinite **ordinate** is called $y$, the quantity $W$ must be a **function** of the two variables $x$ and $y$. Because of this, if any specific curve is considered, and the relationship between $y$ and $x$ derived from its nature is substituted into the formula $W$, it will yield a definite value belonging to that specific curve and its definite **abscissa**. Since the formula $W$ takes on different values for different curves—even if the same **abscissa** is used for all of them—it is clear that among those countless curves

### COROLLARY VI.

30. ...can be reduced <note>original: *reduci possunt*</note>, yet it is helpful to join them with the theory of curved lines. For if we wished to draw the mind away from curved lines and fix it on absolute quantities <term>absolute quantities: variables considered as pure numbers without a geometric or physical context</term> alone, the questions themselves would first become quite abstruse and inelegant, and their use and significance would be less apparent. Secondly, the method of solving questions of this kind, if proposed only in abstract quantities, would be too abstruse and troublesome; whereas the same is wonderfully aided and rendered easy to understand through the inspection of figures and the linear representation of quantities. For this reason, although questions of this sort can be applied to both abstract and concrete quantities, we shall most conveniently translate and solve them in terms of curved lines. That is, whenever an equation between *x* and *y* is sought such that a certain proposed formula composed of *x* and *y* (if the value of *y* is substituted from that sought equation and a determined value is assigned to *x*) becomes a maximum or minimum: then we will always transfer the question to finding a curved line whose **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate, or distance along the axis</term> is *x*, and whose **ordinate** <term>ordinate: the vertical coordinate; Euler uses the Latin term *applicata*</term> is *y*, for which that formula *W* becomes a maximum or minimum, if the abscissa *x* is taken to be of a given magnitude.

These things having been noted, the nature of questions of this kind is seen clearly enough—unless perhaps the ambiguous phrase "of maximum and minimum at the same time" still creates doubt for anyone. Truly, there is no ambiguity here either; for although the method itself shows maximums and minimums equally, yet in any case it will be easy to discern whether the solution provides a maximum or a minimum. Often, however, it can happen that in a given question both a maximum and a minimum hold a place, and in these cases the solution will be twofold, one showing the maximum, the other the minimum. Mostly, however, one or the other—namely, either the maximum or the minimum—is usually impossible; this happens if the formula for the maximum or minimum can grow or decrease infinitely; for in these cases, either a maximum or a minimum will not be given. It can also happen in practice <note>original: *Usu venire*</note> that the proposed formula *W* can both grow and decrease infinitely, and in these cases no solution at all takes place...

### PROPOSITION I. THEOREM.

34. In order that a curve *amz* may be determined by a formula *W* of a maximum or minimum, which satisfies the condition above all other possible curves, the formula *W* must be an **indefinite integral quantity** <term>indefinite integral quantity: a value representing the total accumulation of a function over an interval, rather than a single point</term>, which cannot be integrated unless a relationship between *x* and *y* is assumed.

### DEMONSTRATION.

For let us suppose that the formula *W* does not involve indefinite integrals; it would then be a function of the quantities *x* and *y*, and the values depending on them, *p, q, r, s,* etc. <note>Euler uses these letters to represent the derivatives of the curve: *p* is the first derivative or slope, *q* the second, and so on.</note>, whether algebraic or of such a **transcendental** <term>transcendental: a value, like a logarithm or circular arc, that cannot be produced by simple arithmetic or algebra alone</term> nature that it could be expressed without assuming a relationship between *x* and *y*. This occurs if logarithms of these quantities, circular arcs, or other such defined transcendental quantities—which are to be considered equivalent to algebraic ones—are involved. 

Now, if *W* is set as a function of *x* and *y* alone, it is manifest that the value of the formula *W* (which it obtains for a given curve *amz* related to a given **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate along the axis, usually *x*</term> *AZ*) depends only on the final **ordinate** <term>ordinate: the vertical distance from the axis to the curve; Euler uses the Latin term *applicata*</term> *Zz*; and for all curves having the same ordinate *Zz* at *Z*, the value of *W* would be the same. Thus, the character of the entire curve would not be determined by such a formula *W*, but only the position of its endpoint *z*. If, besides *x* and *y*, the quantity *p* is also present in *W*, then besides the length of the ordinate *Zz*, the position of the **tangent** to the curve at *z*—or the position of the final element at *z*—will be determined. 

If, moreover, *q* is included, then the position of two contiguous elements of the curve at *z* will be determined, and so forth. From this it follows that if *W* were a determinate function of *x, y, p, q, r,* etc., then only an infinitely small portion of the curve around the extremity *z* would be determined by it; and for all curves ending at the same extremity, the same value of *W* would be produced. Therefore, so that the entire curve *amz*, insofar as it corresponds to the whole abscissa *AZ*, may be defined by the formula *W*, the for-

37. Since the formula of the maximum or minimum *W* must be the integral of an indefinite differential formula of the first degree—that is, one whose integral becomes a finite quantity—this differential formula can always be reduced to this form *Zdx*, by means of the letters *p, q, r,* etc. <note>Euler uses these letters to represent the derivatives or slopes of the curve: *p* is the first derivative (dy/dx), *q* the second, and so on.</note>. For this reason, in the following sections, the maximum or minimum formula will perpetually be indicated by us as $\int Zdx$. Moreover, *Z* will be a function not only of the quantities *x* and *y*, but will also contain the letters *p, q, r,* etc. Thus, if the area *AazZ* is to be a maximum or minimum, the formula *W* will become $\int ydx$; and if the surface of a **solid of revolution** <term>solid of revolution: a 3D shape created by spinning a 2D curve around an axis</term> generated by the rotation of the curve *amz* around the axis *AZ* is to be a maximum or minimum, it will be $W = \int ydx\sqrt{(1+pp)}$;

->17<-

and so on; whatever formula is required to be a maximum or minimum in the sought curve, it will always be of this form $\int Z dx$, namely the integral of some finite quantity $Z$ multiplied by the differential <term>differential: an infinitely small change, denoted here as dx</term> $dx$. Moreover, $Z$ must be a quantity of such a kind that if an equation is established between $x$ and $y$, the integral $\int Z dx$ obtains a determined value. From this, $Z$ will be a function of the quantities $x$ and $y$, and of those depending on them, $p, q, r,$ etc. <note>Euler uses $p, q, r$ to represent the first, second, and third derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$.</note>, being either algebraic (that is, determined), or it will furthermore encompass within itself indeterminate integral formulas; this distinction must be carefully maintained. Thus, if the formula of the maximum or minimum $W$ were $\int y dx$, or $\int y dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$; the quantity $Z$ will be algebraic. But if it were $W = \int y dx \int y dx$, then $Z$ would be $y \int y dx$; that is, the quantity $Z$ itself will be indeterminate, for its value cannot be shown unless the relationship between $x$ and $y$ is given. Indeed, it can even happen that the value of $Z$ itself cannot be expressed by an expanded formula of this kind, but must only be extracted through a differential equation, such as if $dZ = y dx + Z^2 dx$; from which equation the value of $Z$ cannot even be displayed in terms of $x$ and $y$. Hence, three classes of formulas $\int Z dx$ arise here, which must become maxima or minima in the sought curves:

The first of these encompasses those formulas in which $Z$ is an algebraic or determined function of $x, y, p, q, r,$ etc. To the second class, we refer those formulas in which the quantity $Z$ itself further involves integral formulas. In the third class are contained those formulas in which the value of $Z$ is determined by a differential equation whose integration is not known.

### PROPOSITION II. THEOREM.

38. *If $amz$ were a curve in which the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, and $Z$ is an algebraic or determined function of $x, y, p, q, r,$ etc., then any portion $mn$ of that same curve will enjoy the same prerogative <note>original: "praerogativa", meaning it shares the same mathematical property</note>, so that for that portion, when referred to its own abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate (the x-axis segment)</term> $MN$, the value of $\int Z dx$ is likewise a maximum or minimum.*

## PROOF.

The value of the formula $\int Z dx$ for the abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate along the x-axis</term> AZ is the sum of all the values of that same formula which correspond to the individual portions of the abscissa AZ. If, therefore, the abscissa AZ is conceived as being divided into any number of parts, one of which is MN, and the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ is shown for each of these individual parts; the sum of all these values will yield the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ that belongs to the whole abscissa AZ, and which will be a maximum or a minimum. However, since $Z$ is assumed to be an algebraic function of $x, y, p, q,$ etc. <note>As noted previously, p and q represent the first and second derivatives (the slope and the rate of change of the slope) of the curve.</note>, the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ corresponding to the portion of the abscissa MN will depend only on the nature of the corresponding portion of the curve $mn$. It will remain the same regardless of how the remaining parts $am$ and $nz$ are varied; for the values of each of the individual letters $x, y, p, q,$ etc., are determined by the portion of the curve $mn$ alone. If, therefore, the values of the formula $\int Z dx$ that fit the portions of the abscissa AM, MN, and NZ are set as $P, Q,$ and $R,$ these quantities $P, Q,$ and $R$ will not depend on one another. Wherefore, since their sum $P + Q + R$ is a maximum or a minimum, it is necessary that each individual part also be endowed with the property of the maximum or minimum. For this reason, if in the curve $amz$ the formula $\int Z dx$ has a maximum or minimum value, and the quantity $Z$ is an algebraic function of $x, y, p, q,$ etc., then for any portion of that curve, the same formula $\int Z dx$ will enjoy the property of being a maximum or minimum. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum)</note>

### COROLLARY I.

39. Therefore, if a curve $amz$ has been found which, for a given abscissa AZ, has a maximum or minimum value of the formula $\int Z dx$, and $Z$ is an algebraic or determined function, then any portion of that same curve, with respect to its own corresponding abscissa, will also enjoy the same property of being a maximum or minimum.

### COROLLARY II.

40. In problems of this kind, therefore, where such a <term>maximum or minimum: the greatest or least value of a quantity</term> is sought, it is not necessary to define the specific length of the <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate along the x-axis</term> to which the maximum or minimum corresponds; rather, if for any single abscissa the formula $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, then for any other abscissa it will possess that same property.

### COROLLARY III.

For then, at the same time, the whole curve and any portion of it will likewise be endowed with the same property of being a maximum or minimum.

### SCHOLION <note>original: "SCHOLION", an explanatory note or commentary common in mathematical and philosophical texts.</note>

42. This property—which is possessed by curves where formulas of the type $\int Z dx$ are a maximum or minimum (where $Z$ is an algebraic or <term>determined function: a function whose value at a point is fixed by the local variables x, y, and their derivatives</term> of $x, y, p, q,$ etc.)—is of the greatest importance; for upon it rests the entire method of solving problems of this kind. However, it seemed best to bring forward this Proposition primarily so that this property—which is unique only to these formulas $\int Z dx$ where $Z$ is either an algebraic or a determined function—should not be thought to be common to absolutely all formulas that can be proposed. For in the following Proposition, we will demonstrate that if <term>integral: the accumulation or sum of values over an interval</term> formulas are contained within $Z$, then that same property no longer holds; from which, at the same time, the nature of questions of this kind will be more clearly understood. Moreover, the proof of this present Proposition is derived from this foundation: that the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ (provided $Z$ is either an algebraic or determined function of $x, y, p, q, r,$ etc.) which fits any portion of the abscissa $MN$, depends only on the corresponding portion of the curve $mn$, and is not affected by the rest of the curve, whether the preceding part $am$ or the following part $nz$. ### ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA.

<meta>catchword: PRO-</meta>

...indeterminate integral formulas. For the values of the quantities *x, y, p, q, r,* etc. <note>Euler uses $p, q, r$ to denote the successive derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$: $p = \frac{dy}{dx}$, $q = \frac{dp}{dx}$, etc.</note> which are obtained for the arc of the curve *mn*, depend only on the position of the elements of this arc *mn*, and on some contiguous elements which do not constitute an arc of finite quantity; from which also a quantity composed in any way from these letters will be determined by the nature of the arc *mn* alone, unless there were present integral quantities, such as $\int y dx$, which would introduce the whole preceding area *AamM*, or $\int dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$, which would involve the whole preceding arc from *m*.

Hence, therefore, it is more clearly understood what we wish to denote by a <term>determined function: a function whose value at any specific point depends only on the coordinates and derivatives at that point</term> of these variables *x, y, p, q, r,* etc.: Namely, a determined function is so constituted that, for any given place, it depends only on the present values of the letters *x, y, p, q,* etc., and does not include their preceding values within itself.

An <term>indeterminate function: a function whose value depends on the entire path or "history" of the curve up to that point</term>, however, is such that its value in any given place cannot be determined solely from the values which these letters *x, y, p, q,* etc. obtain in that place, but additionally requires for its determination all the values which those letters obtained in all the preceding places. Thus it is evident that all <term>algebraic functions: functions involving only the standard operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and roots</term> are at the same time determined; furthermore, all <term>transcendental functions: functions such as logarithms or exponentials that "transcend" simple algebra</term> which do not depend on the relation between *x* and *y* are determined, such as $\log \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, $e^{\frac{p}{y}}$, and the arc-sine of $\frac{p}{q}$; the values of which in any place can be assigned from the values of the letters which they obtain in that place alone.

When, however, indeterminate integral formulas are present in any function, which depend on the mutual relation between *x* and *y* that holds everywhere, then their value in a given place cannot be known from the values which these letters have in that place, but it is necessary additionally to know all the values in every preceding place—that is, the general relation between the <term>coordinates: the x and y values defining a point's position</term> *x* and *y*. We call such functions "indeterminate"; since they are <note>original: "toto cœlo diversæ", literally "different by the whole sky", meaning they are poles apart or diametrically opposed</note> entirely different from those we have called determined.

<vocab>determined function, indeterminate function, integral formulas, quantities, coordinates, algebraic, transcendental, maxima and minima</vocab>

## PROPOSITION III. THEOREM.

43. *If there is a curve amz corresponding to the abscissa <note>The horizontal distance along the axis.</note> AZ, in which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, and if indeterminate integral formulas are contained within Z; then this same property of the maximum or minimum does not apply to every individual portion of the curve, but will be a property belonging only to the whole curve corresponding to the abscissa AZ.*

->DEMONSTRATION.<-

Let the whole curve *amz*, for which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, be conceived as divided into any two parts by the <term>ordinate: the vertical line from the x-axis to the curve (Euler calls this the 'applicate')</term> *Mm*. Let the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ corresponding to the portion *am* be *P*, and let the value of the same formula for the other portion *mz* be *Q*. Therefore, for the whole curve *amz*, the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ will be *P + Q*, which we assume to be a maximum or minimum. To remove all ambiguity and present the matter more clearly, let us assume *P + Q* is a maximum; for whatever is demonstrated regarding a maximum will be easily understood for a minimum. 

Now, if the value of *Q* did not depend on the value of *P*, then the sum *P + Q* could not be a maximum unless both values *P* and *Q* were simultaneously maximums on their own. But in our case, where the quantity *Z* contains indeterminate integral formulas, the value of *Q* will depend not only on the portion of the curve *mz* to which it refers, but also on the entire preceding curve *am*, and thus on the value of *P*. 

Now we assert that for *P + Q* to be a maximum, it is not required that the value of *P* itself be a maximum. For let us suppose the portion of the curve *am* is so arranged that for it, *P* is a maximum, and then imagine that this portion of the curve *am* is changed a tiny bit, so that the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ becomes smaller, say *P — p*. It could certainly happen that because of this change, the value of *Q* increases; let this increment be called *q*. Thus, after the portion *am* has been changed slightly so that $\int Z dx$ is no longer a maximum for it, the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ for the whole curve *amz* will be *P — p + Q + q*. Since it can therefore happen that *q > p* <note>Meaning the gain in the second part of the curve outweighs the loss in the first part.</note>, it is understood that the formu—

## SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary following a proof, common in historical mathematical texts.</note>

61. In this Proposition is contained the entire method for solving Problems in which a curve is sought that makes the value of a certain indeterminate formula, such as $\int Z dx$, a maximum or minimum. For one always conceives of an infinitely small portion of the curve, such as $m n o$, to be varied slightly into $m \nu o$, and then one seeks the difference between the values that the formula $\int Z dx$ takes—first for the true curve $a m n o z$, and then for the imagined curve $a m \nu o z$. This difference, when set equal to zero, gives the nature of the curve being sought. However, this change must be made at an indefinite location so that it pertains to the entire curve and is applicable to every individual point. Furthermore, this change can be set up in any way at all, provided it is infinitely small and extends to either two or more <term>elements of the curve</term> <note>Euler uses "elements" to refer to the tiny, infinitesimal straight-line segments that make up a smooth curve.</note>; for the same final equation must always result. Meanwhile, the convenience of the calculation requires that the change be established in as few elements as are sufficient to complete the solution. Thus, if the goal is to determine the curve—among all possible curves corresponding to the same <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, typically 'x'.</note>—in which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, then it will suffice to conceive of only two elements of the curve being changed. But if the curve must be defined not from among all curves, but only from those that share one or more common properties <note>This refers to "isoperimetric" problems, where, for example, one seeks the largest area among curves of a fixed length.</note>, then one may not take just any change $m \nu o$. Instead, the change must be established such that those shared properties are preserved for all the curves. In these cases, therefore, two elements will not suffice, but more must be taken so that all conditions can be satisfied.

## DEFINITION V.

62. The *Differential Value* corresponding to a given maximum or minimum formula is the difference between the values that this formula obtains, both in the desired curve itself and in the same curve changed by an infinitely small amount.

### COROLLARY I.

63. Therefore, in a curve for which a given formula—suppose $\int Z dx$—must be a maximum or minimum, the corresponding <term>differential value</term> <note>Euler uses the term "differential value" to describe the change in the total integral resulting from a tiny variation in the curve's path. For this reason, if the differential value is set equal to zero, an equation will be obtained by which the nature of the sought curve is expressed.

### COROLLARY II.

64. From the discovered differential value, therefore, which corresponds to the proposed formula for a maximum or minimum, an equation will immediately be obtained expressing the nature of that curve in which the proposed formula holds the maximum or minimum value.

### COROLLARY III.

65. The entire business of finding curves that enjoy the property of being a maximum or minimum is therefore reduced to this: that for each formula of a maximum or minimum, its appropriate differential value be investigated.

## SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is a scholarly commentary or explanatory note intended to clarify the preceding technical proofs.</note>

66. Since, therefore, the general idea has been presented—not only of the nature of the questions in which curves endowed with the property of a maximum or minimum are sought, but also of the method that ought to be used to resolve them—we shall proceed to the actual treatment itself. And first, indeed, we shall present the **absolute method**, by which curves are sought that—among all possible curves related to the same <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually 'x'.</note>—are endowed with some property of a maximum or minimum. Then we shall proceed to the **relative method** of maxima and minima. This refers to questions that do not look among *all* curves corresponding to a given abscissa, but only among those that share one or more specific common properties <note>This refers to "isoperimetric" problems, where, for example, one might seek the shape that encloses the most area among all curves of the *same length*.</note>; from these, one must determine which curve possesses the prerogative of the maximum or minimum.

<summary>Euler summarizes that finding an optimal curve requires setting its "differential change" to zero and introduces the distinction between "absolute" problems (finding an optimum among all curves) and "relative" problems (finding an optimum among curves sharing a common property).</summary>
<keywords>differential value, vanishing, absolute method, relative method, abscissa, optimization, calculus of variations, Euler</keywords>

### PROPOSITION I. PROBLEM.

1. <margin>Fig. 4.</margin> **I**f, in any curve $amz$, any single <term>ordinate</term> <note>original: *applicata*. In 18th-century geometry, the $y$-values are referred to as "applied lines" or ordinates.</note> $Nn$ is increased by an infinitely small particle $n \nu$; to find the increments or decrements which the individual determinate quantities pertaining to the curve will receive from this change.

### SOLUTION.

The determinate quantities pertaining to the proposed curve—besides the <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal $x$-coordinate.</note> $x$, which is not affected—are these: $y, p, q, r, s,$ etc., along with their derived values, which they take on in either subsequent or preceding locations. But if we now let $AM = x$ and $Mm = y$, then $Nn = y'$ <note>Euler uses a notation where $y$ is the current ordinate, $y'$ is the next, $y''$ the one after that, and so on, separated by a constant horizontal interval $dx$.</note>, and its value will be increased by the particle $n \nu$ through the movement of point $n$ to $\nu$; however, the remaining ordinates $y'', y''', y^{IV}$, etc., just like the preceding ones $y_I, y_{II}, y_{III}, y_{IV}$ etc., will not be affected. Since, therefore, only the ordinate $y'$ increases by the particle $n \nu$, it can be gathered from the preceding chapter ($\S\S$ 51 and following) how much of an increment all the remaining quantities take from the increment of this single ordinate $y'$. Namely, all quantities whose value depends on $y'$ will undergo a change, while the others, which do not depend on $y'$, will remain unchanged. Thus, since $p = \frac{y' - y}{dx}$, this quantity $p$ <note>Here $p$ represents the slope or first derivative.</note> will increase by the particle $\frac{n \nu}{dx}$; but since $p' = \frac{y'' - y'}{dx}$, this quantity $p'$ de- <note>The text cuts off here; the next page will explain that $p'$ decreases because $y'$ is subtracted in its formula.</note>

This is a key step in developing the calculus of variations, showing how a local change propagates through the geometric descriptions of a curve.</summary>

### COROLLARY I.

2. Therefore, since the increments <note>Small changes or additions to a value.</note> of these primary quantities pertaining to the curve are known, the increments of all quantities composed from them—which arise from the increased ordinate $y'$ <note>The vertical coordinate of a point on the curve.</note>—can be determined, provided the manner of their composition is considered.

### COROLLARY II.

3. Specifically, the shown increments of these quantities can be considered as their **differentials** <note>In calculus, a differential represents an infinitesimal change in a variable.</note>. And if any quantity composed of them is proposed, its corresponding increment arising from the movement <note>original: *translatione*</note> of point $n$ to $\nu$ will be found by differentiating that quantity; then, in place of the differentials of the individual quantities, one simply writes those increments that have been assigned to these quantities in the previous table.

### COROLLARY III.

4. If, therefore, one has this function $y' \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$, whose increment (arising from the movement of point $n$ to $\nu$) is to be determined, that function should first be differentiated. From this, there will come:
$dy' \sqrt{(1 + pp)} + \frac{y' p dp}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$
Here, in place of $dy'$ and $dp$, let the increments corresponding to the quantities $y'$ and $p$ be written, namely $+ n \nu$ and $+\frac{n \nu}{dx}$; and the increment of the proposed function will be:
$= + n \nu \sqrt{(1 + pp)} + \frac{y' p \cdot n \nu}{dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$

### COROLLARY IV.

5. Thus, through the process of differentiation, the increment of any function arising from the increment $n \nu$ of the ordinate $y'$ can be assigned quickly. This is a task that can be done only with great difficulty, and not at all generally, by simply inspecting a geometric figure.

### SCHOLION <note>original: *scholion*; a scholarly explanatory note or commentary.</note>

6. It must be carefully noted that this method of finding the increments <note>Small, infinitesimal changes in value.</note> of functions or quantities—given from $x$, $y$, $p$, $q$, etc., and their derivatives $y'$, $y''$, $p'$, $p''$, etc.—is applicable only to determined functions <note>A "determined function" is one that can be explicitly written out using standard algebraic or known transcendental operations.</note>; it can by no means be extended to indeterminate ones. For if the proposed function is indeterminate, or an indefinite integral formula that does not admit to being integrated either algebraically or transcendentally, then we achieve nothing through differentiation alone toward finding its increment. In the following sections, however, where we are going to contemplate formulas for the maximum or minimum of the kind $\int Z dx$, in which $Z$ is such an indeterminate function, we shall investigate the increments of functions of this sort. But if $Z$ should be a determined function, the solution of the proposed Problem can suffice to complete the solutions of the problems belonging to this category.

## PROPOSITION II. PROBLEM.

<margin>Fig. 4.</margin>

7. *If $Z$ is a determined function of $x$ and $y$ only, to find the curve $az$, in which the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum.*

### SOLUTION.

Let the abscissa <note>The distance measured along the horizontal axis, usually denoted as $x$.</note> $AZ$, to which the maximum or minimum of the formula $\int Z dx$ must correspond, be conceived as divided into innumerable equal elements, each to be denoted by $dx$. With the indefinite abscissa $AM$ set as $x$, and the ordinate <note>The vertical distance from the axis to the curve, denoted as $y$.</note> $Mm$ set as $y$, the value $Z dx$ will correspond to the element $MN$ from the formula $\int Z dx$. Furthermore, according to the accepted way of notation, the value $Z' dx$ will correspond to the following element $NO$, and the values $Z'' dx, Z''' dx,$ etc., will correspond to the subsequent elements $OP, PQ,$ etc. Conversely, the values $Z_{/} dx, Z_{//} dx, Z_{///} dx,$ etc., will correspond to the preceding elements $LM, KL, IK$. Therefore, if the curve $az$ is the very one being sought, the sum $Z dx + Z' dx + Z'' dx + \&c.$ along with

# ABSOLUTE METHOD FOR FINDING CURVES.
<note>original header: *AD CURVAS INVENIENDAS ABSOLUTA*</note>

E 2
<meta>catchword: Co-</meta>

$Z_{\prime} dx + Z_{\prime\prime} dx + Z_{\prime\prime\prime} dx + \dots$ <note>Euler uses subscripts and primes to denote the values of the function at successive points along the curve.</note> is a maximum or a minimum. If, therefore, a single ordinate $Nn = y'$ is increased by a small particle $n\nu$ <note>This "particle" represents an infinitesimal change in the $y$-value at a specific point, often called a "variation."</note>, that expression must retain the same value. Furthermore, the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$—or the sum of the terms $Z dx + Z' dx + Z'' dx + Z''' dx + \dots$ together with $Z_{\prime} dx + Z_{\prime\prime} dx + Z_{\prime\prime\prime} dx + \dots$—must vanish <note>In calculus, to "vanish" means to equal zero. For a peak or a valley (maximum or minimum), the rate of change must be zero.</note>. The differential values of each of these terms, which arise from shifting the point $n$ to $\nu$, must therefore be investigated; their sum will be the corresponding differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$, which, when set equal to 0, will provide the equation for the sought curve. Since, however, $Z$ is assumed to be a determined function of $x$ and $y$ themselves, its differential $dZ$ will have a form of this kind: $M dx + N dy$; such that $dZ = M dx + N dy$. <note>$M$ and $N$ represent the partial derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$.</note> The differentials of the derived values of $Z$ will therefore be as follows:

| | |
|:---|:---|
| $d Z' = M' dx + N' dy'$ | $d Z_{\prime} = M_{\prime} dx + N_{\prime} dy_{\prime}$ |
| $d Z'' = M'' dx + N'' dy''$ | $d Z_{\prime\prime} = M_{\prime\prime} dx + N_{\prime\prime} dy_{\prime\prime}$ |
| &c. | &c. |

Now, when the differential values of the terms $Z dx, Z' dx, Z'' dx,$ etc., as well as $Z_{\prime} dx, Z_{\prime\prime} dx,$ etc., are found, if these terms are differentiated, and if $n\nu$ is written in place of $dy'$ in the differentials, but 0 in place of all remaining differentials; it is manifest that only the term $Z' dx$ will have a differential value, because $dy'$ occurs in its differential alone. Therefore, with $n\nu$ written in place of $dy'$, the differential value of the term $Z' dx$ will be $N' dx \cdot n\nu$. This will simultaneously be the differential value of the entire formula $\int Z dx$, because the remaining terms besides $Z' dx$ suffer no variation. However, we can put $N$ in place of $N'$, because $N' = N + dN$, and $dN$ vanishes compared to $N$. <note>Because the points are infinitely close together, the value of the derivative $N$ at one point is treated as equal to the value at the next.</note> Therefore, for the curve sought, in which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum, this equation is obtained: $N dx \cdot n\nu = 0$, or $N = 0$; given that $dZ = M dx + N dy$. Which was to be found. <note>original: *Q. E. I.* - *Quod Erat Inveniendum*</note>

<summary>Euler demonstrates that if an integral formula depends only on the coordinates x and y, the curve that maximizes or minimizes that integral is found where the partial derivative of the function with respect to y is zero. This is a foundational step in the development of the calculus of variations.</summary>

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

### Corollary I.

8. If, therefore, a curve must be defined in which the integral $\int Z dx$ <note>This represents the total area or "sum" under the function $Z$ along the x-axis.</note> is a maximum or a minimum, and $Z$ is a determined function of $x$ and $y$ only; then it is necessary to differentiate the quantity $Z$. Since this will take the following form, $dZ = M dx + N dy$, the equation for the sought curve is formed from this, which will be $N = 0$. <note>In modern calculus, $N$ is the partial derivative of $Z$ with respect to $y$. If the total sum is at a peak or valley, changing $y$ slightly shouldn't change the sum, meaning the rate of change $N$ must be zero.</note>

### Corollary II.

9. Since, therefore, $N$ is a determined function of $x$ and $y$, no constant quantity will be present in the equation for the curve $N = 0$ that was not already in the formula of the maximum or minimum $\int Z dx$; and for this reason, the curve found will be unique and perfectly determined.

### Corollary III.

10. Therefore, in the questions contained under this Problem, the satisfying curve is determined solely from the formula of the maximum or minimum; nor will it be permitted, in addition, to prescribe any points through which the sought curve must pass. <note>Euler is pointing out that because the equation $N=0$ is algebraic (it doesn't involve derivatives like $dy/dx$), you cannot force the curve to go through specific start or end points; the formula itself dictates exactly where the curve must be.</note>

### Corollary IV.

11. But if $Z$ were a function of $x$ only, such that it does not involve $y$; then $\int Z dx$ will likewise be a determined function of $x$ only; and thus all curves corresponding to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate $x$.</note> will satisfy it equally. Indeed, the calculus demonstrates this same thing; for in this case, where $y$ is not present in $Z$, $N$ becomes 0; and therefore no equation comes forth for the sought curve.

### Corollary V.

12. It can also be understood immediately whether a curved line is given in which a formula of this kind $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum. For if from the differentiation of $Z$ a value for $N$ of such a kind is found...

### SCHOLION I.

14. We have therefore obtained an easy method for determining, among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa, that one in which the formula $\int Z dx$ constitutes a maximum or minimum value, provided that $Z$ is a determined function of $x$ and $y$ only. At the same time, however, it is also clear that the satisfying curve will always be algebraic <note>An algebraic curve can be described by a polynomial equation, unlike "transcendental" curves like circles or logarithms which are more complex.</note>, provided that $Z$ was an algebraic function of $x$ and $y$. Since, however, it may still be doubtful whether the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ in the found curve is going to be a maximum or a minimum, a judgment will easily be made regarding that in any particular case; in general, however, nothing at all can be decided. Meanwhile, this is certain: if a single equation results, then only a maximum or only a minimum can take place; that is, if the found curve is for a maximum, then a minimum is not given, but the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ can be diminished to infinity. In a similar way, if a single curve has been found, and in it the formula $\int Z dx$ is a minimum, then the value of $\int Z dx$ can be increased to infinity. But if the solution provides no satisfying curve at all, it will be an indication that the value of the formula...

### SCHOLION II

15. From this same solution, those curves endowed with the property of the maximum or minimum of another kind mentioned above can also be found—those which are reached not through vanishing differential values <note>original: "valores differentiales evanescentes," referring to points where the derivative or rate of change is zero</note>, but through infinitely large ones; this kind of maxima and minima differs greatly from the former. These curves will be found if the differential value $N$ <note>In Euler's notation, $N$ represents the partial derivative of the function $Z$ with respect to the vertical coordinate $y$.</note> is set equal not to zero, but to infinity. Whenever, therefore, this equation $N = \infty$ suggests some curved line, then in that line likewise the formula $\int Z dx$ will obtain a maximum or minimum value. This will happen, specifically, when a fraction is produced for $N$ whose denominator, set equal to zero, provides an equation for some curved line. In this way, several curves can be found that satisfy the same question; some of these will contain maxima, others minima. It is even possible for more than two curves satisfying the problem to be found, even though only two equations can arise, namely $N = 0$ and $N = \infty$. For if $N$ is a quantity composed of factors, then any factor set equal to either zero or infinity will give an equation for a satisfying curve; for it is well known that often many maxima and many minima can occur. All of these matters will be explained more clearly in the following examples contained in this problem.

In this case, then, let $Z = XY$; and therefore $dZ = Y dX + X dY = M dx + N dy$. Thus $M = \frac{Y dX}{dx}$ and $N = \frac{X dY}{dy}$;

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

...therefore, a straight line coinciding with the axis itself, for which $y = 0$. For this line, the value of the formula $\int(ax - yy)y dx$ will likewise become $= 0$; for the Parabola, however, the same value will be positive <note>original: "affirmativus"</note>, and therefore $> 0$. From this, it follows that in the Parabola, the value of the proposed formula is not a minimum, but a maximum. We can also indicate algebraically how great the value of the proposed formula will be for the Parabola: for since $yy = \frac{1}{3} ax$, the proposed formula will become $\int \frac{2}{3} ax dx \sqrt{\frac{1}{3} ax} = \frac{4}{15} ax^2 \sqrt{\frac{1}{3} ax}$. If, however, we set another equation, say $y = nx$, the proposed formula will become $\int dx (n a x x - n^3 x^3) = \frac{1}{3} n a x^3 - \frac{1}{4} n^3 x^4$, which is always less than the value of the formula which was found for the Parabola: a fact that anyone can easily experience by substituting definite values in place of $x$.

### E X A M P L E  I I I.

18. *To find the curve in which, among all curves whatever referred to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate or x-axis.</note>, the value of this formula $\int (15 a^2 x^2 y - 15 a^3 xy + 5 a^2 y^3 - 3 y^5) dx$ is a maximum or a minimum.*

Therefore, $Z = 15 a^2 x^2 y - 15 a^3 xy + 5 a^2 y^3 - 3 y^5$. If this is differentiated, with $x$ held constant, it will produce $N dy = 15 a^2 x^2 dy - 15 a^3 x dy + 15 a^2 y^2 dy - 15 y^4 dy$; and from this $N = 15 (a^2 x^2 - a^3 x + a^2 y^2 - y^4)$. This value, set $= 0$, will give the equation for the required curve: it will therefore be $aaxx - a^3x + a^2y^2 - y^4 = 0 = (ax - yy) (ax + yy - aa)$. Because of these two factors, two satisfying curves come forth, one of which will be expressed by this equation $yy = ax$, the other by this $yy = aa - ax$; both are for a Parabola. Now, so that it may appear which one is for the maximum or minimum, let us assume the abscissa to be very small, and the first equation $yy = ax$ substituted into the formula will give $\int - 10 a^3 x dx \sqrt{ax}$. The other formula $yy = aa - ax$, or $y = a$ <note>The author is simplifying for the sake of the test at the limit.</note>, being substituted will give $\int 2 a^5 dx$. But if any other value whatever is assigned to $y$ itself, say $y = 0$, then the proposed formula becomes $\int 0 dx = 0$. From this it is clear that one of the found curves, $yy = aa - ax$, is for the maximum, while the other, $yy = ax$, is for the minimum—specifically for a "negative maximum" <note>In 18th-century calculus, a "maximum negative" refers to a value that is very large in the negative direction, what we would now simply call a minimum.</note>.

### EXAMPLE IV.

19. *Among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa, define the one in which the value of the formula* $\int (3ax - 3x^2 - y^2) (ax - x^2 - \frac{4}{3}xy + y^2) dx$ *is a maximum or a minimum.*

From this formula, therefore, the following expanded value of $Z$ <note>Euler uses $Z$ to represent the function inside the integral.</note> will be produced:

-> + 3a²x² - 4ax²y + 2axyy + $\frac{4}{3}$xy³ - y⁴ <-
-> $Z =$ - 6ax³ + 4x³y - 2xxyy <-
-> + 3x⁴ <-

Which, when differentiated—with $x$ held constant—and divided by $dy$, will provide the following value for $N$ <note>In Euler’s method, $N$ represents the partial derivative of $Z$ with respect to $y$. Finding where $N=0$ is a necessary condition for a maximum or minimum.</note>:

-> - 4ax² + 4axy + 4xyy - 4y³ <-
-> $N =$ + 4x³ - 4xxy <-

This expression, set equal to zero, will give the equation for the required curve. It will therefore be:

-> y³ - xyy + xxy + axx = 0 <-
-> - axy - x³ <-

which has two factors, which provide these two equations:

-> I. $y - x = 0$, for a straight line. <-
-> II. $y^2 - ax + x^2 = 0$, for a circle. <-

# EXPLANATORY NOTE <note>original: "SCHOLION"</note>

20. Problems can also be solved through the common Method of maxima and minima <note>Euler refers to the standard calculus of his day, used to find the peak or valley of a single function.</note>. For when a curve is sought for which the value of $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum, and this for any given abscissa <note>The horizontal $x$-coordinate.</note>; it is obvious that if $Z$ is a specific function of $x$ and $y$, the formula $\int Z dx$ cannot be a maximum or minimum unless its element $Z dx$, and consequently $Z$ itself, is of such a nature. For this reason, the question is satisfied if the quantity $Z$ is differentiated while $x$ is held constant, and its differential is set to zero. For then $Z$ will constantly have a maximum or minimum value, and therefore so will $Z dx$ and the formula $\int Z dx$ itself. But if the function $Z$ is differentiated with $x$ held constant, $N dy$ will result; since we have generally established in our differentiation that $dZ = M dx + N dy$; the condition is satisfied by setting $N = 0$: which is the same solution we found through the method handed down. However, although it may seem from this that these questions can be resolved in the same way as in the common Method of maxima and minima, this only occurs if $Z$ is a function of $x$ and $y$ alone; for if $Z$ also contains quantities derived from differentials, such as $p, q, r,$ etc. <note>In Euler's notation, $p$ usually represents the first derivative (the slope $dy/dx$), $q$ the second derivative, and so on.</note>, then the common Method can no longer be of any use. For even if the function $Z$ were then differentiated with $x$ held constant, the differentials $dp, dq, dr,$ etc., would still enter into the resulting differential. Since their relationship to $dy$ is not established, an equation suitable for determining a maximum or minimum cannot be derived from them. In these cases, therefore, the utility and necessity of our Method <note>Referring to the Calculus of Variations.</note> will be most clearly seen.

# PROPOSITION III. PROBLEM.

<margin>Fig. 4.</margin>
21. If $Z$ is a specific function of $x, y,$ and $p$ <note>Where $p$ represents the first derivative or slope of the curve.</note>, such that $dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp$; find, among all the curves corresponding to the same abscissa, that curve in which the value of $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum.

->COMPLETE [METHOD] FOR FINDING CURVES.<-

# SOLUTION.

Let $a m z$ be the curve satisfying the requirement, and conceive of any ordinate <note>The vertical "height" of a point on a graph.</note> $N n = y$ being increased by the small particle $n \nu$; the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$—or of the quantity equivalent to it, namely $Z dx + Z' dx + Z'' dx + Z''' dx + \text{etc.}$ together with $Z_{,,} dx + Z_{,,,} dx + \text{etc.}$—must be $= 0$ <note>Euler treats the integral as a sum of many small rectangles. To find the minimum or maximum, he "jiggles" one point ($n$ to $\nu$) and calculates the change. If the curve is already at a maximum or minimum, this change must be zero.</note>. Therefore, the differential value of the entire quantity $\int Z dx$ resulting from the translation of point $n$ to $\nu$ will be obtained if the differential values of each of those terms that are affected by this translation are sought and added into one sum. However, from the translation of point $n$ to $\nu$, only those terms undergo a change in which the quantities $y$, $p$, and $p'$ are present <term>p</term><note>Euler uses $p$ to represent the slope of the curve, or $dy/dx$.</note>; and therefore only the terms $Z dx$ and $Z' dx$ change; for just as $Z$ is a function of $y$ and $p$ (besides $x$), so $Z'$ is a similar function of $y'$ and $p'$ <note>The primes ($'$) indicate the values at the next successive point on the curve.</note>. For this reason, these terms must be differentiated, and in their differentials, in place of $dy$, $dp$, and $dp'$, one must write the values indicated above: $+ n \nu$; $+ \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ and $- \frac{n \nu}{dx}$. Now, just as $dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp$, so will $dZ' = M' dx + N' dy' + P' dp'$. From this, therefore, the differential value of $Z$ itself will be $P \cdot \frac{n \nu}{dx}$, and that of $Z'$ will be $N \cdot n \nu - P' \cdot \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ <note>Euler is showing how a change in the height of one point affects the slope of the segment leading *to* it and the segment leading *away* from it.</note>; from which the differential value of both terms $Z dx + Z' dx$, and thus of the entire formula $\int Z dx$, will be $= n \nu \cdot (P + N' dx - P')$. But $P' - P = dP$, and in place of $N'$, $N$ can be written; hence the differential value will be $= n \nu \cdot (N dx - dP)$. Wherefore, since the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ set equal to zero provides the equation for the sought curve, this will be $0 = N dx - dP$, or $N - \frac{dP}{dx} = 0$, by which equation the nature of the curve sought is expressed. Which was to be found.

## COROLLARY VI.

27. In these cases, therefore, in which $Z = V(n + p)$ and *V* is a function of *x* and *y* alone, one does not arrive at a second-order differential equation <term>second-order differential equation</term><note>An equation involving the second derivative, which usually defines the "curvature" of the path. In fact, one does not even arrive at a first-order differential equation; but rather at an algebraic one <term>algebraic equation</term><note>An equation without derivatives. In the context of geometry, this means the relationship between x and y is fixed and cannot be adjusted to meet boundary conditions.</note>. For since $pdx = dy$, then $(n + p) Ndx = nNdx + Ndy$; which, when set equal to $Mdx + Ndy$, will give an equation divisible by $dx$, and thus an algebraic one, namely $nN = M$, provided that *V* was an algebraic function.

## COROLLARY VII.

28. Whenever this happens, the formula for the maximum or minimum, which is $\int Zdx$, will be of such a form as $\int (Vndx + Vdy)$, or, if *n* is set to 0, of the form $\int Vdy$. Formulas for maxima and minima of this kind likewise lead to a determined equation for the sought curve, such that it is not permitted to prescribe one or more points through which the curve must pass. <note>Usually, when finding the shortest path between two points, the points are fixed. Euler is noting that in these specific mathematical cases, the "best" path is determined solely by the formula, and you cannot force that path to go through a specific starting or ending point.</note>

## COROLLARY VIII.

29. Given that *V* is a function of *x* and *y*, that maximum or minimum formula $\int Vdy$ is handled in the same way as $\int Vdx$. For, having set $dV = Mdx + Ndy$, the formula $\int Vdx$ corresponds to the equation for the curve $N = 0$; likewise, the other formula $\int Vdy$ corresponds to the equation $M = 0$. From this, it is clear that the coordinates *x* and *y* can be interchanged with one another. <note>This demonstrates the symmetry of the coordinate system; whether we look at the change in height (y) relative to width (x) or vice versa, the logic of the "best" path remains consistent.</note>

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

### S C H O L I O N  I. <note>original: "Scholion I." A scholion is a scholarly note or commentary used to explain a preceding theorem or proof.</note>

30. It is therefore evident in the solution of problems of this kind—where one seeks a curve possessing the maximum or minimum value of the formula $\int Zdx$ (where $Z$ is a function of $x$, $y$, and $p$ <note>original: $p$; Euler uses $p$ to represent the slope of the curve, $dy/dx$.</note>)—that one arrives at a second-order differential equation <term>second-order differential equation</term><note>An equation involving the second derivative, or the "rate of change of the slope." These are generally more difficult to solve than first-order equations.</note>, unless the quantity $p$ appears as a single dimension <note>i.e., it is a first-degree term, not squared or cubed.</note> in $Z$. Often, however, this second-order differential equation allows for integration <term>integration</term><note>The mathematical process of finding the original function from its rate of change; here, it "lowers" the order of the equation from second to first.</note>, which must be examined in individual cases. In the meantime, it will be useful to note here that, generally, integration is successful if $x$ does not appear in the function $Z$ at all; that is, if in its differential $dZ = Mdx + Ndy + Pdp$, the value $M$ <note>The partial derivative with respect to $x$.</note> vanishes, so that it is simply $dZ = Ndy + Pdp$. 

For since, for the discovered curve, we have this equation $N - \frac{dP}{dx} = 0$, let it be multiplied by $dy$; and because $dy = pdx$, it will be transformed into $Ndy - pdP = 0$. This is equivalent to $Ndy + Pdp = Pdp + pdP = dZ$, the integral of which is $Z + C = Pp$. This equation is now only a first-order differential equation. Therefore, whenever one seeks from among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as $x$.</note> that curve in which the value of the formula $\int Zdx$ is a maximum or minimum, and $Z$ is a function of $y$ and $p$ only (such that $dZ = Ndy + Pdp$), then, for the satisfying curve, the first-order differential equation $Z + C = Pp$ can be presented immediately. 

Furthermore, if $Z$ were a function of $x$ and $p$ only, and $dZ = Mdx + Pdp$ (with the term $Ndy$ vanishing), then a first-order differential equation will also result for the curve. For, because $dP = 0$, then $P = C$, which will provide an equation of only the first differential order for the sought curve. 

But if, in addition, $M$ also vanishes—that is, if $Z$ is a function of $p$ alone and $dZ = Pdp$—then the discovered equation $P = C$ will be transformed into $Pdp = Cdp = dZ$, which, when integrated once more, gives $Z + D = Cp$. In this case, because both $Z$ and $P$ are functions of $p$ alone, both equations $P = C$ and $Z + D = Cp$ will yield a constant value for $p$. This results in an equation of the form $dy = ndx$, which indicates that for a problem of this kind, [straight lines] satisfy...

# ABSOLUTE METHOD FOR FINDING CURVES.
