...to produce straight lines, and indeed any lines drawn however one wishes. For in the equation $P = C$, since $C$ is an arbitrary constant, the value of $p$ itself <note>Recall that $p$ represents the slope, $dy/dx$.</note> will turn out to be not only constant, but also arbitrary; from which any straight line will result. Therefore, if a curve must be drawn through two given points in which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or a minimum, and $Z$ is a function of $p$ only, then the straight line drawn through those two given points will satisfy the condition.

->### SCHOLION II.<-

31. Since we have already seen above that in problems of this kind, the coordinates $x$ and $y$ are exchanged with each other, and, if it seems convenient, the ordinate <note>original: *applicata*; in modern geometry, the $y$-coordinate.</note> $y$ can be treated as the abscissa <note>the $x$-coordinate</note>, it will be helpful to confirm this same thing in this case as well. Let, therefore, the curve to be investigated be that in which $\int Z dy$ is a maximum or minimum, where $Z$ is a function of $x, y$, and $p$, and $dZ = Mdx + Ndy + Pdp$. However, this formula $\int Z dy$, when reduced to our form, becomes $\int Zp dx$ <note>Since $dy = p dx$, substituting $p dx$ for $dy$ changes the variable of integration to $x$.</note>: in which $d(Zp) = Mp dx + Np dy + (Z + Pp) dp$: from which the corresponding differential value of the proposed formula will be $(Np dx - dZ - P dp - p dP) \eta v = (- M dx - 2P dp - p dP) \eta v$: and the equation for the sought curve will be $0 = - M dx - 2P dp - p dP$; or $0 = - M dy - d(Pp^2)$. 

But if now, to show the similarity—because here we consider $y$ as the abscissa—we set $dx = \pi dy$ <note>Euler uses the Greek letter $\pi$ here as a variable representing the reciprocal of the slope, $dx/dy$, not as the mathematical constant 3.14159.</note>, then $p = 1/\pi$ and $dp = - d\pi/\pi^2 = - p^2 d\pi$; $dZ = M dx + N dy - P p^2 d\pi = M dx + N dy + \Pi d\pi$, by setting $\Pi = - P p^2$; so that the similarity of the terms is preserved. Therefore, the equation for the curve will be $0 = - M dy + d\Pi$; which same equation would have appeared if, in the formula $\int Z dy$, the ordinate $y$ were transformed into the abscissa and vice-versa, the abscissa into the ordinate. Therefore, whatever indeterminate formula composed of $x$ and $y$ and their differentials is proposed, which must be a maximum or minimum, it will be permitted to treat either of the coordinates $x$ and $y$ as the abscissa, and to adapt the maximum or minimum to it.

He also proves that if an integrand depends only on the slope, the shortest or longest path between two points is a straight line.</summary>

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA.

### EXAMPLE I.

32. *Among all curves referred to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal $x$-coordinate.</note>, to determine that one in which the integral $\int (Z dx + [Z] dy)$ is a maximum or a minimum; where $Z$ and $[Z]$ are any functions of $x$ and $y$, such that $d Z = M dx + N dy$ and $d [Z] = [M] dx + [N] dy$.*

In order for this formula $\int (Z dx + [Z] dy)$ to be reduced to the standard form, let $p dx$ be substituted for $dy$ <note>Here $p$ represents the slope, $dy/dx$.</note>; one will then have this formula $\int (Z + [Z] p) dx$ to be made a maximum or minimum. Therefore, let the value $Z + [Z] p$ be differentiated; its differential will be $= + M dx + N dy + [M] p dx + [N] p dy + [Z] dp$.

Now, by the rule discovered, the following equation for the sought curve will be produced: $0 = (N + [N] p) dx - d [Z] = (N + [N] p) dx - [M] dx - [N] dy$. Because $[N] p dx = [N] dy$ <note>Since $p dx = dy$.</note>, this equation, when divided by $dx$, will give this algebraic or finite <note>meaning an equation without derivatives or integrals</note> equation for the sought curve: $N - [M] = 0$, or $N = [M]$. From this, it is understood that if the proposed formula $\int (Z dx + [Z] dy)$ were "determined" <note>In modern terms, if the differential form is "exact."</note>—that is, if the differential $Z dx + [Z] dy$ is such that it admits integration—then no single line would satisfy the requirement, or rather all lines would satisfy it equally. For if $Z dx + [Z] dy$ admits integration <note>original: *integrationem admittit*; if the integral depends only on the endpoints and not the path.</note>, it will be $N = [M]$ by its very nature, as we have demonstrated elsewhere regarding "determined" differential formulas of two variables; therefore, in these cases, the identical equation $0 = 0$ is produced. From this it is clearly understood, as we have already noted before, that the formula for a maximum or minimum must be an "indeterminate" formula <note>an "inexact" differential, where the path taken between two points actually changes the result</note>; otherwise, all curved lines would satisfy the condition equally.

Therefore, the formula $\int dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$ <note>The formula for arc length, where $p$ represents the slope $dy/dx$.</note> being compared with the general formula $\int Z dx$, we have $Z = \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$, and its differential $dZ = \frac{p dp}{\sqrt{(1+pp)}}$; from which it follows that $M = 0, N = 0,$ and $P = \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1+pp)}}$ <note>These letters refer to Euler's specific notation for components of the differential equation.</note>. Wherefore, since in general the equation for the sought line is $N - \frac{dP}{dx} = 0$, we will have in this case $dP = 0$; and therefore $P = \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1+pp)}} = Constant$. From this equation arises $p = Constant = n$, or $dy = n dx$, which, when integrated again, gives $y = a + nx$. Not only is it clear, then, that the sought line is a straight line, but also, because of the two arbitrary constants $a$ and $n$, it is a straight line drawn in any way. Wherefore, if a line is ordered to be drawn shortest through two given points, it will be that straight line. Moreover, it is understood in a similar way that if a line must be found in which the integral $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, where $Z$ is a function of $p$ only, then only a straight line satisfies the condition; as we have already noted before.

### EXAMPLE IV.

## EXAMPLE V.

36. *Among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually $x$.</note>, to determine that one in which the integral* $\int \frac{y dy^3}{dx^2 + dy^2}$ *is a maximum or a minimum.*

This formula, reduced to the customary form by means of the substitution $dy = p dx$, changes into this: $\int \frac{y p^3 dx}{1 + p^2}$; and this is usually found if one seeks a solid of revolution <note>A 3D shape created by rotating a 2D curve around an axis.</note> created by the rotation of a curve around an axis, which experiences the least resistance when moved through a fluid in the direction of that axis: for in this case, the resistance is considered proportional to the formula $\int \frac{y dy^3}{dx^2 + dy^2}$ or $\int \frac{y p^3 dx}{1 + p^2}$ <note>This is known as Newton's solid of least resistance problem, one of the first major successes of the calculus of variations.</note>. Therefore, $Z = \frac{y p^3}{1 + p^2}$, and $dZ = \frac{p^3 dy}{1 + p^2} + \frac{y dp (3 p^2 + p^4)}{(1 + p^2)^2}$; so that it becomes $M = 0$, $N = \frac{p^3}{1 + p^2}$, and $P = \frac{p^2 y (3 + p^2)}{(1 + p^2)^2}$ <note>In Euler’s method, $M, N,$ and $P$ are the components of the differential of $Z$ relative to $dx, dy,$ and $dp$.</note>. Since $M = 0$, one integration generally succeeds, and the equation for the sought-after curve will be $Z + C = Pp$, or $\frac{y p^3}{1 + p^2} + a = \frac{p^3 y (3 + p^2)}{(1 + p^2)^2}$; which simplifies into this: $a (1 + p^2)^2 = 2 p^3 y$. However, the development of this equation cannot be carried out such that $p$ is eliminated; therefore, it is convenient to define both coordinates $y$ and $x$ through the same variable $p$. And first, indeed, $y = \frac{a (1 + p^2)^2}{2 p^3}$. Then, because $dy = p dx$,

### E X A M P L E VI.

37. *To find a curve in which this formula $\int xy dx \sqrt{1+p^2}$ <note>The OCR omitted the $x$ in the problem statement, but the subsequent derivation confirms the integrand is $xy\sqrt{1+p^2}$. This formula relates to the moment of a surface area.</note> results in a maximum or a minimum.*

Therefore, $Z = xy \sqrt{1+p^2}$, and $dZ = ydx \sqrt{1+p^2} + xdy \sqrt{1+p^2} + \frac{xyp dp}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}$. For this reason, we will have $M = y \sqrt{1+p^2}$, $N = x \sqrt{1+p^2}$, and $P = \frac{xyp}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}$ <note>In Euler's method, $M$, $N$, and $P$ are the partial derivatives of the integrand $Z$ with respect to $x$, $y$, and $p$ respectively.</note>; from which the equation for the curve will be formed as $N dx = dP$, which suggests:
$x dx \sqrt{1+p^2} = \frac{p^2 x dx + yp dx}{\sqrt{1+p^2}} + \frac{xy dp}{(1+p^2)^{3/2}}$, or
$x dx - y dy = \frac{xy dp}{1+p^2}$, because $dy = p dx$. This is a differential equation of the second degree <note>term: **differential equation of the second degree** — an equation involving the second derivative of a function, here represented by the change in slope $dp$.</note>, and although, by means of suitable substitutions, it can be reduced to a simple differential form (due to the variables $x$ and $y$ constituting the same number of dimensions everywhere), nevertheless, that differential equation is so structured that it can neither be integrated nor separated. It can, indeed, be reduced to an equation of this form: $\frac{du}{u^3} + \frac{dv}{v^3} = \frac{v dv (1+u^3)^3}{u^3}$. Since this is the case, the discovered equation $x dx - y dy = \frac{xy dp}{1+p^2}$ cannot be restored to a simpler or more convenient form; and from this, almost nothing can be judged concerning the nature of the discovered curve. In the meantime, however, that equation implicitly <note>original: "potentiâ"</note> involves two arbitrary constants, from which a satisfying curve can be drawn through any two given points.

## EXAMPLE VII.

38. To find a curve in which the integral $\int (x^2 + y^2)^n dx \sqrt{1 + p^2}$ <note>Euler uses $xx$ and $yy$ to denote $x^2$ and $y^2$. The term $\sqrt{1+p^2} dx$ represents an element of the arc length ($ds$).</note> is a maximum or a minimum.

Since in this case $Z = (x^2 + y^2)^n \sqrt{1 + p^2}$, then $dZ$ will be:
$2n (x^2 + y^2)^{n-1} (x dx + y dy) \sqrt{1 + p^2} + \frac{(x^2 + y^2)^n p dp}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$ ,
therefore $N = 2n (x^2 + y^2)^{n-1} y \sqrt{1 + p^2}$ and $P = \frac{(x^2 + y^2)^n p}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$ <note>In Euler’s method, $N$ is the partial derivative of the function $Z$ with respect to $y$, and $P$ is the partial derivative with respect to $p$ (the slope $dy/dx$).</note>;
from which, for the sought-after curve, this equation will be held:
$2n (x^2 + y^2)^{n-1} y dx \sqrt{1 + p^2} = d \left( \frac{(x^2 + y^2)^n p}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}} \right) =$
$\frac{2n(x^2 + y^2)^{n-1} p(x dx + y dy)}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}} + \frac{dp (x^2 + y^2)^n}{(1 + p^2)^{3/2}}$ , which, when divided by $(x^2 + y^2)^{n-1}$ and multiplied by $\sqrt{1 + p^2}$, becomes:
$2ny dx = 2nx dy + \frac{(x^2 + y^2) dp}{1 + p^2}$ or $\frac{2n (y dx - x dy)}{x^2 + y^2} = \frac{dp}{1 + p^2}$.
Both sides of this equation are integrable through the quadrature of the circle <note>term: **quadrature of the circle** — a classical term here referring to integration that results in inverse trigonometric functions, specifically the arctangent.</note>, and let the integral be $2n \arctan \frac{x}{y} = \arctan p + \arctan k = \arctan \frac{p + k}{1 - pk}$ <note>original: "A tang." stands for *Arcus tangentis* or arctangent. $k$ is a constant of integration.</note>: from which it follows that $\frac{x}{y} = \tan \left( \frac{1}{2n} \arctan \frac{k + p}{1 - kp} \right) = T$; and $T$ will be an algebraic function of $p$ itself, provided that $2n$ is a rational number. Since, therefore, $x = Ty$, or $y = \frac{x}{T}$, then $dy = p dx = \frac{dx}{T} - \frac{x dT}{T^2}$, or $x dT = T dx - p T^2 dx$; and therefore $\frac{dx}{x} = \frac{dT}{T - p T^2} + \frac{T dp}{1 - p T} - \frac{T dp}{1 - p T}$; from which results $\ln x = \ln \frac{T}{1 - p T} - \int \frac{T dp}{1 - p T}$ <note>original: "l x" refers to the natural logarithm of $x$.</note>, which certainly suffices abundantly for constructing the curve. But so that the nature of these curves, which emerge for specific values of the exponent $n$, may be better understood, we shall contemplate several cases.

*I.* Let $n = 1/2$, and $2n = 1$; then $\arctan \frac{x}{y} = \arctan \frac{k + p}{1 - kp}$;

$N - \frac{d P}{d x} = 0$. However, since we noted in the preceding Problem that if $Z$ were only a function of the variables $x$ and $y$ themselves, then the solution could be completed by the common Method <note>Euler refers here to standard differential calculus, as opposed to the "Calculus of Variations" he is currently inventing.</note>: for in order for the integral $\int Z dx$ to be a maximum or minimum, it is necessary that $Z dx$ (and accordingly $Z$ itself) also be so, with respect to the variable $x$; and for this reason the differential of $dZ$, taking $x$ as a constant and setting it equal to zero, will give the equation for the sought-after curve. A similar Method would succeed in the present Problem, if only in the differential of $Z$ itself—which arises when $x$ is set as a constant and is $Ndy + Pdp$—the relationship between the <term>differentials</term> <note>Differentials like $dy$ or $dp$ represent infinitely small changes in those variables.</note> $dy$ and $dp$ were evident, so that a division by $dy$ could be performed and a finite value to be set equal to zero could be extracted. Since, however, it is not yet possible to define this relationship between $dy$ and $dp$ *a priori* <note>original: "a priori," meaning from theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>—without which the common method of maxima and minima cannot be applied—we will be able to assign it *a posteriori* <note>original: "a posteriori," meaning derived from the results of the calculation.</note>: For because this equation for the sought curve was found to be $N - \frac{d P}{d x} = 0$; it is understood that this could have arisen from $Ndy + Pdp$, or $N + \frac{Pdp}{dy}$, if it had been established that $- \frac{d P}{d x} = \frac{Pdp}{dy}$, or $0 = dP + \frac{Pdp}{p}$, since $dy = p dx$. Therefore, that relationship between the differentials $dy$ and $dp$ will be so arranged that it is contained in the equation $p dP + Pdp = 0$; which property comes down to this: that $Pp$ must be considered as a constant. Hence, for resolving Problems in which a curve is sought having the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ as a maximum or minimum, where $dZ = Mdx + Ndy + Pdp$ exists; the value of $Z$ itself must be differentiated, and in the differential $Mdx + Ndy + Pdp$, zero must be put in place of $Mdx$, $Ndy$ should be left unchanged, and then in place of $Pdp$, $- pdP$ must be written; and that which emerges should be set equal to zero. For in this way $Ndy - pdP = 0$ will be obtained; which equation, since $dy = pdx$, changes into $N - \frac{d P}{d x} = 0$, which is the very one we found. Therefore, a Method free from geometric and linear resolution is desired, by which it may be clear that in such an investigation of a maximum or minimum, $- pdP$ ought to be written in place of $Pdp$.

## PROPOSITION IV. PROBLEM.

40. *If Z is a function of x, y, p, and q <note>In Euler’s notation, $p = \frac{dy}{dx}$ and $q = \frac{dp}{dx} = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$. These represent the slope and the rate of change of the slope (curvature) respectively.</note>, such that dZ = Mdx + Ndy + Pdp + Qdq; find, among all curves corresponding to the same <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as x.</note>, the one in which the integral $\int Zdx$ is a maximum or minimum.*

## S O L U T I O N.

The value of the integral formula $\int Zdx$ is expanded into these two series $Zdx + Z'dx + Z''dx + Z'''dx + \&c.$ and $Z,dx + Z,,dx + Z,,,dx + \&c.$ <note>Euler uses primes ($Z'$) and subscripts ($Z,$) to denote the values of the function at successive or preceding points along the curve, separated by an infinitesimal distance $dx$.</note> the sum of which will be a maximum or minimum if the differential values of each term—which arise by increasing the <term>ordinate</term> <note>The vertical coordinate, $y$.</note> $y'$ by a small particle $nv$—are collected and set equal to zero. However, by such an increase to the ordinate $y'$, only the letters $y' ; p, p', q, q, q'$ undergo change; and therefore only those terms in which these letters are present, that is, the terms $Z,dx$, $Zdx$, and $Z'dx$, are affected. To find the increases of these terms, arising from the movement of the point $n$ to $v$, let them be differentiated, and it will be:

-> $d. Z'dx = dx ( M'dx + N'dy' + P'dp' + Q'dq' )$ <-
-> $d. Zdx = dx ( Mdx + Ndy + Pdp + Qdq )$ <-
-> $d. Z,dx = dx ( M,dx + N,dy, + P,dp, + Q,dq, )$ <-

Now indeed, because the abscissa $x$ is not affected by that movement, $dx = 0$ must be set everywhere: then, the values of the remaining differentials arising from the movement of point $n$ to $v$—according to the first Proposition of this Chapter—will be as follows:

| $dy' = + nv$ | $dp' = - \frac{nv}{dx}$ | $dq' = + \frac{nv}{dx^2}$ |
|--------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|
| $dy = 0$     | $dp = + \frac{nv}{dx}$  | $dq = - \frac{2nv}{dx^2}$ |
| $dy, = 0$    | $dp, = 0$               | $dq, = + \frac{nv}{dx^2}$ |

The reduction of <term>integral</term><note>In calculus, an integral calculates the area under a curve or the total accumulation of a quantity.</note> formulas of the form $\int Z q dx$, or $\int Z \frac{ddy}{dx}$, can be reduced to a form such as $Y + \int V dx$, in which $Y$ and $V$ are functions of $x, y,$ and $p$ alone, no longer involving $q$ <note>original: "non amplius involventes q". In Euler's notation, $x$ and $y$ are coordinates, $p$ is the first derivative (slope), and $q$ is the second derivative (curvature).</note>. Since, therefore, $Y$ is an <term>absolute quantity</term><note>A term that stands outside the integral and does not change during the optimization process.</note>, and for that reason does not fall into the investigation of the maximum or minimum, the formula $\int Z q dx$ will become a maximum or minimum if $\int V dx$ is rendered as such; thus, formulas of this kind $\int Z q dx$ can be reduced to the state of the preceding Problem; whence it is not surprising that for the satisfying curves, only a <term>differential equation of the second order</term> is found.

But so that the mentioned reduction of the formula $\int Z q dx$ or $\int Z dp$ to $Y + \int V dx$ may be better understood; let us suppose, since $Y$ is a function of $x, y,$ and $p$, that $dY = \rho dx + \sigma dy + \tau dp = (\rho + \sigma p) dx + \tau dp$; and from the equality $\int Z dp = Y + \int V dx$, it will be $Z dp = (\rho + \sigma p) dx + \tau dp + V dx$; from which it is concluded that $\tau = Z$ and $V = -\rho - \sigma p$. 

On which account, this very reduction shall be established in the following way: let the formula $\int Z dp$ be <term>integrated</term> while treating $x$ and $y$ as constants, and the integral will be a function of $x, y,$ and $p$, which shall be called $Y$. Then let this function $Y$ be <term>differentiated</term><note>The process of finding the rate at which a function changes.</note>, setting $p$ as a constant, and the differential taken negatively will give $V dx$, and $V$ will be a function of $x, y,$ and $p$ not containing $q$. Whenever, therefore, a formula of this kind $\int Z q dx$ must be made a maximum or minimum, and $Z$ is a function of $x, y,$ and $p$; then the question, even if it seems to pertain to the present Problem, will nonetheless be immediately reduced to the preceding Problem.

Setting the <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal x-coordinate.</note> $A M = x$, and the <term>ordinate</term><note>The vertical y-coordinate.</note> $M m = y$; the radius of curvature will be $m R = \frac{(1 + p^2)^{3/2}}{q}$; however, the area $A R m$ is $= \int \frac{1}{2} m R \cdot dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$; from which it is required that this formula be a minimum: $\int \frac{(1 + p^2)^2 dx}{q}$ <note>Euler uses $p$ for the slope ($dy/dx$) and $q$ for the change in slope ($d^2y/dx^2$).</note>. Therefore, $Z = \frac{(1 + p^2)^2}{q}$, and $dZ = \frac{4(1 + p^2) p dp}{q} - \frac{(1 + p^2)^2 dq}{q^2}$; from which it follows $M = 0$, $N = 0$, $P = \frac{4(1 + p^2) p}{q}$, and $Q = - \frac{(1 + p^2)^2}{q^2}$. Since now $M = 0$ and $Z = 0$ <note>original: "Cum nunc fit M = 0 & Z = 0". In Euler's method, these conditions allow for a simplified differential equation.</note>; the equation for the sought curve, by Corollary 6, will be $Z = D + Cp + Qq$, or $\frac{(1 + p^2)^2}{q} = D + Cp - \frac{(1 + p^2)^2}{q}$, which is $2(1 + p^2)^2 = Dq + Cpq$. Furthermore, since $dp = q dx$, or $q = \frac{dp}{dx}$, it will be $2dx = \frac{(D + Cp) dp}{(1 + p^2)^2}$, the integral of which is $x = \frac{a}{1 + p^2} + 2b \int \frac{dp}{(1 + p^2)^2} = \frac{a + bp}{1 + p^2} + b \int \frac{dp}{1 + p^2} + c$: by changing the constants at will, we will have $x = \frac{a + bp + cp^2}{1 + p^2} + b \text{ arctangent } p$. Then because $dy = p dx$, it will be $y = \int p dx = px - \int x dp$; and therefore $y = \frac{ap + bp^2 + cp^3}{1 + p^2} + bp \text{ arctangent } p - \int \frac{(a + bp + cp^2) dp}{1 + p^2} - b \int dp$

Moreover, $by - ax$ expresses a multiple of the <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal distance along an axis.</note> assumed upon some other fixed axis, to which the square of the corresponding arc is proportional. ### EXAMPLE IV.

53. *To find the curve in which the value of this formula $\int \frac{y dy dx^2}{d^2 y}$ is the minimum of all possible values.*

It is clear, first of all, that a maximum cannot exist <note>In variational calculus, some problems only have a lower bound (minimum) or an upper bound (maximum). Here, Euler explains why a maximum is impossible for this specific integral.</note>, because in a **straight line**, $d^2 y = 0$; therefore, the value of the proposed formula would be infinitely large. For this reason, we must see in what sort of curved line the value of the formula $\int \frac{y dy dx^2}{d^2 y}$ becomes a minimum. This formula, through our substitutions <note>Euler uses the standard substitutions $p = \frac{dy}{dx}$ and $q = \frac{dp}{dx} = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ to turn higher-order derivatives into a system of first-order variables.</note>, transforms into this: $\int \frac{y p dx}{q}$.
Thus, let $Z = \frac{y p}{q}$, and its differential $d Z = \frac{p dy}{q} + \frac{y dp}{q} - \frac{y p dq}{q q};$ 
therefore, $M = 0, N = \frac{p}{q}, P = \frac{y}{q},$ and $Q = - \frac{y p}{q q}.$ <note>In Euler's method, M, N, P, and Q represent the partial derivatives of the function Z with respect to x, y, p, and q respectively.</note>
Since, however, $M = 0$, the sought curve will be expressed by the following equation:
$Z - P p - Q q + \frac{p d Q}{dx} = C$
as was shown in **Corollary 5**. <note>Euler is referencing a previous rule he derived for when the function Z does not explicitly contain the variable x.</note>

$\frac{y p}{q} - \frac{p}{dx} d . \frac{y p}{q q} = C$, or $\frac{y dy}{p q} + \frac{a dx}{p} = \frac{p dy}{q q} + \frac{y dp}{q q} - \frac{2 y p dq}{q^3}$, 
since $dy = p dx$. But since $dp = q dx$,

### 55. To find the curve in which $\int \frac{x p dx}{y q}$ is a maximum or a minimum.

Because $Z = \frac{x p}{y q}$, it will be $d Z = \frac{p dx}{y q} - \frac{x p dy}{y^2 q} + \frac{x d p}{y q} - \frac{x p d q}{y q^2}$; and therefore $M = \frac{p}{y q}$; $N = - \frac{x p}{y^2 q}$; $P = \frac{x}{y q}$, and $Q = - \frac{x p}{y q^2}$ <note>These variables represent the partial derivatives of the expression inside the integral with respect to the coordinates and their derivatives.</note>. (\frac{p dx}{y q} - \frac{x p dy}{y^2 q^2} + \frac{x dp}{y q^2} - \frac{2 x p dq}{y q^3})$; or $0 = q^2 dx^2 (3 y q - 2 p^2) (y - x p) - 4 y q dx dq (xy q - x p^2 + y p) + 6 x y^2 p d q^2 - 2 x y^2 p q d dq$. ## PROPOSITION V. PROBLEM.

56. *To find the curve in which the value of the formula* $\int Z dx$ *is a maximum or a minimum, where Z is a function of such a kind that it involves differentials of any degree, so that* $d Z = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + T dt + \dots$ <note>original: "et caetera." Euler is using $M, N, P, Q, R, S, T$ to represent the partial derivatives of the expression $Z$ with respect to $x, y, y', y'', y''', y'''',$ and $y'''''$.</note>

### SOLUTION.

<margin>Fig. 4.</margin>
Since shifting the point *n* to *$\nu$* <note>In Euler's geometric method, he varies the curve by moving a single point $n$ by an infinitesimal distance to $\nu$ and calculating the change in the total integral.</note> affects the preceding elements more than the following ones—for it affects only a single following element, whereas its effect extends further back into the preceding elements depending on the presence of higher-order differentials—for this reason, it will be convenient to take some earlier ordinate <term>ordinate: the vertical $y$ distance of a point from the $x$-axis</term>, such as *Hh*, as the first. This ensures that the change resulting from adding the small piece *n$\nu$* to the ordinate *Nn* does not extend back beyond *Hh*; this will happen if the differentials in *Z* do not rise beyond the sixth order. It will be sufficient, however, to extend the value of *d Z* as far as the term *Tdt*, because from the solution itself, the method for adapting it to any number of further terms will be easily gathered. Furthermore, because all the preceding problems are contained within this one, it will simultaneously be clear that the solution always turns out the same, regardless of which ordinate is increased by some infinitely small piece, such as *n$\nu$*. Therefore, let *AH = x* and *Hh = y*; then to the individual points of the abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal $x$ distance of a point from the $y$-axis</term> H, I, K, L, M, N, O, etc., there will correspond the values of the letters *p, q, r, s, t*, etc., as follows:

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $dy = 0$ | $dy' = 0$ | $dy'' = 0$ | $dy''' = 0$ | $dy^{IV} = 0$ | $dy^V = + n \nu$ |
| $dp = 0$ | $dp' = 0$ | $dp'' = 0$ | $dp''' = 0$ | $dp^{IV} = + \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ | $dp^V = - \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ |
| $dq = 0$ | $dq' = 0$ | $dq'' = 0$ | $dq''' = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^2}$ | $dq^{IV} = - \frac{2n \nu}{dx^2}$ | $dq^V = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^2}$ |
| $dr = 0$ | $dr' = 0$ | $dr'' = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^3}$ | $dr''' = - \frac{3n \nu}{dx^3}$ | $dr^{IV} = + \frac{3n \nu}{dx^3}$ | $dr^V = - \frac{n \nu}{dx^3}$ |
| $ds = 0$ | $ds' = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^4}$ | $ds'' = - \frac{4n \nu}{dx^4}$ | $ds''' = + \frac{6n \nu}{dx^4}$ | $ds^{IV} = - \frac{4n \nu}{dx^4}$ | $ds^V = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^4}$ |
| $dt = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^5}$ | $dt' = - \frac{5n \nu}{dx^5}$ | $dt'' = + \frac{10n \nu}{dx^5}$ | $dt''' = - \frac{10n \nu}{dx^5}$ | $dt^{IV} = + \frac{5n \nu}{dx^5}$ | $dt^V = - \frac{n \nu}{dx^5}$ |

<note>This table is a masterpiece of early variational calculus. It shows how a variation $n\nu$ at a single point affects the fifth derivative ($t$) five steps back, the fourth derivative ($s$) four steps back, and so on. The coefficients (1, -5, 10, -10, 5, -1) are the binomial coefficients with alternating signs, reflecting the nature of finite differences.</note>

Furthermore, since the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ corresponds to the horizontal distance <term>abscissa: the coordinate along the horizontal axis, usually $x$</term> $AH$, and this is not changed by the shift of point $n$ to $\nu$, the values of the formula $\int Z dx$ that correspond to the subsequent horizontal segments <term>elements: infinitesimal parts of the whole, here referring to the segments of the x-axis</term> are shown in this table:

| To the Element | corresponds |
| :--- | :--- |
| HI | $Z dx$ |
| IK | $Z' dx$ |
| KL | $Z'' dx$ |
| LM | $Z''' dx$ |
| MN | $Z^{IV} dx$ |
| NO | $Z^V dx$ |

Euler is now substituting the specific increments (small changes) calculated for the derivatives into the differential of the expression $Z dx$ at various points along the curve (represented by $Z', Z'', Z'''$, etc.) to find the total change in the integral $\int Z dx$ caused by shifting a single point $n$ to $\nu$.</meta>

# COMPLETE METHOD FOR FINDING CURVES

To find the increments of these values, arising from the displacement of the point $n$ to $\nu$, each of these values must be differentiated, and in the place of the differentials $dy, dp, dq, dr, ds, dt$ and their derivatives, it is necessary to substitute the values assigned above and expressed by $n\nu$; and it will be as follows:

$d. Z dx = n\nu . dx (\frac{T}{dx^5})$
$d. Z' dx = n\nu . dx (\frac{S'}{dx^4} - \frac{5T'}{dx^5})$
$d. Z'' dx = n\nu . dx (\frac{R''}{dx^3} - \frac{4S''}{dx^4} + \frac{10T''}{dx^5})$
$d. Z''' dx = n\nu . dx (\frac{Q'''}{dx^2} - \frac{3R'''}{dx^3} + \frac{6S'''}{dx^4} - \frac{10T'''}{dx^5})$
$d. Z^{IV} dx = n\nu . dx (\frac{P^{IV}}{dx} - \frac{2Q^{IV}}{dx^2} + \frac{3R^{IV}}{dx^3} - \frac{4S^{IV}}{dx^4} + \frac{5T^{IV}}{dx^5})$
$d. Z^V dx = n\nu . dx (N^V - \frac{P^V}{dx} + \frac{Q^V}{dx^2} - \frac{R^V}{dx^3} + \frac{S^V}{dx^4} - \frac{T^V}{dx^5})$

Since now only these elements are altered and receive increments by the transposition of the point $n$ to $\nu$, the sum of these increments will give the total differential value that the formula $\int Z dx$ receives when extended across the entire abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal $x$-coordinate along the base axis</term> $AZ$; which therefore will be:

$$
n\nu . dx \left\{
\begin{aligned}
& + N^V \\
& - \frac{P^V + P^{IV}}{dx} \\
& + \frac{Q^V - 2Q^{IV} + Q'''}{dx^2} \\
& - \frac{R^V + 3R^{IV} - 3R''' + R''}{dx^2} \\
& + \frac{S^V - 4S^{IV} + 6S''' - 4S'' + S'}{dx^4} \\
& - \frac{T^V + 5T^{IV} - 10T''' + 10T'' - 5T' + T}{dx^5}
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$
<note>In the fourth line of the bracketed expression, the denominator is printed in the original as $dx^2$, though the mathematical progression and the pattern of finite differences clearly indicate it should be $dx^3$.</note>

Furthermore, each of these individual terms can be expressed conveniently and succinctly through differentials: for it will be,

# ON THE METHOD OF MAXIMA AND MINIMA

$- P^V + P^{IV} = - d P^{IV}$
$+ Q^V - 2 Q^{IV} + Q^{III} = + dd Q^{III}$
$- R^V + 3 R^{IV} - 3 R^{III} + R^{II} = - d^{3} R^{II}$
$+ S^V - 4 S^{IV} + 6 S^{III} - 4 S^{II} + S^I = + d^{4} S^{I}$
$- T^V + 5 T^{IV} - 10 T^{III} + 10 T^{II} - 5 T^I + T = - d^{5} T$

<note>These lines represent the differences between the values of the functions at successive points on the curve. Euler is showing that these combinations of discrete values correspond exactly to the definition of higher-order differentials (the change of a change).</note>

Therefore, the total differential value <note>Euler uses "differential value" to mean the "variation" or change in the total integral</note> of the formula $\int Z dx$ arising from the small particle $n \nu$ <note>the vertical shift of a point $n$ to a new position $\nu$</note>, will be $= n \nu . dx ( N^V - \frac{d P^{IV}}{dx} + \frac{dd Q^{III}}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 R^{II}}{dx^3} + \frac{d^4 S^I}{dx^4} - \frac{d^5 T}{dx^5} )$. In this case, however, because all the terms are homogeneous <note>original: "homogenei"; meaning they are of the same mathematical order</note>, the markings <note>the Roman numeral superscripts</note> can safely be omitted, for the distinction between $N^V$ and $N$ vanishes, as does the distinction between $d P^{IV}$ and $d P$, and the rest. For this reason, that differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ will be:

-> $n \nu . dx ( N - \frac{d P}{dx} + \frac{dd Q}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 R}{dx^3} + \frac{d^4 S}{dx^4} - \frac{d^5 T}{dx^5} ) :$ <-

From this, the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ can be gathered at the same time even if higher differentials were contained in $Z$. Therefore, if a curve is sought which has a maximum or minimum value for $\int Z dx$ for a given abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal $x$-coordinate</term>, and if the differential of $Z$ was $d Z = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + T dt + \&c.$, the first differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ will be this:

-> $n \nu . dx ( N - \frac{d P}{dx} + \frac{dd Q}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 R}{dx^3} + \frac{d^4 S}{dx^4} - \frac{d^5 T}{dx^5} + \&c. )$ <-

And from this, for the curve being sought, this equation will arise:

-> $0 = N - \frac{d P}{dx} + \frac{dd Q}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 R}{dx^3} + \frac{d^4 S}{dx^4} - \frac{d^5 T}{dx^5} + \&c.$ Which was to be found. <note>original: "Q. E. I." for "Quod Erat Inveniendum"</note> <-

## COROLLARY I.

57. In the formula $\int Z dx$, as we have treated it, the quantity $Z$ contains differentials of the fifth order <note>original: "quinti gradus"</note>: since indeed in its differential...

<summary>Euler simplifies the complex sum of discrete changes into a general differential equation, establishing the primary formula used to find the path of a curve that minimizes or maximizes an integral.</summary>
<keywords>Euler's equation, calculus of variations, differential value, homogeneity, maximum and minimum, fifth order differentials</keywords>

--- Page 81 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the differential equation derived to find a curve that maximizes or minimizes a given integral. On the previous page, Euler established the general form of this equation by considering the variations of the integral.</meta>

<header>THE ABSOLUTE METHOD FOR FINDING CURVES.</header>

...of the expression $d Z = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + T dt$, the term $T dt$ is the final one. Since $T$ still contains differentials of the fifth order <note>original: "gradus" (degree). In modern calculus, we refer to these as "orders" of derivatives.</note> or $t$, it is evident that the equation for the sought curve will be a differential equation of the tenth order.

### COROLLARY II.

58. From this, it is understood that the differential equation for the curve must always rise to an order twice as high as that of the formula for the maximum or minimum itself. For we assume that, in the last term $T dt$, the quantity $T$ still contains $t$ <note>In Euler's notation, $p, q, r, s, t$ represent the first through fifth derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$.</note> within itself; for if this were not so, the order of the equation would be reduced by two, as can be gathered from paragraph 50.

### COROLLARY III.

59. If, therefore, differentials of the $n$-th order are contained in $Z$, then the equation for the curve will be a differential equation of the $2n$-th order; and for this reason, it contains within itself just as many <note>i.e., $2n$</note> new arbitrary constants.

### COROLLARY IV.

60. Because of so many arbitrary constants, just as many points must be proposed to determine the Problem; thus, so that the Problem may be defined, it must be stated as follows: *Among all curves passing through $2n$ given points, determine that one in which the integral $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum, provided that the quantity $Z$ contains differentials of the $n$-th order.*

### COROLLARY V.

61. Because $n$ is an integer, the number of points by which the Problem will be determined will always be even. Thus, either zero points, or two, or four, or six, or eight points, and so on, are required for the determination of the Problem.

<summary>Euler establishes that the differential equation (the Euler-Lagrange equation) for a variational problem is always twice the order of the highest derivative in the integrand. He explains that this $2n$-th order equation requires $2n$ boundary points to reach a unique solution.</summary>

### SCHOLION I. <note>original: "Scholion". In mathematical texts of this era, a scholion is an explanatory note or commentary following a proposition or corollary.</note>

62. Therefore, from the degree of differentiality <note>original: "gradu differentialitatis". In modern calculus, we refer to this as the "order" of the differential equation.</note> to which the equation found for the curve rises, or from the number of points through which the satisfying curve must pass, problems of this kind can be conveniently distributed into classes. To the **first class**, therefore, those problems will be referred in which a curved line is sought absolutely, which for a given abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate, typically $x$.</note> has the value $\int Z dx$ as a maximum or minimum; such problems are contained both in the second Proposition and also in the third, in those cases which we explained in §26 and 27; for these cases, the solution provides a specific determined curve satisfying the requirement. The **second class** encompasses those problems whose solution leads to a differential equation of the second order: and these require two points for their determination; and they ought to be proposed in such a way that, among all curves passing through two given points, that one is defined in which $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum: we have given the solution to problems of this kind in the third Proposition. Furthermore, to the **third class** belong the problems treated in the fourth Proposition, which are formulated such that among all curves passing through four given points, that one is determined which has $\int Z dx$ as a maximum or minimum. In a similar way, the **fourth class** demands six points for determination, the **fifth** eight, and so on; all of these classes we have encompassed in the present Problem. Moreover, although the found equation rises to such a high degree of differentials, it nevertheless quite often admits one or more integrations <note>original: "integrationem". Euler means that the high-order differential equation can be simplified or reduced to a lower order by finding its integral.</note> in a general sense, several cases of which we have exhibited in the preceding Problems. For this reason, let us also see in which cases our general equation admits integration, either one or several; so that in the provided Examples it may be immediately seen whether they are contained in these cases or otherwise. There are, however, two primary cases of this kind: in one of them $N = 0$, in the other $M = 0$, upon which other cases subsequently depend, which we shall develop here.

### CASE I.

63. ## SCHOLION II.

70. With the help of these cases—the number of which could be increased even further if it seemed convenient—problems can often be resolved quite expeditiously. For if any problem is contained within one of these cases, which admits one or more integrations by itself, an equation for the curve can be formed immediately, already integrated once or several times; because of this, it can thereafter be handled more easily. So that this may appear more clearly, and at the same time to declare the use of this last problem, in which derivatives exceeding the second degree are present in the formula for the maximum or minimum $\int Z dx$, it will be helpful to bring forward a single example. <note>Euler is explaining that his general "Cases" act like shortcut templates. If a scientist's specific problem matches the structure of one of his cases, they can skip the difficult calculus and jump straight to a simplified equation.</note>

# CHAPTER III.

## *On finding curves endowed with a property of maximum or minimum, if indeterminate quantities are contained within the formula for the maximum or minimum itself.*

## PROPOSITION I. PROBLEM.

1. To **find** the increments which an indeterminate integral quantity, <margin>Fig. 4.</margin> at any point of the abscissa, receives when one ordinate *Nn* is increased somewhere by a small part *n ν*.

### S O L U T I O N.

Let the <term>abscissa<gloss>the horizontal coordinate along the axis, usually denoted by x</gloss></term> *AH* = *x*, the corresponding <term>ordinate<gloss>the vertical distance from the axis to the curve, usually denoted by y</gloss></term> *Hh* = *y*, and let any indeterminate quantity Π be proposed, corresponding to the abscissa *AH*, which is an integral formula that does not allow for indefinite integration. This quantity Π is so constructed that, insofar as it corresponds to the abscissa *AH* (or point *H*), it is not changed by the increase of the ordinate *Nn*; this will occur if the <term>differentials<gloss>the derivatives or rates of change of the curve's height</gloss></term> in Π do not rise beyond the fifth degree. For this purpose, we assume that it is only the fifth ordinate *Nn*, counting from *Hh*, that is changed. <note>In Euler’s method of variations, he imagines the curve as a series of points. Changing one point *n* affects the derivatives (slopes, curvature, etc.) at that point and several subsequent points, depending on how many derivatives are in the formula.</note> For if differentials of higher degrees were contained in Π, then a further ordinate beyond *Nn* would have to be increased by an infinitely small part. It will suffice, however, to extend the solution only to the five degrees of differentials contained in Π; since from that point, even if higher differentials were present, it would be possible to adapt the solution to them. Therefore, just as the value Π corresponds to the point *H* on the abscissa, so according to our method of notation, the value Π' will correspond to the next point *I*, the value Π'' to point *K*, the value Π''' to point *L*, and so on. We must therefore investigate how much of an increase each of these derivative values Π', Π'', Π''', Π'''', etc., receives from the shifting of point *n* to *ν*, or to define—

2. If, therefore, $\pi$ were an indeterminate quantity of this kind—or an integral formula that does not admit to indefinite integration <note>Euler is referring to "definite" integrals where the value depends on the limits of integration</note>—then all its values after the location of the <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal x-coordinate</note> where one <term>ordinate</term> <note>The vertical y-coordinate</note> is conceived to be increased will undergo a change; and even some of its values *before* that place [will change], the number of which depends on the degree of the differentials <note>The order of the derivatives (first, second, third, etc.)</note> which are contained in that formula $\pi$.

### COROLLARY III.

4. In these cases, therefore, it is necessary that the <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as x.</note> for which the maximum or minimum is sought be determinate. Consequently, the curve which is found to possess the property of the maximum or minimum for this specific abscissa will not be endowed with this same property for other abscissas. <note>Euler is explaining that if the condition for a maximum depends on a fixed endpoint, changing that endpoint changes the "ideal" curve.</note>

### SCHOLION.

5. Soon, the distinction between those questions in which $Z$ is a determinate quantity and those where it is indeterminate will be more clearly perceived when we begin to treat problems of this kind. Furthermore, such questions can be varied in many ways, depending on whether the quantity $Z$ in the formula for the maximum or minimum, $\int Z dx$, is merely a function of an indeterminate formula $\Pi$ <note>The Greek letter Pi, used here to represent a previously defined integral.</note> of the sort we have just contemplated, or if it additionally includes the determinate quantities $x, y, p, q, r, s,$ etc. <note>In Euler’s notation, $p, q, r, s$ usually represent the successive derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$: $p = \frac{dy}{dx}$, $q = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, and so on.</note> Next, several such indefinite integral formulas, distinct from one another, could also be contained within $Z$. However, a single rule, added to those already handed down above, will be sufficient for these various cases. The most important point, however, lies in the indeterminate formula $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$ itself, for which we have assumed here that $[Z]$ is a determinate function. But if this very quantity $[Z]$ should again encompass indefinite integral formulas of this kind, a special solution will be needed once more. Indeed, this complication of indeterminate formulas can be extended to infinity; this will happen if the quantity $[Z]$ again includes the quantity $\Pi$ within itself, such that $d[Z] = [L] d\Pi + [M] dx + [N] dy + [P] dp + [Q] dq + [R] dr +$ etc. Then, because $d\Pi = [Z] dx$, it will again be necessary to consider the value $d[Z] = [L] d\Pi + [M] dx +$ etc., and this progression will continue to infinity. From this, a method will arise for resolving those problems in which a curve is sought that has a maximum or minimum value of the formula $\int Z dx$ when the quantity $Z$ is not given [simply]...

## PROPOSITION II. PROBLEM.

<margin>Fig. 4.</margin>
6. *If $Z$ is a function of an indeterminate quantity $\Pi$, such that $d Z = L d \Pi$, and if $\Pi = \int [Z] d x$, where $d[Z] = [M] d x + [N] d y + [P] d p + [Q] d q + [R] d r +$ etc., find the curve $az$ which, for a given abscissa $AZ$, results in a maximum or minimum value for the formula $\int Z dx$.* <note>Original: "inveneri curvam az quae pro data abscissa AZ habeat valorem formulae $\int Z dx$ maximum vel minimum." Euler is defining a "nested" variation problem where the main integral depends on another integral.</note>

### SOLUTION.

Setting the <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, $x$.</note> $AH = x$ and the <term>ordinate</term> <note>The vertical coordinate, $y$.</note> $H h = y$, the total abscissa $AZ$, to which the maximum or minimum must correspond, is set as $= a$. Therefore, by dividing the space $HZ$ into countless infinitely small elements $HI, IK, KL, LM$, etc., the sum $\int Z dx + Z dx + Z' dx + Z'' dx + Z''' dx +$ etc. must be a maximum or minimum until the endpoint $Z$ is reached. To achieve this, we must seek the differential values <note>In modern terms, these are the "variations" of the integral.</note> which each of these terms receives from the shifting of point $n$ to $\nu$. The sum of these values, when set to zero, will yield the equation for the required curve. However, since we assume the change arising from the movement of $n$ to $\nu$ does not extend beyond $H$ toward $A$, the differential value of the term $\int Z dx$ <note>This refers to the fixed part of the integral before the point where the curve is being "nudged."</note> will be zero. The differential values of the remaining terms will be found if they are differentiated, and if those increments—which we found in the preceding Proposition to arise from the shifting of point $n$ to $\nu$—are substituted into the differentials. In this expression, because all terms are <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Terms are homogeneous when they have the same mathematical dimensions or degrees, allowing them to be combined or compared.</note> with one another, the numerical indices can now be ignored. 7. 11. Since $Z$ is a function of $\Pi$ only, such that it contains no other variable quantities in itself, then because $dZ = L d\Pi$, $L$ will also be a function of $\Pi$ only.

### SCHOLION I.
<note>A "Scholion" is an explanatory note or commentary intended to clarify a specific point in a mathematical or scientific text.</note>

13. Several primary cases occur here to be considered, the first of which is if $[Z]$ were a function of $x$ and $y$ only, so that $d[Z] = [M] dx + [N] dy$. If a curve is now sought in which the formula $\int Z dx$ is a maximum or minimum for a given <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually $x$.</note> $AZ = a$, where $Z$ is any function of $\int [Z] dx = \Pi$, such that $dZ = L d\Pi$; for the curve sought, this equation will be held:

-> $0 = [N] (H - \int L dx)$ <-

Therefore, either $[N] = 0$ or $H = \int L dx$ (which implies $L = 0$). If either one or both of these equations yield a curved line, that line will satisfy the problem not only for the specific abscissa $AZ = a$, but also for any other indefinite abscissa $x$. This is inferred from the fact that the quantity $H$—which depends on the specific fixed abscissa $a$—has dropped out of the calculation <note>original: "ex calculo excesserit." If the result doesn't depend on the endpoint $a$, the solution is "universal" for that curve.</note>. Regarding the equation $L = 0$ specifically: because $L$ is a function of $\Pi$ (which is $\int [Z] dx$), it would follow that $\int [Z] dx$ equals a certain constant, which cannot happen unless $[Z] = 0$. Therefore, the two equations that satisfy this case will be $[N] = 0$ and $[Z] = 0$.

### SCHOLION II.
<note>A "Scholion" is an explanatory note or commentary intended to clarify a specific point in a mathematical or scientific text.</note>

14. Next, it is worth considering the case in which $[N]$ <note>In Euler’s notation, $[N]$ typically refers to the partial derivative of the function with respect to the $y$-coordinate.</note> vanishes; this occurs if $[Z]$ is a function of $x, p, q, r, \&\text{c.}$ that does not involve $y$. Let us assume that $[Z]$ is a function of $x$ and $p$ <note>Here, $p$ usually denotes the first derivative or slope, $dy/dx$.</note>, and let $d[Z] = [M]dx + [P]dp$. If, therefore, we set $\int[Z]dx = \Pi$, and a curve is sought in which—for a fixed <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, $x$.</note> $AZ = a$—the formula $\int Zdx$ is a maximum or minimum, where $Z$ is a function of $\Pi$ such that $dZ = Ld\Pi$; then the equation for the sought curve will arise as $0 = \frac{d.[P](H - \int Ldx)}{dx}$; and therefore $Const. = [P](H - \int Ldx)$. This constant, however, introduced through integration, is not arbitrary; for it must be so determined that when $x = a$ (in which case $\int Ldx = H$), the expression $\frac{Const.}{[P]}$ becomes $0$. This cannot happen unless either this constant is set to $0$, or the quantity $[P]$ is such that it becomes infinite when $x = a$. In the first case, we have either $[P] = 0$ or $\int Ldx = H$, which means $L = 0$, or $\int[Z]dx = Const.$ or rather $[Z] = 0$. In the latter case, however, the constant still cannot be chosen at will; for it will be determined by setting $x = a - dx$, in the same way that expressions which appear indeterminate in certain cases are usually defined. From this, it is clear that in problems of this kind, the number of arbitrary constants entering into the solution—which must equal the number of points through which the satisfying curve must pass—cannot be judged from the degree of the differentials. For by removing all integral formulas through differentiation, one often arrives at a differential equation of a higher degree, upon which the determination of the problem (via a set number of points) will by no means depend.

15. If $\Pi$ denotes the area of the curve $\int ydx$, and $Z$ is any function of $\Pi$, find the curve which, for a given abscissa $= a$, has a maximum or minimum value for the formula $\int Zdx$.

Because $Z$ is a function of $\Pi$, it follows that $dZ = L d\Pi$, and $L$ will be a function of $\Pi = \int y dx$ <note>$\Pi$ represents the area under the curve from the starting point to $x$.</note>. Then, since $d\Pi = y dx$, the value of $[Z]$ will be $y$; and because $d[Z] = [M] dx + [N] dy + [P] dp$ etc., it follows that $[M] = 0, [N] = 1, [P] = 0, [Q] = 0$, etc. <note>These bracketed letters are Euler’s way of denoting partial derivatives: $[N]$ is the derivative with respect to $y$, and $[P]$ is the derivative with respect to the slope $p$.</note> From this, for the curve we are seeking, we obtain the following equation: $0 = H - \int L dx$; and therefore $L = 0$. From this, it follows that $\Pi = \int y dx$ is equal to a certain constant, and furthermore $y = 0$. Therefore, the only solution is a straight line falling directly upon the axis itself; and this holds true for any <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate, $x$.</note> just as much as for a defined value $= a$.

->E X A M P L E II.<-
<note>original: "E X E M P L U M II."</note>

16. If $\Pi$ denotes the arc of a curve $= \int dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$ <note>The standard formula for the length of a curve, where $p$ is the slope $dy/dx$.</note> and $Z$ is any function of that arc; find the curve which, for a given abscissa $AZ = a$, yields a maximum or minimum value for the formula $\int Z dx$.

Since $dZ = L d\Pi$, $L$ will be a function of the arc $\Pi$ itself; and because $d\Pi = dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$, it follows that $[Z] = \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}$ and $[M] = 0, [N] = 0, [P] = \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}, [Q] = 0$, etc. From this, for the sought curve, the following equation is obtained: $0 = - d. \frac{p}{dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} (H - \int L dx)$; and hence $C = \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} (H - \int L dx)$: where the constant $C$ must be determined in such a way that, when $x = a$, it becomes $C = \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} \times 0$. Therefore, because the term $\frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$ cannot become infinite, it is necessary that $C = 0$. Consequently, either $\frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} = 0$, or $\int L dx = H$. From the latter case, it follows that $L = 0$ and $\Pi$ equals some constant; from which it is further deduced that $d\Pi = dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)} = 0$, a condition that cannot be satisfied in any way. From the former case, however, we deduce that $p = 0$ (or $dy = 0$), which is the equation for a straight line parallel to the axis $AZ$. This line satisfies the question for any abscissa.

### EXAMPLE III.

17. *Let* $\Pi$ *denote the surface area of a solid of revolution* <note>A shape formed by rotating a 2D curve around a straight line, like a vase or a sphere.</note> *generated by the rotation of the curve $ah$ around the axis $AZ$, which is expressed as* $\int y dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$ <note>In modern notation, $p$ represents the derivative $dy/dx$, so $pp$ is $(dy/dx)^2$. This is the standard formula for the surface area of a revolving curve.</note>, *and let $Z$ be any function of this surface area; find the curve in which, for a given abscissa* $AZ = a$, *the integral* $\int Z dx$ *is a maximum or a minimum.*

Since $d Z = L d \Pi$, $L$ will be a function of $\Pi = \int y dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$; and since $d \Pi = y dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$, it follows that $[Z] = y \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$, and $d[Z] = dy \sqrt{(1 + pp)} + \frac{yp dp}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$ : from which it follows that $[M] = 0$, $[N] = \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$; and $[P] = \frac{yp}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$, while the remaining values $[Q], [R], [S]$, etc. will all be $= 0$. <note>These bracketed letters are Euler's notation for partial derivatives: $[N]$ is the derivative with respect to $y$, and $[P]$ is the derivative with respect to the slope $p$.</note> Therefore, for the curve being sought, the following equation will be obtained: $0 = (H - \int L dx) \sqrt{(1 + pp)} - \frac{1}{dx} d. \frac{yp}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}} (H - \int L dx)$. Let us set, for the sake of brevity, $H - \int L dx = V$; thus $V dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)} = d. \frac{yp V}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}} = \frac{V pp dx}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}} + \frac{Vy dp}{(1 + pp)^{3:2}} + \frac{yp dV}{\sqrt{(1 + pp)}}$, or $V dx = \frac{Vy dp}{1 + pp} + yp dV = \frac{Vy dp}{1 + pp} - yp L dx$, because $dV = - L dx$. Let us suppose that $Z = \Pi$, so that the integral $\int dx \int y dx \sqrt{(1 + pp)}$ must be a maximum; then $L = 1$ and $\int L dx = x$, and furthermore $V = a - x$, because $H = a$. This results in the equation $(a - x) dx = \frac{(a - x) y dp}{1 + pp} - yp dx$. Let $a - x = u$; then $dx = - du$, and $dy = - p du$, and we obtain the following equation: $0 = u du - y dy + \frac{uy dp}{1 + pp}$, or $u du - y dy - \frac{uy du ddy}{du^2 + dy^2} = 0$. <note>Euler is transforming the differential equation into a form that can be solved by substitution.</note> Let $u = e^t$ and $y = e^t z$: then $du = e^t dt$, and $ddu = 0 = e^t (ddt + dt^2)$, or $ddt = - dt^2$; furthermore $dy = e^t (dz + z dt)$ and $ddy = e^t (ddz + 2 dt dz)$; by substituting these, there arises

### SCHOLION III.

18. The case of this example, in which we investigated the curve where $\int dx \int y dx \surd (1 + pp)$ <note>In modern notation, $p$ is the derivative $dy/dx$. This expression is a "double integral," which calculates the accumulation of an accumulation.</note> is a maximum or minimum, even though it contains a double integral sign, can still be resolved by the method of the preceding Chapter. It is worth showing this for the following reason: so that the agreement between both methods may be declared. Especially, however, through this work a new way will be opened for solving many other problems regarding maxima and minima, which until now, as far as is known, has not been touched upon.

The question, namely, is that for a given <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate, usually $x$.</note> $AZ = a$, this expression $\int dx \int y dx \surd (1 + pp)$ becomes a maximum or minimum. This expression is transformed into the following: $x \int y dx \surd (1 + pp) - \int xy dx \surd (1 + pp)$ <note>Euler is using a technique similar to modern "integration by parts" to turn a double integral into a single integral that is easier to work with.</note>. In order for this form to be rendered a maximum or minimum, it is necessary that its value, for the abscissa $AZ = a$, be the same for the sought curve $az$ itself and for that same point $n$ moved to $\nu$ <note>This "movement" from $n$ to $\nu$ represents a tiny variation or "wiggle" in the curve, which is the heart of the calculus of variations.</note>. 

Let us therefore suppose that $\int y dx \surd (1 + pp) = A$ when $x = a$ is set, and in the same case $\int xy dx \surd (1 + pp) = B$. Now, with the elements $m n o$ changed into $m \nu o$, the value of $A$ will be increased by its differential value, which, by the preceding Chapter, is $= n \nu \cdot dx (\surd (1 + pp) - \frac{1}{dx} d \cdot \frac{yp}{\surd (1 + pp)})$; moreover, by the same rules, the differential value of the quantity $B$ comes out to $= n \nu \cdot dx (x \surd (1 + pp) - \frac{1}{dx} d \cdot \frac{xyp}{\surd (1 + pp)})$. Wherefore, for the proposed formula $\int dx \int y dx \surd (1 + pp)$, with the point $n$ moved to $\nu$, for the abscissa $AZ = a$

## PROPOSITION III. PROBLEM.

19. *Given that $\Pi$ is an indeterminate integral function $\int [Z] dx$, such that $d [Z] = [M] dx + [N] dy + [P] dp + [Q] dq + [R] dr +$ etc. Let $Z$ be any function of both this quantity $\Pi$ and the determined quantities $x, y, p, q, r, s,$ etc., so that $dZ = L d\Pi + M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr +$ etc. Find the curve $az$, which, for a given abscissa $AZ = a$, has a maximum or minimum value of the formula $\int Z dx$.*

### SOLUTION.

The increment $n\nu$ <note>Euler uses the Greek letter $\nu$ (nu) to represent a tiny, virtual change in the vertical position of a point on the curve.</note>, which is conceived to be added to a single <term>ordinate</term><note>The vertical y-coordinate.</note> $Nn$, is taken to be so far removed from the first ordinate $Hh$ that it causes no change in the value of the formula $\int Z dx$ corresponding to the abscissa $AH$. Consequently, only the values of this formula corresponding to the elements of the abscissa following $H$ undergo changes; these are $Z dx, Z' dx, Z'' dx, Z''' dx,$ etc., up to the final element of the abscissa in $Z$. Therefore, if the increments of these values arising from the movement of point $n$ to $\nu$ are collected into a single sum and set equal to zero, they will provide the equation for the sought-after curve. Moreover, the increments of these values will be obtained by differentiating them and substituting in place of the <term>differentials</term><note>The small changes or rates of change in the variables.</note> those values which we found above—both in the final Proposition of the preceding Chapter and the first of this one—to arise from the movement of $n$ to $\nu$: thus it will be

->COROLLARY I.<-

20. The rule found in the preceding Chapter has therefore been made more extensive; for we can now define the curve that possesses a maximum or minimum value for the formula $\int Z dx$ in cases where $Z$ is not only a function of the specific quantities $x, y, p, q, r, \text{etc.}$ but also contains within itself one <term>indeterminate integral quantity</term><note>An integral whose value depends on the upper limit $x$, meaning it evolves as you move along the curve.</note> $\Pi$—provided that $\Pi$ is a specific function.

### COROLLARY II.

21. Furthermore, if there are multiple such <term>indeterminate integral quantities</term><note>Integrals like $\int Z dx$ where the upper limit is the variable $x$, rather than a fixed value.</note> in *Z*, the solution can still be applied. For just as a certain expression entered into the differential value from one such indeterminate formula, similar expressions will arise from each individual formula, if more are present, and will be added to the differential value.

### COROLLARY III.

22. Since *Z* is here assumed to be a <term>function</term><note>A mathematical relationship where one quantity depends on others.</note> not only of the defined quantities *x*, *y*, *p*, *q*, *r* etc., but also of the indeterminate quantity $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$, because $dZ = L d\Pi + M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + \&c.$, then the quantities *M*, *N*, *P*, *Q* etc. will also involve this integral formula $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$. This applies even to the quantity *L* itself, unless perhaps $\Pi$ has only a single <term>dimension</term><note>Meaning if $\Pi$ appears only linearly (to the first power) within the function *Z*.</note> in *Z*.

### COROLLARY IV.

23. For this reason, in the equation found for the curve, there will be integral quantities of two kinds—namely, $\int L dx$ and $\int [Z] dx$. Consequently, if the resulting equation is to be freed from these formulas through differentiation, it will rise to a much higher <term>differential degree</term><note>What we today call the "order" of a differential equation (e.g., first-order, second-order).</note> than the form itself initially suggests.

### COROLLARY V.

24. By eliminating these integral formulas, one will arrive at a differential equation two degrees higher. For if the resulting equation, when expanded, is of the $n$-th differential degree, then first the value of the formula $\int L dx$ is determined from it; and once differentiation is performed, one arrives at a differential equation of $n+1$ degrees. This will still contain the formula $\int [Z] dx$, which, after being further reduced and freed from the formula $\int [Z] dx$ by differentiation, will become of the differential degree $n+2$.

### SCHOLION I.
<note>original: "SCHOLION," a scholarly commentary or explanatory note.</note>

25. Although the number of points through which the sought-after curve must pass depends on the <term>differential degree</term><note>The "order" of the differential equation, such as second-order or third-order.</note>, in this case it cannot be defined simply by the number $n + 2$. For this differential equation of $n + 2$ degrees potentially involves $n + 2$ <term>constants</term><note>Fixed values that appear when solving equations, often labeled C1, C2, etc.</note>, but not all of them are truly <term>arbitrary</term><note>Values that can be freely chosen to fit the curve to specific points.</note>. One constant is determined by the fact that the <term>integral</term> $\int [Z] dx$ must result in a specific value—not a vague one, but the exact value found in the quantity $Z$; that is, it must vanish (become zero) when $x = 0$, provided this condition was assumed in the formula $\int Z dx$. Furthermore, in the same way, one constant is defined by the formula $\int L dx$, which, as we established, must also vanish when $x = 0$. Because of this, only $n$ strictly arbitrary constants will remain, which will provide the same number of points by which the problem is determined. Therefore, just as in the previous chapter, for the problem to be determined, it must be proposed such that: among all the curves passing through $n$ given points, that one is determined which contains the <term>maximum or minimum</term> value of the formula $\int Z dx$ for a given <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal or x-coordinate.</note> $x = a$. To carry out this judgment, the discovered equation must be expanded; that is, all the indicated <term>differentiations</term> must actually be performed. Once this is done, it will be clear what degree of differentials are present, and from this degree, the number $n$ will be obtained. However, we shall see in the following examples what more can be observed regarding this number $n$.

---

### EXAMPLE I.

*26. To find the curve which, for a given abscissa $AZ = a$, has the maximum or minimum value of the formula $\int ydx \int ydx$, where the integral $\int y dx$ is taken such that it vanishes when $x = 0$.*

Therefore, let $\Pi = \int y dx$, and $[Z] = y$; from this, we get $[N] = 1$, with the remaining letters $[M], [P], [Q]$, etc. being $= 0$. Furthermore, $Z = y \times \Pi$ and $d Z = y x d \Pi + y \Pi dx + x \Pi dy$; from which we have $L = yx; M = y \Pi$ and $N = x \Pi, P = Q = R, \&c. = 0.$
<note>The variable 'x' appearing in these terms likely refers to the differential relationships Euler derived in his general formula; he is breaking down the complex integral into components his formula can solve.</note>

28. To find the curve in which, for a given <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate, typically x.</note>, the expression $\int \frac{dx}{p} \int y dx$ is a maximum or a minimum.

In this case, let $\Pi = \int y dx$, and $[Z] = y$ and $[N] = 1$; then since $Z = \frac{\Pi}{p}$, it follows that $L = \frac{1}{p}$ and $P = - \frac{\Pi}{pp}$; all other letters <term>vanish</term><note>original: "evanescunt"; they become zero in the general formula Euler is applying.</note>. From this, the following equation is produced: $0 = H - \int \frac{dx}{p} + \frac{1}{dx} d. \frac{\Pi}{pp}$; or $0 = H - \int \frac{dx}{p} + \frac{y}{pp} - \frac{2 \Pi dp}{p^3 dx}$

Therefore, having set $x = a$, in which case $\int \frac{dx}{p} = H$, it will be $y dx = \frac{2 \Pi dp}{p}$. If that equation is differentiated, it will be $0 = - \frac{dx}{p} + \frac{dx}{p} - \frac{2 y dp}{p^3} - \frac{2 y dp}{p^3} + \frac{6 \Pi dp^2}{p^4 dx} - \frac{2 \Pi ddp}{p^3 dx}$. Or $0 = 3 \Pi dp^2 - 2 yp dx dp - \Pi p ddp$; which equation conveniently becomes integrable if it is divided by $\Pi p dp$, for it yields $0 = \frac{3 dp}{p} - \frac{2 y dx}{\Pi} - \frac{ddp}{dp}$, the <term>integral</term><note>The result of the integration process.</note> of which is $C = 3 l p - 2 l \Pi - l \frac{dp}{dx}$ <note>Euler uses "l" for the natural logarithm.</note>. Or $C \Pi^2 dp = p^3 dx$; therefore, having set $x = a$, since it must be that $y dx = \frac{2 \Pi dp}{p}$, then from this equation $C \Pi y = 2 p^2$, by which one constant will be defined. It will therefore be $\Pi = \sqrt{ \frac{p^3 dx}{C dp} } = \frac{2 y p dx dp}{3 dp^2 - p ddp}$, or $3 dp^2 - p ddp = \frac{2 y dp \sqrt{dx dp}}{b \sqrt{bp}}$, which is a <term>third-degree differential equation</term><note>An equation involving the third derivative of the curve.</note>, and therefore, besides the constant $b$ (we have indeed substituted $\frac{1}{b^3}$ in place of $C$), it involves three new constants. One of these will be determined by the fact that, when $x = a$, it must happen that $\frac{\Pi y}{b^3} = 2 pp$; and another from the fact that, when $x = 0$, it must be that $\Pi = 0$, or $\frac{p^3 dx}{dp} = 0$. ### EXAMPLE IV.

29. To find the curve *az* related to the <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate on a graph, usually denoted as x.</note> *AZ = a*, in which the expression $\int dx \left( \frac{\int yx dx}{\int y dx} \right)$ is a maximum or a minimum.

It seemed appropriate to bring forward this example so that it might appear how questions of this kind are to be resolved if two or more <term>indefinite integral</term><note>An integral without specific limits, representing a family of functions; here, Euler is treating the internal integrals as variables themselves.</note> formulas are present. Let therefore $\int y x dx = \Pi$ and $\int y dx = \pi$; and having set $d \Pi = [ Z ] dx$ and $d \pi = [ z ] dx$, it will be $[ Z ] = yx$ and $[ z ] = y$. Now if the lowercase letter $[ z ]$ is treated in the same way as the uppercase $[ Z ]$, such that $d [ z ] = [ m ] dx + [ n ] dy + [ p ] dp + \text{etc.}$, it will be $[ M ] = y$ and $[ N ] = x$, and likewise $[ n ] = 1$. Next, since $z = \Pi / \pi$, it will be $dz = d \Pi / \pi - \Pi d \pi / \pi^2$. Let $1 / \pi = L$ and $\Pi / \pi^2 = l$ be set; and we will have, because $N$ and $P, Q, R, \text{etc.} = 0$, this following equation for the sought curve:

-> $0 = x ( H - \int \frac{dx}{\pi} ) - 1 ( h - \int \frac{\Pi dx}{\pi^2} )$ <-

where $\int \frac{dx}{\pi} = H$ and $\int \frac{\Pi dx}{\pi^2} = h$ are set, if $x = a$ is assumed. Since therefore $H x - x \int \frac{dx}{\pi} = h - \int \frac{\Pi dx}{\pi^2}$, it will be, by differentiating:

-> $H - \int \frac{dx}{\pi} - \frac{x}{\pi} = - \frac{\Pi}{\pi^2}$ <-

Therefore, having set $x = a$, it must be that $\Pi / \pi^2 = x / \pi$. If it is differentiated again, there will come forth:

-> $- \frac{2}{\pi} + \frac{xy}{\pi^2} = - \frac{yx}{\pi^2} + \frac{2 \Pi y}{\pi^3}$ <-

or $xy - \pi = \Pi y / \pi$; and from here $\Pi = \pi x - \frac{\pi \pi}{y}$. If the differentiation is carried out further, we will have:

-> $yx dx = \pi dx + yx dx - 2 \pi dx + \frac{\pi \pi dy}{y^2}$ <-

or $y^2 dx = \pi dy$, or $\frac{y dx}{\pi} = \frac{dy}{y}$. However, since,

With $x = 0$ set, $\pi$ becomes 0, and in this case $\frac{y^2 dx}{dy} = 0$ will occur. However, the equation $\frac{y dx}{\pi} = \frac{dy}{y}$, because $y dx = d\pi$ <note>original: "ob y dx = d$\pi$"; this is the fundamental relationship where the derivative of the integral $\pi$ is the integrand $y$</note>, integrated gives $\pi = by$; and therefore, once $x = 0$ is set, $y$ must vanish <note>vanish: in mathematics, to reach a value of zero</note>. From the equation $\pi = by$, it follows that $y dx = b dy$; and hence $x = b \text{ logarithm } y - b \text{ logarithm } 0$, provided that $\pi = by$ must vanish when $x = 0$ is set; in which case $y$ would become 0, and the curve would depart into a straight line falling upon the axis *AZ*.

But if we suppose that, with $x = 0$ set, the value of the integral $\pi = \int y dx$ does not need to vanish, but instead becomes $= bc$, then $x = b \text{ logarithm } \frac{y}{c}$, which is the equation for the **Logarithmic Curve** <note>A curve where the x-value is proportional to the logarithm of the y-value; this was a primary focus of 18th-century analysis</note>. To determine this fully, let the value $\Pi = \int y x dx$ be sought; because $y dx = b dy$, then $y x dx = b x dy$, and $\Pi = b x y - b \pi + \text{Constant}$, or $\Pi = b^2 y \text{ logarithm } \frac{y}{c} - b^2 y + C$. Since however $\Pi$ must be 0 when $x = 0$ (or $y = c$) is set, it will be $\Pi = b^2 y \text{ logarithm } \frac{y}{c} + b^2 (c - y)$.

Now let $x = a$ be set, which results in $\text{logarithm } \frac{y}{c} = \frac{a}{b}$, and $y = c e^{a/b}$ <note>Euler uses "e" to denote the base of the natural logarithm, a notation he popularized</note>. In this case, however, it is necessary that $\Pi = \pi x$, or $a b c e^{a/b} + b^2 c - b^2 c e^{a/b} = a b c e^{a/b}$, and from this $e^{a/b} = 1$, from which it follows that either $a = 0$ or $b = \infty$.

This inconvenience <note>Euler uses "incommodum" to describe a mathematical contradiction or a result that fails to define a unique, useful curve</note> arises from the fact that we assumed $\Pi = 0$ when $x = 0$ was made. Let us therefore suppose that when $y = g$ is set, in that case $\Pi$ vanishes; then $\Pi = b^2 y \text{ logarithm } \frac{y}{c} - b^2 y + b^2 g - b^2 g \text{ logarithm } \frac{g}{c}$. Now with $x = a$ set, in which case it must be that $\Pi = \pi x = a \pi$; then $a b c e^{a/b} - b^2 c e^{a/b} + b^2 g - b^2 g \text{ logarithm } \frac{g}{c} = a b c e^{a/b}$, and from this $e^{a/b} = \frac{g}{c} (1 - \text{logarithm } \frac{g}{c})$, or $b = \frac{a}{\text{logarithm } \frac{g}{c} (1 - \text{logarithm } \frac{g}{c})}$, and therefore $x = \frac{a (\text{logarithm } y - \text{logarithm } c)}{\text{logarithm } g (1 - \text{logarithm } \frac{g}{c}) - \text{logarithm } c}$. This is the equation [for] the curve

### SCHOLION II.

30. Through this Problem, therefore, not only can those questions be resolved which seek a curve having a maximum or minimum formula $\int Z dx$ for a given **abscissa** <note>The horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as x</note>—where $Z$, besides the determined quantities $x, y, p, q, r, s,$ etc., includes one integral formula $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$—but also those where several formulas of this kind are present. Meanwhile, however, it must be noted that these integral formulas $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$ contained in the function $Z$ must be so composed that $[Z]$ is a **determined function** <note>In Euler’s terminology, a "determined function" is one composed of variables and their derivatives, but which does not itself contain another integral</note>; that is, a function of the quantities $x, y, p, q, r$, etc., involving no further integral formulas. For this reason, let us now investigate a method of resolving problems of this kind when that function $[Z]$ is not determined, but besides $x, y, p, q$, etc., it involves a new integral formula $\pi = \int [z] dx$. But lest the solution become too lengthy, we shall not consider beyond differentials of the second degree <note>Second-order derivatives</note>. For it is already understood that if the solution has been prepared up to differentials of the second degree, then by **induction** <note>A logical step where the pattern for higher orders is inferred from the lower ones</note>, the solution can be extended to any further degrees. To this end, we must designate the first **ordinate** <note>The vertical coordinate, y</note> $Ll$ by $y$, from which the third following ordinate $Nn = y''$ is conceived to be increased by a small part $n \nu$: From this increase, there will arise the following increments of the quantities $y, p,$ and $q,$ with their derivatives:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| change in $y = 0$ | change in $p = 0$ | change in $q = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^2}$ |
| change in $y' = 0$ | change in $p' = + \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ | change in $q' = + \frac{2n \nu}{dx^2}$ |
| change in $y'' = + n \nu$ | change in $p'' = - \frac{n \nu}{dx}$ | change in $q'' = + \frac{n \nu}{dx^2}$ |

which Table will suffice for resolving any problems whatsoever, as will be understood from the following Proposition.

### PROPOSITION IV. PROBLEM.

31. Let $\pi = \int [z] dx$ and $d[z] = [m] dx + [n] dy + [p] dp + [q] dq$, and let the quantity $[Z]$ involve the integral formula $\pi$ such that $d[Z] = Z d\pi + [M] dx + [N] dy + [P] dp + [Q] dq$. <note>In Euler’s notation, these brackets and letters represent specific functions of the variables; the letters like m, n, p, and q represent what we would today call partial derivatives.</note> Now, having set $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$, let $Z$ be a function of $x, y, p, q$, and also of $\pi$, so that $dZ = L d\pi + M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq$. Given these conditions, it is required to define the curve $az$ which, for a given **abscissa** <note>The horizontal distance along the axis</note> $AZ = a$, has a maximum or minimum value for the formula $\int Z dx$.

-> S O L U T I O N <-

As we advised in the preceding **Scholion** <note>An explanatory note or commentary</note>, let the abscissa be $AL = x$ and the **ordinate** <note>The vertical height of the curve, labeled 'applicata' in Latin</note> be $Ll = y$; moreover, let the value $\int Z dx$ correspond to the abscissa $AL = x$, which will not be affected by the small variation $n \nu$ <note>The variation $n \nu$ represents a tiny shift in the curve's path at a specific point, used to test if the total integral remains at a maximum or minimum</note>. From this, the differential value must be determined from the following elements of the abscissa, to which will correspond the values $Z dx, Z' dx, Z'' dx, Z''' dx$, $Z^{IV} dx$, and so on, up to the final element of the entire proposed abscissa $AZ$ at $Z$. <note>Euler uses the prime marks ($Z', Z''$, etc.) to indicate the values of the function at successive points $x+dx, x+2dx$ along the curve.</note> The differential values of each of these terms will be found through differentiation, by substituting in place of the differentials $dy, dp, dq$ the values indicated in the preceding paragraph. It will therefore be:

$d. Z dx = dx ( L d\pi + \frac{Q. n \nu}{dx^2} )$
$d. Z' dx = dx ( L' d\pi' + \frac{P' n \nu}{dx} - \frac{2 Q'. n \nu}{dx^2} )$
$d. Z'' dx = dx ( L'' d\pi'' + N''. n \nu - \frac{P''. n \nu}{dx} + \frac{Q''. n \nu}{dx^2} )$
$d. Z''' dx = dx. L''' d\pi'''$
$d. Z^{IV} dx = dx. L^{IV} d\pi^{IV}$
&c.

It remains, therefore, for us to define through the variation $n \nu$ the differentials $d\pi, d\pi', d\pi'', d\pi'''$ etc.—that is, the differential values of the quantities $\pi, \pi', \pi'', \pi'''$ etc. Indeed, it is:

### COROLLARY I.

32. Therefore, the differential value <note>In modern calculus, this is known as the variation of the integral.</note> for the formula $\int Z dx$ has been found, and it is more widely applicable than what was assumed in the Proposition: namely, if $dZ = L d\pi + M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr +$ etc. <note>Euler uses $p, q, r$ to represent the first, second, and third derivatives ($y', y'', y'''$).</note> and there exists $d\pi = [Z] dx$, if $d[Z] = [L] d\pi + [M] dx + [N] dy + [P] dp + [Q] dq + [R] dr +$ etc. and likewise if, with $d\pi = [z] dx$ being set, it were $d[z] = [m] dx + [n] dy + [p] dp + [q] dq + [r] dr +$ etc. Indeed, no matter how many degrees of differentials are contained in the quantities $Z$, $[Z]$, and $[z]$, the given solution will be applicable.

### COROLLARY II.

33. But if it is set that $H - \int L dx = T$, and $G - \int [L] dx (H - \int L dx) = V$, the differential value will be:

$= n \nu . dx (N - \frac{dP}{dx} + \frac{dd Q}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 R}{dx^3} + \text{etc.})$
$+ n \nu . dx ([N] T - \frac{d. [P] T}{dx} + \frac{dd. [Q] T}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 [R] T}{dx^3} + \text{etc.})$
$+ n \nu . dx ([n] V - \frac{d. [p] V}{dx} + \frac{dd. [q] V}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3 [r] V}{dx^3} + \text{etc.})$
<note>The term $n \nu . dx$ represents the infinitesimal change in the curve at a specific point, which is why it appears as a factor in every line of the variation.</note>

### COROLLARY III.

34. From this, therefore, the equation for the sought curve <note>The "sought curve" is the function $y(x)$ that satisfies the condition for a maximum or minimum.</note> will be this:
$0 = N + [N] T + [n] V - \frac{d(P + [P] T + [p] V)}{dx} + \frac{dd(Q + [Q] T + [q] V)}{dx^2} - \frac{d^3(R + [R] T + [r] V)}{dx^3} + \text{etc.}$
the law of which progression <note>original: "progressio"—referring to the pattern of terms in the series.</note>, if by chance more terms are needed, is obvious by itself.
