### SCHOLION.

37. The solution of this Problem is therefore very broadly applicable, because it not only encompasses all the preceding Problems and satisfies the specific case proposed, but can also be adapted by induction to any cases that are even more intricate. To make this easier to understand, let us suppose that $[z]$ additionally contains an integral formula $\pi = \int \zeta dx$, such that $d[z] = [l] d\pi + [m] dx + [n] dy + [p] dp + [q] dq +$ etc. <note>In Euler’s notation, $p, q, r...$ represent the derivatives $y', y'', y'''...$ of the curve.</note> where $d\zeta = u dx + v dy + \Phi dp + \chi dq +$ etc. Now, to determine the differential value <note>The "differential value" is the mathematical expression for the change in the total integral when the path of the curve is slightly altered.</note>, besides the two integral quantities $T$ and $V$, a third must be defined, $W$, constructed such that it is:
$W = F - \int [l] dx (G - \int [L] dx (H - \int L dx))$ 
which vanishes when $x = a$ is set. And once this is done, the differential value will be:
$= \nu \cdot dx (N + [N] T + [n] V + u W - \frac{d(P + [P] T + [p] V + \Phi W)}{dx} + \frac{dd (Q + [Q] T + [q] V + \chi W)}{dx^2} - $ etc.) 
Therefore, no formula for a maximum or minimum could even be devised that would not be contained in this solution, or composed of such formulas to which this solution applies. Furthermore, one could extend this expression to infinity if every indeterminate formula were to contain yet another new indefinite integral formula within itself; nor would any difficulty arise, except in providing a sufficient number of characters <note>original: "characterum"—Euler means the difficulty would lie only in having enough different letters and symbols to label all the variables.</note>. ### COROLLARY III

### COROLLARY IV

42. Since the quantity $H$—which depends on a given <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as x.</note> $AZ$—has been removed from this equation through division, it is clear that in these cases, a curve that satisfies the condition for one abscissa will satisfy it for every other abscissa. Thus, these problems are similar to those in which the quantity $Z$ is a <term>determinate function</term><note>A function whose value depends only on the current coordinates and derivatives, rather than on the path taken (the integral).</note>.

### COROLLARY V

43. If, therefore, the quantity $\Pi = \int [Z] dx$ must be a maximum or minimum, where $d[Z] = [L] d\Pi + [M] dx + [N] dy$ $+ [P] dp + [Q] dq + \text{etc.}$ <note>Euler uses $p, q, r$ to represent the first, second, and third derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$.</note>, a curve can be shown which, by itself, enjoys this property for any abscissa. Its nature is expressed by this equation: $0 = [N] e^{-\int[L]dx} - \frac{d.[P]e^{-\int[L]dx}}{dx}$ $+ \frac{dd.[Q]e^{-\int[L]dx}}{dx^2} - \text{etc.}$ From which, moreover, once the individual terms are expanded, the exponential quantity $e^{-\int[L]dx}$, and even the integral formula $\int [L] dx$ itself, will cancel out.

### SCHOLION I. <note>original: "SCHOLION"; a scholarly note or explanatory remark added to a mathematical proof.</note>

44. The use of this Proposition is remarkably useful in problems so structured that the <term>indefinite quantities</term><note>Quantities that change along the length of the curve, often represented by integrals with variable limits.</note> contained within them cannot be expressed by integral formulas alone, but instead require the construction of differential equations. This solution is equally valid whether one such quantity $\Pi$ is present in the formula for the maximum or minimum $\int Z dx$, or if several are present. For if several such quantities $\Pi$ are involved, one will simply have more values for the letters *L*, $[L]$, $[M]$, $[N]$, $[P]$, $[Q]$, etc., as well as for the letter $V = e^{-\int [L] dx}(H - \int e^{\int [L] dx} L dx)$. When all of these are introduced into the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ in the manner we have discovered, they will provide the equation for the curve; the treatment will be exactly the same as if only a single such quantity were present.

However, since that letter $\Pi$—the absolute value of which cannot be expressed by quantities pertaining to the curve—remains in almost all the terms, the equation found for the curve will not only consist of the letters *x*, *y*, *p*, *q*, *r*, etc., but will also involve that very quantity $\Pi$, as well as other integral formulas usually depending on it, such as $\int [L] dx$ and $\int L dx$. Therefore, so that a <term>pure equation</term><note>An equation containing only coordinates (x, y) and their derivatives (p, q, etc.), without any integral signs.</note> for the curve may be produced (one contained only by the letters *x*, *y*, *p*, *q*, etc.), it is necessary to combine the discovered equation—after it has been freed from the integral formulas $\int [L] dx$ and $\int L dx$—with the equation $d\Pi = [Z]dx$, and by its help, eliminate the value of $\Pi$.

Although one arrives at <term>differentials of higher orders</term><note>Higher-order derivatives, such as the second or third derivative.</note> in this way, one should not think that just as many <term>arbitrary constants</term><note>The constants of integration (like "+ C") that appear when solving differential equations.</note> are included. For both the equation $d\Pi = [Z]dx$ itself and the other preceding equations require a certain determination, by which several constants will be determined. Furthermore, it should be noted that the truth of this Method can be verified by the preceding ones whenever the equation $d\Pi = [Z]dx$ is so composed that it allows for integration. In such cases, the same problems can be resolved by the methods previously handed down, and from there, one may observe their agreement. Thus, if $[Z]$ consists only of *x* and $\Pi$, then it will be certain that $\Pi$ is a function—

$0 = - d. [P] e^{-\int [L] dx}$, or $[P] e^{-\int [L] dx} = C$;

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the word "determinari" from the previous page.</note> ...the quantity Π would be determined, and in this way the equation for the curve being sought would be found. $\frac{C dp}{g p^2} = \frac{(n + \frac{1}{2}) dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\Pi \sqrt{\Pi}} - \frac{n C dx (1 + p^2)}{\Pi p}$, and $D - \frac{C}{gp} = \frac{1}{\Pi^n \sqrt{\Pi}} - \frac{C \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\Pi^n p}$.
If Π <term>Π (Pi): used here as a variable representing velocity or a function of it, rather than the circular constant 3.14</term> is eliminated from these, an equation between $p$ <note>The slope of the curve</note> and $x$ will be obtained of such a kind that $x$ occurs nowhere, but instead only $dx$ <note>the differential or tiny change in x</note> occurs everywhere, from which that equation can be constructed, and thus the curve itself. Or more easily, let $p$ be determined in terms of Π from the latter equation, and this value, substituted into the fundamental equation $dx = \frac{d\Pi}{g - \alpha \Pi^n \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$, will give the value of $x$ in terms of Π; namely, it will be $x = \int \frac{d\Pi}{g - \alpha \Pi^n \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$ and $y = \int \frac{p d\Pi}{g - \alpha \Pi^n \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$.
Moreover, the constant $D$ must be chosen in such a way that, by setting $x = a$, in which case it becomes $C = \frac{p}{\sqrt{\Pi (1 + p^2)}}$, $D$ becomes $\frac{1}{g \sqrt{\Pi (1 + p^2)}}$, or it must then be that $\frac{C}{D} = gp$.

COMPLETED FOR FINDING CURVES.

...as a function of the variables *x, y, p, q, r, etc.*, whether it be determinate or indeterminate. A <term>determinate function</term> <note>original: "functio determinata"</note> for us is one which, if the values of the letters *x, y, p, q, r, etc.* are given at any point, can itself be assigned, whether it be algebraic or transcendental. An <term>indeterminate function</term> <note>original: "functio indeterminata"</note>, however, is one which cannot be assigned through the given values of those letters obtained at a single location, but instead involves all preceding values together, just as happens if <term>integral signs</term> <note>original: "signa integralia"; referring to the symbol ∫</note> occur. In Chapter Two, therefore, we handed down the method of resolving all problems in which *Z* is a determinate function; in this third chapter, we have pursued those formulas in which *Z* is either itself an indefinite function or involves one or more such functions. At the same time, we have exhibited a method for those cases in which that indefinite function cannot even be represented by integral formulas, but truly requires the resolution of a <term>differential equation</term>. Now, therefore, let us develop those cases in which the expression that must be a maximum or minimum is not a simple integral formula, as we have held until now, but is composed in any way from several formulas of this kind; and at the same time, we will open a method for expeditiously resolving many other problems that do not relate to <term>orthogonal coordinates</term> <note>original: "coordinatas orthogonales"; refers to the standard Cartesian system where axes meet at right angles</note>.

### COROLLARY V.

6. For if a Circle $CAME$ is described upon any diameter $CE$ ending at $C$, the arc $AM$ intercepted between the radii $ACM$ for a given area $ACM$ will be a minimum. That is to say, if any other curve is described through any two points situated on this Circle, and an area equal to the area $ACM$ is cut off by two radii drawn from $C$, the corresponding arc of that curve will always be greater than the arc $AM$. To make this clear, let $CD$ be drawn from $C$ perpendicular to $CE$, and let the perpendicular $SQ$ be dropped upon it from $S$: the triangle $SCQ$ will be similar to the triangle $CEM$, and hence $CE : CM [y] = CS [1] : SQ$ or $SQ = \frac{y}{CE} = \sin \angle DBS$, or $DBS$.

<margin>Fig. 10.</margin>
11. *On any surface, whether convex or concave, to draw a line which is the shortest of all between its endpoints.* <note>This is the definition of a "geodesic," the straightest possible path on a curved surface, like the routes followed by airplanes over the Earth.</note>

Let any plane be taken to which the surface may be referred, $APQ$, and in it let the straight line $AP$ be taken for the axis. Now, from each point of the sought line, let perpendiculars be conceived to be dropped onto this plane, by which the line $AQ$ is described, which will be the projection of the shortest line onto this plane; once this is known, the shortest line itself on the proposed surface will simultaneously become known. Let $AP = x$, $PQ = y$; and since the nature of the surface is given, the length of the perpendicular $QM$ to the plane $APQ$ can be defined from the given values $AP = x$ and $PM = y$, until it intersects the surface at $M$. <note>Euler is using a 3D coordinate system where $x$ and $y$ are on a flat ground plane and $z$ (the perpendicular $QM$) represents the "height" of the surface.</note> If therefore we set $QM = z$, the length of this line $z$ will be given in terms of $x$ and $y$, such that $z$ is a defined function of $x$ and $y$ themselves. Since, then, $z$ is a function of $x$ and $y$, which is given by the local equation for the surface, let us set $dz = T dx + V dy$; and $T$ and $V$ will be functions of $x$ and $y$ of such a kind that $T dx + V dy$ is a definite differential formula: namely, if we set $dT = Edx + Fdy$, then $dV = Fdx + Gdy$ will hold, with the letter $F$ being common to both differentials. <note>In modern terms, $T$ and $V$ are partial derivatives ($\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$), and $F$ represents the mixed second partial derivative, showing the surface is smooth and continuous.</note> Now the element of the line drawn on the surface <note>The infinitesimal segment of the path length, $ds$.</note> is $= \sqrt{(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)} = \sqrt{(dx^2 + dy^2 + (Tdx + Vdy)^2)}$. Therefore, setting $dy = p dx$, this formula must be a minimum: $\int dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2 + T^2 + 2 TVp + V^2 p^2)}$; so that $Z = \sqrt{(1 + p^2 + T^2 + 2 TVp + V^2 p^2)}$, from which it follows

### SCHOLION II.

13. From these examples, the excellent use that our method has in resolving problems even of diverse kinds is abundantly clear. In particular, the last example provides several circumstances most worthy of note, from which the nature of the solution can be illustrated. Since a double equation arose from two factors, a double solution also emerged. The first of these absolutely determines the satisfying line, such that it cannot be drawn through two given points: for it gives either a straight line or a semicircle. The straight line solves the question in two ways: it is either normal (perpendicular) to the axis $AP$, or parallel to it. How each satisfies the condition is manifest: for in the case of the line normal to the axis, the portion of the curve that encloses the given space with the axis and the normal is always infinitely small, and therefore indeed a minimum. The other straight line, parallel to the axis, is somewhat more broadly applicable, since it can be drawn through a given point; and because the <term>ordinates<gloss>The vertical coordinate, or the distance from the axis to the curve</gloss></term> themselves are normal to it, and the space cut off becomes the abscissa itself, that straight line will certainly be the shortest in that respect. Then the semicircle, which came from the first solution, satisfies the condition so absolutely that, once the quantity of space to be cut off is proposed, the semicircle itself is determined,

Having explained these things, let us proceed to show the use of the method handed down in those investigations of the maximum or minimum in which the formula of the maximum or minimum is not such a simple <term>integral expression<gloss>A formula representing the area under a curve or the accumulation of values</gloss></term> $\int Z dx$, of the form we have treated exclusively until now; but is instead composed of two or more formulas of this kind in any way whatsoever. 

And first indeed, if the maximum or minimum ought to be the <term>aggregate<gloss>The sum or total</gloss></term> of two or more integral formulas, say $\int Z dx + \int \Upsilon dx - \int X dx$, the operation involves no difficulty: for because the formula of the maximum or minimum is $\int dx (Z + \Upsilon - X)$, <note>Euler shows that you can simply combine the terms under a single integral sign.</note> this can be treated just like a simple integral formula, and its differential value can be assigned. The operation, however, will come down to this: that for each individual formula $\int Z dx$, $\int \Upsilon dx$, and $\int X dx$, their differential values are sought; and in their place in the formula $\int Z dx + \int \Upsilon dx - \int X dx$ they are substituted; and what arises is set equal to zero: and thus the equation satisfying the search will be obtained.

## PROPOSITION II. PROBLEM.

14. *To find the equation between x and y, such that, when x == a is set, this expression $\int Z dx \times \int \Upsilon dx$, which is the product of two integral formulas $\int Z dx$ and $\int \Upsilon dx$, becomes a maximum or a minimum.*

### SOLUTION.

Let us suppose that the equation between $x$ and $y$ has already been found, and that from it, when $x == a$ is set, the value of the Formula $\int Z dx == A$, and $\int \Upsilon dx == B$; these quantities $A$ and $B$ will be constants; and their product $AB$ will be a maximum or minimum. Now let it be assumed that at the <term>indefinite value<gloss>A variable point along the axis</gloss></term> $x$, the variable $y$ is increased by a small particle...

<meta>This page continues Euler's mathematical derivation from page 145. In the previous section, he established how to handle the sum of two integral formulas. Here, he moves to a more complex case: finding the maximum or minimum of the product of two integrals, which he labels A and B.</meta>

$n \nu$, from this variation, both quantities *A* and *B* will receive an increment; specifically, each will be increased by a <term>differential value<gloss>A very small, infinitesimal change in a mathematical quantity</gloss></term> to be defined from the preceding principles. Therefore, let *dA* be the differential value of *A*, which corresponds to the <term>integral formula<gloss>A mathematical expression representing the area under a curve or the total accumulation of values</gloss></term> $\int Z dx$, given the condition *x = a*. In a similar way, let *dB* be the differential value of *B* arising from the formula $\int Y dx$, given *x = a*. Since, therefore, by adding the particle $n \nu$ to the variable *y*, *A* becomes *A + dA* and *B* becomes *B + dB*, the product *AB* will be transformed into *AB + A dB + B dA + dA dB*. Because *AB* must be a maximum or a minimum, it is necessary that *AB = AB + A dB + B dA + dA dB*. Therefore, $0 = A dB + B dA$, because the term *dA dB* <note>In the calculus of variations, the product of two differentials (dA dB) is considered "infinitely small" compared to the other terms and is ignored to find the equilibrium point.</note> vanishes compared to the rest. From these steps, the following solution to the Problem arises: Let the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ be sought, which we call *dA*, and let *A* be the total value that the formula $\int Z dx$ obtains when *x = a*. Next, let the differential value of the formula $\int Y dx$ be sought, which we call *dB*, and let *B* denote the total value that the formula $\int Y dx$ receives when *x = a*. Once these are found, one will have this equation $0 = A dB + B dA$, in which the required relationship between *x* and *y* will be contained. <note>original: "Q. E. I." - Quod Erat Inveniendum, meaning "Which was to be found."</note>

### COROLLARY I.

15. Although the constant quantities *A* and *B* are present in the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$, they are nonetheless not arbitrary; rather, each is defined by this very equation itself. That is to say, if the values of $\int Z dx$ and $\int Y dx$ are elicited from this equation, and *x* is set to *a*, those quantities *A* and *B* ought to result; from this, they will be determined by *a* and by the remaining arbitrary constants that enter through the process of <term>integration<gloss>The mathematical process of finding the whole from the parts, often used to find areas or volumes</gloss></term>.

### COROLLARY II.

16. If *Z* and *Y* were determined functions of the quantities *x, y, p, q, r*, etc., then the differential values *dA* and *dB* will not depend on *a*; nevertheless, the quantity *a* enters into the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$. From this, the curve discovered will satisfy the requirement only for the defined value of the <term>abscissa<gloss>The horizontal coordinate (x) in a graph</gloss></term> *x = a*.

### COROLLARY III.

17. In the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$, the particle <term>nν<gloss>A notation used by Euler where 'n' represents an infinitesimal quantity and 'ν' (nu) represents the variation applied to the curve</gloss></term> will be removed entirely. Since each <term>differential value<gloss>The specific change in the total integral caused by a small variation in the function</gloss></term> $dA$ and $dB$ was produced as a result of being multiplied by $n \nu$, the $n \nu$ will again be eliminated through division. In this way, an equation relating $x$, $y$, and various constants will be produced, which satisfies the Problem.

### SCHOLIUM I.

18. No one should be troubled by the form of the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ found here, even though it bears the appearance of a standard <term>differential formula<gloss>A mathematical rule, such as the product rule, used to find the rate of change of a function</gloss></term>. Furthermore, no one should conclude from this that the <term>integral<gloss>The 'whole' or 'sum' of a differential; the inverse operation of differentiation</gloss></term> of the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ can be taken as **Constant** = $AB$. We have already explained the specific meanings we assign to the letters $A$ and $B$, as well as to the differential forms $dA$ and $dB$; from this, it can be understood that the common method of notation does not apply in this case.

I have chosen to use this method of notation, even though it differs from the usual practice, so that the connection between the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ and the formula for the maximum or minimum $\int Z dx \cdot \int \Upsilon dx$ <note>original: "$\int Z dx \cdot \int \Upsilon dx$" — Euler uses the Greek letter Upsilon ($\Upsilon$) to represent a second function</note> can be better understood. For when the maximum or minimum must correspond to the value $x = a$, let us suppose that in this case $\int Z dx$ becomes $A$ and $\int \Upsilon dx$ becomes $B$; once this is done, the maximum or minimum will be the product $AB$.

From this, the discovered equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ arises naturally, provided that $AB$ is differentiated while treating the letters $A$ and $B$ as variables. When this has been done, it must be remembered that for the differentials $dA$ and $dB$, one must use the "differential values" that correspond to the integral formulas $\int Z dx$ and $\int \Upsilon dx$, from which the constant quantities $A$ and $B$ themselves were produced. It will be helpful to have noted this connection because we shall show below that this same principle applies equally to any method of composition by which a formula for a maximum or minimum is constructed from integral formulas. In a similar way, the required equation can be obtained from the expression of the maximum or minimum itself through differentiation.

### EXAMPLE I.

19. *To find the equation between x and y such that, assuming x = a, the expression $\int y dx \times \int x dy$ becomes a maximum.* <note>original: "Invenire æquationem inter x & y, ut, posito x = a, fiat ista expressio $\int y dx \times \int x dy$ maximum."</note>

Let $\int y dx = A$, and $\int x dy = B$, assuming $x = a$. We seek the <term>differential values<gloss>The change in the value of an integral resulting from a slight variation in the shape of the curve</gloss></term> of the formulas $\int y dx$ and $\int x dy$ (or $\int x p dx$). The differential value of the formula $\int y dx$ is $n \nu dx \cdot 1$. For the formula $\int x dy$, or $\int x p dx$, it is $n \nu dx (-\frac{1}{dx} d \cdot x) = - n \nu dx$. Therefore, $dA = n \nu dx$, and $dB = - n \nu dx$. From this, the equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ will transform into this: $0 = - A \cdot n \nu dx + B \cdot n \nu dx$, or $A = B$. Thus, all equations between $x$ and $y$ satisfy the search equally well, provided that in the case where $x = a$, it happens that $\int y dx = \int x dy$. This means the <term>area of the curve<gloss>The space bounded by the curve, the x-axis, and the vertical lines representing the limits</gloss></term> must be equal to $\frac{1}{2} x y$. <note>This result implies the area under the curve must equal half the area of the rectangle formed by the coordinates x and y.</note>

### EXAMPLE II.

20. *To find the equation between x and y such that, in the case where x = a, the expression $\int y dx \times \int dx \sqrt{1+p^2}$ becomes a minimum.*

In the case $x = a$, let $\int y dx = A$, and $\int dx \sqrt{1+p^2} = B$. <note>Here, $A$ represents the area and $B$ represents the arc length or perimeter of the curve.</note> Furthermore, by taking the differential values, $dA = n \nu dx \cdot 1$, and $dB = n \nu dx (-\frac{1}{dx} d \cdot \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}) = - n \nu d \cdot \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}$. From this comes the following equation: $0 = - A \cdot n \nu d \cdot \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^2}} + B \cdot n \nu dx$, or $B dx = A d \cdot \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}$. This, when <term>integrated<gloss>The process of finding the original function from its rate of change (differential)</gloss></term>, gives $x + b = \frac{Ap}{B\sqrt{1+p^2}}$, where $\frac{A}{B}$ denotes the ratio that $\int y dx$ holds to $\int dx \sqrt{1+p^2}$ at the moment when $x = a$. For the sake of brevity, let $\frac{A}{B} = c$; then $(x+b)\sqrt{1+p^2} = cp$, and $p = \frac{x+b}{\sqrt{c^2 - (x+b)^2}} = \frac{dy}{dx}$. Therefore, after integrating this equation—

### EXAMPLE III.

21. *To find the curve in which, for a given abscissa $x = a$, this expression becomes a minimum: $\int yx dx \times \int x dx \sqrt{1 + p^2}$.* <note>original: "Invenire curvam, in qua, pro data abscissa x = a, minimum fiat hac expressio $\int y x dx \times \int x dx \sqrt{(1 + p p)}$."</note>

Assuming $x = a$, let $\int yx dx = A$, and $\int x dx \sqrt{1 + p^2} = B$. <note>Here, $p$ represents the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ or the slope of the curve.</note> Furthermore, $dA = n \nu \cdot dx \cdot x$ and $dB = - n \nu \cdot dx \cdot \frac{1}{dx} d \cdot \frac{xp}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$; from which this equation will be obtained: $B \cdot dx = A d \cdot \frac{px}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$, which when integrated gives $x^2 \pm b^2 = \frac{2Apx}{B\sqrt{1 + p^2}} = \frac{2cpx}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$, assuming $\frac{A}{B} = c$. From this, $p = \frac{x^2 \pm b^2}{\sqrt{4c^2x^2 - (x^2 \pm b^2)^2}} = \frac{dy}{dx}$, and therefore the equation for the curve will be $y = \int \frac{(x^2 \pm b^2) dx}{\sqrt{4c^2x^2 - (x^2 \pm b^2)^2}}$. Concerning this, it should be noted that if we set $b = 0$, then the equation for a Circle results, $y = \int \frac{x dx}{\sqrt{4c^2 - x^2}}$, the radius of which is $2c$.

### PROPOSITION III. PROBLEM.

23. *Find an equation between x and y of such a condition that, assuming x = a, the fraction* $\frac{\int Z \, dx}{\int Y \, dx}$ *obtains a maximum or minimum value: where Z and Y are any functions of x, y, p, q, r, etc., whether determinate or indeterminate.* <note>In modern terms, Euler is looking for the extremum of a functional defined as a ratio of two integrals.</note>

### S O L U T I O N.

In the case where $x = a$, let $\int Z \, dx = A$, and $\int Y \, dx = B$. The ratio $\frac{A}{B}$ will be a maximum or minimum provided that the relationship between $x$ and $y$ has been correctly assigned. Therefore, the fraction $\frac{A}{B}$ will be equal to this same fraction $\frac{\int Z \, dx}{\int Y \, dx}$ in the case where $x = a$, even if at some point a single ordinate <term>y|The vertical coordinate or height of the curve at a given point.</term> is increased by a small particle $n v$. But then $\int Z \, dx$ will become equal to $A$ itself, together with the differential value of the formula $\int Z \, dx$, which becomes $= dA$; and in a similar way, $\int Y \, dx$ will change into $B$ increased by the differential value of the formula $\int Y \, dx$, which becomes $= dB$. Thus, by adding the particle $n v$ to the ordinate $y$, in the case where $x = a$, the fraction $\frac{\int Z \, dx}{\int Y \, dx}$ will pass into this: $\frac{A + dA}{B + dB}$; which must be equal to the fraction

### COROLLARY I.

24. ### COROLLARY II.

25. Although two unknown constants $A$ and $B$ seem to be present in this discovered equation $B dA = A dB$, they can nevertheless be combined into one. For by setting $\frac{A}{B} = C$, it will be $dA = C dB$; and once the equation is found, the value of $C$ itself will be determined by substituting the value $a$ in place of $x$.

### SCHOLION

<note>A scholion is an explanatory note or commentary used to clarify the relationship between different mathematical results.</note>

26. If the solutions of this and the preceding Problem are compared with each other, a great agreement will be detected between them. For if the product <term>factum<gloss>The result of multiplication</gloss></term> $\int Z dx \times \int Y dx$ must be a maximum or minimum, that equation $0 = A dB + B dA$ arose; but if the quotient <term>quotus<gloss>The result of division</gloss></term> $\frac{\int Z dx}{\int Y dx}$ must be either a maximum or a minimum, this equation $0 = A dB - B dA$ was found; in both cases, however, the letters $A, B$ and $dA, dB$ retain the same values. Therefore, since $A$ and $B$ are constant quantities, both equations differ only by the sign of the constant; for by setting $\frac{A}{B} = C$, in the former case we have $dA = - C dB$, and in the latter case $dA = + C dB$. From this, almost the same solution will emerge for both cases, because the whole difference will be located only in the sign of the constant quantity $C$. Therefore, if the equation between $x$ and $y$ has been found, which

Indeed, the very nature of the matter demands this agreement: for if $\frac{\int Z dx}{\int Y dx}$ is a maximum, then by that very fact $\frac{\int Y dx}{\int Z dx}$ will be a minimum, and vice versa; thus it is necessary that the same solution satisfies both questions. The former equation, $x = b + c + t$, cannot hold; because, since $dx = dt$, it is impossible for $\frac{\int x dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\int dt \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$ or $(b + c + \frac{\int t dt \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\int dt \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}) = c$. 

Therefore, let $x = c - b - t$, in which case the abscissas descend downward from some higher point on the axis $AC$: and it would have to be $\frac{\int x dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\int dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}$ or $c - b - \frac{\int t dt \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\int dt \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} = c$, which likewise cannot happen; from which it must be concluded that no one portion satisfies the condition more than any other. 

This, however, seems to arise from the fact that the <term>Catenary<note>The shape a hanging chain takes under its own weight.</note></term> has two <term>conjugate parts<note>Symmetrical branches or sections of a curve that mirror each other, much like the two sides of a hyperbola.</note></term> just like a conic Hyperbola, and from this it can always be that $\frac{\int x dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}{\int dx \sqrt{(1 + p^2)}} = 0$, which is the minimum value. This can be more clearly confirmed from the found value $p = \frac{b}{\sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)}}$, whence it becomes $\sqrt{(1 + p^2)} = \frac{c - x}{\sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)}} = (c - x) r$, having set for the sake of brevity $r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)}}$. 

It would therefore be necessary in the sought case for $\frac{\int (c - x) xr dx}{\int (c - x) r dx} = c$ or $\int (c - x)^2 r dx = 0$; and since this must <term>evanesce<note>original: "evanescere"; to disappear or become zero.</note></term> in the case where $x = 0$, it ought to vanish in another case as well. But the integral is:
$\int (c - x)^2 r dx = \int \frac{(c - x)^2 dx}{\sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)}} = -\frac{1}{2} (c - x) \sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)} - \frac{b^2}{2} \log \frac{c - x + \sqrt{((c - x)^2 - b^2)}}{c + \sqrt{(c^2 - b^2)}} + \frac{1}{2} c \sqrt{(c^2 - b^2)}$, which expression, since it was once equal to $0$, will afterwards continually increase and not de[crease] <note>The text cuts off mid-word "descendet" (decrease) or "desinet" (cease).</note> because $(c - x)^2$ is perpetually <term>positive<note>original: "affirmativum"; Euler uses this to mean the value is always greater than zero because it is squared.</note></term>.

30. *To find a curve in which, for a given **abscissa** <term>abscissa<note>The horizontal coordinate, typically denoted as $x$.</note></term> $x = a$, this expression* $\frac{\int y x d x}{\int d x \sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$ *is a maximum or a minimum.*

By setting $x = a$, let $\int y x d x = A$, and $\int d x \sqrt{(1 + p p)} = B$. Now, the **differential value** <term>differential value<note>In the calculus of variations, this refers to the small change or variation in the value of an integral.</note></term> of the formula $\int y x d x$ is $d A = n v . d x . x = n v . x d x$, and the differential value of the formula $\int d x \sqrt{(1 + p p)}$ is $d B = - n v . d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$ <note>Here, $p$ represents the slope of the curve, $dy/dx$.</note>. Therefore, since $B d A = A d B$, we will have this equation: $B x d x = - d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$, or $x d x = - c^2 d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$, by setting $A = B c^2$. From this, by integrating, we obtain $x^2 = C - \frac{2 c^2 p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$, and from there $p = \frac{b c - x x}{\sqrt{(4 c^4 - (b c - x x)^2)}} = \frac{d y}{d x}$; which provides $y = \int \frac{(b c - x x) d x}{\sqrt{(4 c^4 - (b c - x x)^2)}}$, which is the general equation for the **Elastic Curve** <term>Elastic Curve<note>Latin: *curva Elastica*. This is the shape formed by a thin, flexible rod (like a metal spring) when it is bent by forces applied at its ends.</note></term>. 

This curve has the property that the **radius of curvature** <term>radius of curvature<note>Latin: *radius osculi*. This is the radius of the circle that best fits the curve at any given point; a smaller radius means a sharper bend.</note></term> is everywhere inversely proportional to the abscissa $x$: this is evident from the equation $x d x = - c^2 d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}$, which becomes $\frac{d x}{d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}} = \frac{c^2}{x}$, and since $\frac{- d x}{d . \frac{p}{\sqrt{(1 + p p)}}} = \frac{d x (1 + p p)^{3/2}}{d p}$ is the radius of curvature in the curve. Furthermore, so much of this curve, calculated from the beginning, satisfies the condition in which $\int y x d x$ will be...

## PROPOSITION IV. PROBLEM.

31. *To find an equation between two variables* x *&* y *so arranged that, when the variable* x $= a$ *is set, the expression* W *becomes a maximum or minimum, where* W *is any function of the integral formulas* $\int Z dx, \int Y dx, \int X dx$, *&c. in which* Z, Y, X *&c. denote any functions of* x, y, p, q, *&c. whether they be definite or indefinite.*

### S O L U T I O N.

Let us assume that a suitable equation between x & y has already been found, and when $x = a$ is set, it results that $\int Z dx = A; \int Y dx = B; \int X dx$ $= C$ &c. Once these values are substituted into the expression *W*, a maximum or minimum will truly be obtained. Now, if the other variable y is assumed to be increased at one single location by a small increment $n \nu$ <note>Euler uses $n \nu$ to represent a virtual displacement or variation of the curve at a point, a foundational concept in the calculus of variations.</note>, and the resulting changes in each individual formula $\int Z dx, \int Y dx, \int X dx$ &c. are introduced, the same value for *W* must be produced <note>Because at a maximum or minimum, a tiny change in the input results in no change to the output—the slope is zero.</note>. But from that small increment $n \nu$, the formulas $\int Z dx, \int Y dx$, and $\int X dx$ &c. will each be increased by their own **differential values** <term>differential values<note>Known today as "variations" (denoted by $\delta$). Euler is explaining that a change in the curve's shape ripples through every integral that depends on that curve.</note></term>. If, therefore, the differential value of the formula $\int Z dx$ is set $= dA$, that of the formula $\int Y dx = dB$, and that of the formula $\int X dx = dC$, &c., then in place of the quantities *A, B, C,* &c., these increased values $A + dA, B + dB, C + dC$ &c. will arise from the small increment $n \nu$. When these are substituted into *W*, they must produce the same value which *A, B, C,* &c. produced. Let us assume that, with $A + dA, B + dB, C +$ $dC$ &c. substituted in place of $\int Z dx, \int Y dx, \int X dx$ &c., there results *W* $+ dW$; it will be that $W + dW = W$, and therefore $dW = 0$. Moreover, this value $dW$, as is clear from the nature of differentiation, is found—

->ON THE USE OF THE METHOD<-

...[this will be found] if the quantity *W*, after substituting the letters *A, B, C*, etc., into it in place of the integral formulas, is differentiated, with these very letters *A, B, C*, etc., treated as variables themselves; and in this differential <note>In this context, the "differential" refers to the variation or the small change in the expression.</note>, let *dA, dB, dC*, etc., designate the differential values <note>These represent the "variations" of the integrals $\int Zdx, \int Ydx, \int Xdx$ respectively.</note> of the corresponding formulas $\int Zdx, \int Ydx, \int Xdx$, etc. Therefore, if the differential of the proposed quantity *W* taken in this sense is set equal to zero, it will give the desired equation between *x* and *y*. **Which was to be found.** <note>original: "Q. E. I." (*Quod Erat Inveniendum*), a standard concluding phrase in mathematical proofs.</note>

### COROLLARY I.

32. If, therefore, an expression *W* is proposed which is a function of integral formulas $\int Zdx, \int Ydx, \int Xdx$, etc., and which must be a maximum or minimum for a determined value of *x* = *a*: then let the letters *A, B, C*, etc., be written in place of the formulas $\int Zdx, \int Ydx, \int Xdx$, etc. Once this is done, let the expression *W* be differentiated, with only these letters *A, B, C*, etc., being treated as variables, and let the differential be set equal to 0.

### COROLLARY II.

33. In this differential, in which the letters *A, B, C*, etc., will appear with their differentials *dA, dB, dC*, etc., the letters *A, B, C*, etc., will denote respectively the values that the formulas $\int Zdx, \int Ydx, \int Xdx$, etc., take when *x* = *a* is set; however, the differentials *dA, dB, dC*, etc., express the differential values of those same integral formulas corresponding to the <term>abscissa<gloss>The horizontal or x-coordinate in a graph.</gloss></term> *x* = *a*.

### COROLLARY III.

34. From the preceding, however, it is clear that if *Z, Y, X*, etc., were <term>definite functions<gloss>Functions where the value depends only on the current coordinates and their derivatives at a specific point.</gloss></term> of the quantities *x, y, p, q,* etc., then the differential values *dA, dB, dC*, etc., do not depend on the value *a*: on the contrary, if *Z, Y, X*, etc., were <term>indefinite functions<gloss>Functions that might include further integrals or quantities whose values depend on the entire path of the curve.</gloss></term>, then the differential values *dA, dB, dC*, etc., must simultaneously depend on the value *a*.

36. However, to develop this equation further, taking the <term>differentials</term> <note>Differential: an infinitesimal change in a variable quantity.</note> gives:

-> — b dp / p² √(1 + p²) = e^{n ∫ dx √(1 + p²)} dx <-

This expression, when multiplied by √(1 + p²) and integrated, gives n b / p + c = e^{n ∫ dx √(1 + p²)}. When this <term>exponential value</term> <note>Exponential value: the value of the quantity involving $e$ raised to a power.</note> is substituted back into the previous equation, it will yield:

-> n b dx / p + c dx = — b dp / p² √(1 + p²) <-

or

-> dx = — b dp / p (nb + cp) √(1 + p²) <-

A more convenient <term>equation</term> arises if we set ∫ dx √(1 + p²) = s, where s will be the <term>arc of the curve</term> <note>Arc of the curve: the distance measured along the path of the curve, often called arc length.</note>, assuming x and y are <term>normal coordinates</term> <note>Normal coordinates: standard Cartesian coordinates (x, y) meeting at right angles.</note>. Therefore, we will have this equation:

-> n b + cp = e^{ns} p <-

which, when multiplied by dx (since dy = p dx), transforms into this:

-> n b dx + c dy = e^{ns} dy <-

Since, however, with the assumption that $x = 0$, the arc $s$ <note>The variable $s$ denotes the arc length of the curve.</note> must vanish <note>Original: "evanescere"; in this context, it means the value becomes zero at the starting point.</note>, it is necessary that in this case $\frac{nb}{p} + c = 0$; from here, therefore, either the constant $c$ will be determined from the given beginning of the curve, or conversely, the position of the first tangent will become known from $c$. Furthermore, if we contemplate this question more carefully, we shall find it already contained in a certain Example in Section 45 of the preceding Chapter. Moreover, we treated that question, which encompasses this one, above in Section 45 of the preceding Chapter, where this very case may be seen as an addition. However, once a comparison is made, the greatest agreement will be seen between the various solutions of the same Problem that can indeed be attempted.

## SCHOLION II.

42. With these Chapters, therefore, we have completely concluded that part of the **Method of maxima and minima** <note>This refers to the Calculus of Variations, a field Euler was pioneered.</note> adapted for finding **curved lines**, which we have called **absolute**. In this part, a curved line is typically sought that possesses, for a given value of the **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal $x$-coordinate on a graph</term> or another **variable $x$**, some indeterminate expression that is a maximum or minimum. For that expression, which must be a maximum or minimum, will either be a single **integral formula** of the form $\int Z dx$—where $Z$ is any function of the variables $x, y, p, q,$ etc., whether **definite or indefinite**, for which cases we provided the Method in the preceding Chapters—or that maximum or minimum expression will contain within itself several such integral formulas, being a function of two or more integral formulas. For this latter case, the appropriate Method has been set out in this Chapter and illustrated with Examples. 

The entire Method presented here relies on finding **differential values**, which apply to each integral formula—whether the formulas themselves must be a maximum or minimum, or are merely contained within the maximum or minimum expression. Therefore, the entire method of solution is reduced to those **Cases** that we represented collectively in § 7 of this Chapter. Anyone, therefore, who keeps those cases in mind or has them ready at hand will be prepared to solve all problems of this type with ease. Indeed, the cases enumerated there do not only constitute the **absolute** Method of maxima and minima; they will also suffice for the other **relative** Method, which we will take up in the following pages. From this, the great utility of those cases in both Methods will be clearly seen. We shall complete this treatment in two chapters: in the first, we will assign a certain **common property** to all the curves from which the desired curve must be extracted; in the second, we will assign several such properties. <note>This is a preview of "isoperimetric" problems, where a curve is found that maximizes one property (like area) while keeping another property (like perimeter) constant.</note>

# CHAPTER V.

## The method for finding, among all curves endowed with the same property, that which enjoys the property of a maximum or minimum.

### D E F I N I T I O N.

1. A **common property** is an **integral formula**, or an indefinite expression, which applies equally to all curves from which the required one must be determined.

### S C H O L I O N I.

2. Up to this point, we have presented the **absolute method** of maxima and minima. In that method, among every possible curve corresponding to the same **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal $x$-coordinate on a graph</term>, we typically sought the one that would enjoy some specific maximum or minimum property. Now, however, we proceed to the **relative method**. In this method, we will teach how to determine a single line endowed with a maximum or minimum property, chosen not from absolutely all lines corresponding to the same abscissa, but only from those curves—innumerable though they may be—which share one or more proposed properties. In this Chapter, we shall first consider the countless curves corresponding to the same abscissa that have one specific property in common; from these, we shall investigate the single line in which any indefinite expression obtains its maximum or minimum value. In this field, the **Isoperimetric Problem** <note>original: "Problema Isoperimetricum." From the Greek for "same perimeter," this refers to problems where the length of the curve is held constant while maximizing another property, like area.</note> is especially famous. Publicly proposed at the beginning of this century <note>Euler is referring to the famous challenge issued by Jakob Bernoulli in 1697 regarding the "isoperimetric" curves.</note>, it required finding, among all curves of the same length corresponding to the same abscissa, the one which possessed some maximum or minimum property. Later, however, this question was understood in a broader sense, so that this determina-

<meta>catchword: -tion</meta>

the determination would be made not only among all curves of the same length, but also among all curves endowed with any other common property; which is the very question we have undertaken to treat in this Chapter. Therefore, since a curve must be chosen, not from absolutely all curves corresponding to the same **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate (x-value) on a graph</term>, but from those—innumerable though they may be—in which some proposed property applies equally, this property must be considered above all else; we indicate this here by the name of **common property**. Therefore, this common property, such as the equality of the length of the curves, must affect all intermediate points, and for this reason it will be an **indefinite function** <note>In Euler’s time, this referred to a quantity whose value depends on the entire path or shape of the curve, rather than just a single point.</note> which is determined not from the position of a single element of the curve, but from the position of the whole curve. For this reason, a common property of this kind will be either a simple indefinite integral formula, or an expression comprising several such integral formulas. It will therefore be structured in exactly the same way as the formula or expression for the maximum or minimum itself. Consequently, the same categories and divisions that we previously established and treated regarding the expression of the maximum or minimum will apply equally to the common property.

## COROLLARY I.

3. If, therefore, a common property is proposed, which we call *B*, then all curves must be considered which contain the same value for *B* given the same abscissa; and from among these, that curve must be defined which possesses the maximum or minimum.

## COROLLARY II.

4. In problems belonging to this category, two things must be given: the common property *B*, and the expression for the maximum or minimum *A*. Once these are given, one must define, among all curves containing the same value *B* for a given abscissa, that which has the maximum or minimum value of *A* for that same abscissa.

<summary>Euler generalizes the isoperimetric problem, explaining that "common properties" (constraints) are expressed as integral formulas just like the properties being maximized or minimized. He establishes that for these problems, both the constraint (B) and the target property (A) must be defined.</summary>

## COROLLARY III.

5. Not only do there exist infinite curves which, for a given **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or x-value on a graph</term>, possess the same common property, but they also exist in an infinite variety of ways. For if any curve is chosen at will, it will have a specific, determined value for the proposed common property; however, besides that one, there will be countless other curves containing the very same value for that common property given the same abscissa.

## COROLLARY IV.

6. Therefore, once any **indefinite expression** <note>original: "expressione quacunque indefinita"; in this context, an integral formula that depends on the path of the curve.</note> is proposed, countless categories of infinite curves will be produced; any one of these categories encompasses within itself infinite curves which, for the same given abscissa, contain the same value for that expression.

## COROLLARY V.

7. Since, therefore, there are infinite categories, each of which comprises countless curved lines for which the expression proposed as the common property applies equally; in each and every category there will be one curve which, compared to the remaining curves of the same category, contains the *other* expression <note>The "other" expression refers to the second property one wishes to maximize or minimize, such as area or time of descent.</note> in the maximum or minimum degree.

## COROLLARY VI.

8. Since, then, from any category, one curve is found endowed with the property of the maximum or minimum; there will altogether be found infinite curves of this sort satisfying the requirement, any of which will be so constructed that, among all other curves enjoying the same common property, it is endowed with the maximum or minimum property.

### SCHOLIUM II.
<note>Scholium: a scholarly note or explanatory commentary intended to clarify a preceding point.</note>

9. All these points will be further clarified if we define the **common property** <note>original: "proprietatem communem"; this refers to a fixed constraint shared by a group of curves, such as having the same total length.</note> about which we have spoken generally until now. Let the common property, then, be a formula expressing the length of the arc of a curve, and let the expression for the maximum or minimum be **∫ Z dx**; so that, among all curves having equal arc lengths corresponding to the same **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or x-value on a graph</term>, that curve must be determined in which the value **∫ Z dx** becomes a maximum or minimum for that same abscissa.

It is obvious, however, that not only are there infinite curved lines of equal length for the same abscissa, but this can also occur in infinite ways. For if the common abscissa is set as **a**, and any length **c** is taken that is greater than **a**, infinite lines—both straight and curved—can be presented, each of which has a length equal to **c**; and among these, one can be identified in which **∫ Z dx** is a maximum or minimum. However, in place of **c**, infinite quantities can be selected, as there is no other condition except that **c > a** <note>The arc length "c" must be greater than the straight-line distance "a" for a curve to exist between two points.</note>. Each value chosen for **c** will yield one curve endowed with the maximum or minimum property. Consequently, for the infinite values of **c**, infinite curved lines satisfying the question will be found. 

Yet the Question should not be considered **indeterminate** <note>original: "indeterminata"; meaning a problem with no definite or single solution.</note> for this reason: for the solution itself, which provides infinite satisfying curves, is to be interpreted in such a way that every one of these discovered curves possesses the maximum or minimum value of the formula **∫ Z dx** compared to all other curves of the same length. Moreover, it is clear that what we have demonstrated here regarding equal arcs of curves must also hold for any other formula or **indeterminate expression** <note>original: "expressione indeterminata"; a variable integral formula that depends on the path of the curve.</note>. Thus, if among all curves which contain the same value for the formula **∫ Y dx** for a given abscissa **x = a**, that curve is required in which **∫ Z dx** is a maximum or minimum, then indeed infinite satisfying lines will be found. However, these will differ from one another in such a way that any one of them, compared to all other possible curved lines sharing the same value for the formula **∫ Y dx**, will contain the maximum or minimum value of the formula **∫ Z dx**.

## PROPOSITION I. THEOREM.

10. *Whatever curve, among all possible curves corresponding to the same abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or x-value on a graph</term>, possesses the property of some proposed maximum or minimum; that same curve will simultaneously, among all curves endowed with any common property shared with it, possess that same property of the maximum or minimum.*

### PROOF.

Let the expression for the maximum or minimum be **A**, and the common property be **B**; both **A** and **B** will be either an indefinite integral formula, or an expression composed of several such formulas. Let us now suppose that a curve has been found which, among all possible curves corresponding to the same abscissa, contains the maximum or minimum of expression **A**; that curve will contain a certain specific value of expression **B**. However, besides this curve, there will be countless others to which the same value of expression **B** applies; and all these countless curves are already included within that total set of all possible curves from which the one where expression **A** is a maximum or minimum was identified. Therefore, since this curve possesses the proposed maximum or minimum property among *all* possible curves, it will also possess the maximum or minimum value of expression **A** among those infinite curves that share the common expression **B** with it. Which was to be demonstrated. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum)</note>

### COROLLARY I.

11. Therefore, the absolute method <note>The "absolute method" refers to finding a maximum or minimum without external constraints like a fixed perimeter.</note> also serves for resolving problems of the relative method <note>The "relative method" involves constraints, such as finding the largest area for a fixed perimeter.</note>, provided it always yields a curve that satisfies the conditions. Nevertheless, it does not grant a complete solution. <note>Euler means that the absolute method only finds one specific case, whereas the relative method needs to find a family of solutions for every possible value of the constraint B.</note>

### COROLLARY II.

12. Thus, the curve which, among all others, has the expression **A**

maximum or minimum, it will be one of those infinite curves, each of which, among all others sharing the common property *B*, possesses the same maximum or minimum value of expression *A*.

### COROLLARY III.

13. Therefore, the solution to the problem in which—among all curves endowed with the same common property *B*—one seeks that curve in which expression *A* is a maximum or minimum, will be more widely applicable than if one were to search absolutely among all curves for the one in which *A* is a maximum or minimum. That solution will include the absolute case within itself as a special case.

### PROPOSITION II. PROBLEM.

14. *To outline in general the method of solving problems in which, among all curves sharing a certain common property, that one is required which possesses the property of some proposed maximum or minimum.*

### SOLUTION.

<margin>Fig. 15.</margin>
Every maximum or minimum is characterized by the fact that, when an infinitely small change is made, its value is not changed at all. <note>Euler is describing the fundamental principle of the calculus of variations: at an extreme point, the "derivative" or variation is zero.</note> For this reason, if the curve *az* has a maximum or minimum value for expression *A* among all curves corresponding to the same <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or x-value</term> *AZ* which share a common property *B*, it will retain that same value if an infinitely small change is introduced, provided that the common property *B* is not disturbed. To achieve this, however, it is not sufficient (as we did previously) to increase a single <term>applicata: the vertical coordinate or y-value</term> (for instance, *Nn*) by an infinitely small particle *nv*. Since a total change made in this way is determined by only a single condition, it cannot be made to ensure both that the common property *B* remains equally applicable to the changed curve and that the expression *A* for the maximum or minimum is satisfied. For this reason, a change must be applied involving two condition—

<meta>catchword: —s [nibus]</meta>

<summary>Euler explains that constrained optimization problems (relative maxima/minima) are broader than absolute ones. He establishes that to find such a curve, one must vary at least two vertical coordinates to satisfy both the constraint and the extremum condition.</summary>
<keywords>constrained optimization, calculus of variations, abscissa, ordinate, infinitely small change, mathematical proof</keywords>

--- Page 187 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Solution" to Proposition II started on the previous page. It explains the core technical method for solving "isoperimetric" or constrained optimization problems, where a curve must satisfy a shared property (like a specific length) while maximizing or minimizing another property (like the area beneath it).</meta>

<page-num>177</page-num>
<header>RELATIVE MAXIMA AND MINIMA.</header>

...be determined by [these conditions]; this will be obtained if two <term>ordinates: the vertical $y$-coordinates of the points on the curve</term> $Nn$ and $Oo$ are increased by infinitely small particles $n\nu$ and $o\omega$. <note>Euler is introducing the "method of variations." To keep a constraint (like the total length of the curve) constant while changing the curve's shape, he must adjust at least two points ($n$ and $o$) simultaneously so that the change in one offsets the change in the other.</note> If, therefore, the curve is conceived to be changed in this way, two things must first be achieved: that the common property applies equally to the original curve and the changed one; and second, the expression of the maximum or minimum must retain the same value in both curves. The first condition will be met if the differential value of the expression containing the common property is investigated—arising from the displacement of the two points $n$ and $o$ to $\nu$ and $\omega$—and that value is set to vanish. The second condition will be satisfied if, in a similar way, the differential value of the expression which must be a maximum or minimum is sought—arising from the two particles $n\nu$ and $o\omega$—and is set equal to zero. In this way, two equations will be obtained, one from the common property and the other from the expression of the maximum or minimum; each will have a form such as $S \cdot n\nu + T \cdot o\omega = 0$, in which $S$ and $T$ will be quantities pertaining to the curve. From these two equations, the particles $n\nu$ and $o\omega$ can be eliminated; and the resulting equation will describe the sought curve which, among all others endowed with the same common property $B$, possesses a maximum or minimum value for expression $A$. <note>original: "Q. E. I." — Quod Erat Inveniendum: Which was to be found.</note>

### COROLLARY I.

15. The solution of problems of this kind is therefore also reduced to finding differential values. However, these differential values differ from those we gave previously in this: they must be defined from the displacement of *two* points of the curve.

### COROLLARY II.

16. Therefore, in any such problem, it is necessary to investigate two such differential values arising from the two particles $n\nu$ and $o\omega$: one for the common property, and the other for the expression of the maximum or minimum.

<header>ON THE METHOD</header>

### COROLLARY III.

17. Once these two differential values have been found for any given problem, each must be set equal to zero. From this, two equations will be generated which, by eliminating the assumed small changes <note>original: "particulis," referring to the infinitesimal displacements $n\nu$ and $o\omega$ mentioned on the previous page</note> $n\nu$ and $o\omega$, will yield a single equation expressing the nature of the curve being sought.

### COROLLARY IV.

18. If, therefore, among all curves corresponding to the same <term>abscissa: the horizontal x-coordinate along the axis</term> that are equally endowed with a common property $B$, we seek that one in which the expression $A$ becomes a maximum or minimum, then the differential values of both expressions $A$ and $B$ arising from the two small changes $n\nu$ and $o\omega$ must be found and set equal to zero. If the particles $n\nu$ and $o\omega$ are then eliminated from these two equations, the resulting equation for the curve being sought will emerge.

### COROLLARY V.

19. Thus, in this operation, both expressions $A$ and $B$ are treated in exactly the same way; it does not even matter which one represents the common property and which represents the maximum or minimum. From this it is clear that the same solution must be produced even if the expressions $A$ and $B$ are swapped with one another.

### COROLLARY VI.

20. Therefore, the same solution will hold regardless of whether one seeks the curve that makes $A$ a maximum or minimum among all curves sharing property $B$, or conversely, whether one seeks the curve that makes $B$ a maximum or minimum among all curves sharing property $A$. <note>This is a fundamental principle in optimization known as "reciprocity." For example, the shape that encloses the maximum area for a fixed perimeter is the same shape that has the minimum perimeter for a fixed area: the circle.</note>

### SCHOLIUM.

21. It is spontaneously evident by the very nature of the solution that both expressions **A** and **B**, although they signify entirely different things when viewed in themselves, are interchangeable with each other. For if we consider the two small particles *n ν* and *o ω* <note>original: "particulas n ν & o ω," referring to the infinitesimal changes or "variations" made to the curve's shape</note>, by which the <term>ordinates: the vertical y-coordinates of the curve</term> *N n* and *O o* are increased; first, it is necessary that they be so compared that the common property **B** obtains the same value in the curve itself as in the changed one; namely, the common property **B** must apply equally to the curve *a m n o p z* and to *a m ν ω p z*: then, in the same way, it must be brought about through those same particles *n ν* and *o ω* that the expression **A**, which ought to be a maximum or minimum, receives the same value for the curve *a m n o p z* as for *a m ν ω p z*. And so, both the common property and the nature of the maximum or minimum introduce plainly the same condition into the calculation; from which it is manifest that both given expressions, of which one contains the common property and the other the ratio of the maximum or minimum, can be swapped and interchanged with one another without affecting the Solution. Therefore, for this reason, in the Solution of Problems of this kind, it is sufficient to know those two expressions; nor is it necessary for completing the Solution to know which signifies the common property or the maximum or minimum. Thus if, among all curves equal in length, that one is sought which encompasses the maximum area; the same curve is found which comes forth if, among all curves enclosing equal areas, that one is sought which is the shortest, or has the minimum length. These things hold true if the nature of the maximum or minimum being sought is such that its **differential value is = 0** <note>In modern terms, this means the first derivative is zero at a peak or valley</note>. However, we have already observed above that there are two kinds of maxima and minima: in one, the differential value is = 0, but in the other it is = $\infty$ <note>original: "$\infty$" or infinity</note>. Here, however, we only contemplate maxima and minima of the former kind; for, in this relative Method, the latter kind cannot take place at all. For if the differential value which corresponds to the expression of the maximum or minimum is set as infinitely large, then the equation for the curve is found from this alone; and therefore the common property does not enter into the calculation. Next, because terms of two types occur in these differential values—one involving the particle $n \nu$ and the other the particle $o \omega$—the differential value of any indeterminate expression of this kind will have the form $n \nu \cdot I + o \omega \cdot K$. Regarding this form, it is first manifest that the former member $n \nu \cdot I$ is the differential value of that same expression which arises if only the particle $n \nu$ is considered. Therefore, $n \nu \cdot I$ will be that very differential value which we taught how to define above for any given expression; so that this member may be displayed for any indeterminate expression using the rules handed down previously. 

As for the other member $o \omega \cdot K$, because the individual terms in which $o \omega$ is present always correspond to the quantities following those to which similar terms involving the particle $n \nu$ correspond, it is clear that the quantity $K$ will be the value which the quantity $I$ takes on in the next subsequent position. Therefore, $K = I' = I + d I$. <note>In Euler's notation, the prime (') or adding $dI$ indicates the value of the function at the very next point along the horizontal axis.</note> Wherefore, since we can assign the member $n \nu \cdot I$ from the rules already given above, the other member $o \omega \cdot K = o \omega (I + d I)$ will henceforth be known from it. Let $V$ therefore be any indeterminate expression whose differential value arising from the two particles $n \nu$ and $o \omega$ must be defined. Let us suppose its differential value arising from the single particle $n \nu$ to be $= n \nu \cdot I$; the differential value which arises from both particles $n \nu$ and $o \omega$ will be $= n \nu \cdot I + o \omega \cdot I'$, or $= n \nu \cdot I + o \omega (I + d I)$; which therefore can be easily assigned by the help of the rules given above.

sponding <note>Completing "corresponding" from the previous page.</note>, let that one be sought in which the expression *V* obtains a maximum or minimum value; for that, we have the equation *d A* = 0; where *d A* denotes the differential value <note>In modern calculus, this "differential value" is called the "variation." It represents how the total value of an integral changes when the shape of the curve is slightly altered.</note> of the expression *V*.

### COROLLARY V.

32. To find a maximum under a constraint, you add the variation of the target (A) to the variation of the constraint (B), each scaled by a constant.</note>

### COROLLARY VI.

33. It is therefore clear that the curve which, among absolutely all curves, has *V* as a maximum or minimum—the equation for which is *d A* = 0—is contained within the equation *α d A* + *β d B* = 0, which expresses the curve that, among all those sharing the same common property *W*, has *V* as a maximum or minimum.

### COROLLARY VII.

34. Therefore, in the very first equation which the Solution provides, *α d A* + *β d B* = 0, there is already one arbitrary constant; this constant must be determined by the requirement that the value of expression *W* obtains its given value. <note>The constants α and β allow the solution to be tuned so it fits the specific "given" value of the constraint, such as a specific length of a string.</note>

### COROLLARY VIII.

35. Thus, the problem can be solved so that, among all curves corresponding to the same abscissa *A Z*, in which the expression *W* obtains the same given value, that curve is defined in which the value of *V* itself is maximum or minimum.

For first, it appears—as we have already demonstrated above—that the solution will be the same whether, among all curves endowed with the common property *W*, one seeks the curve which has *V* as a maximum or minimum; or conversely, among all curves endowed with the common property *V*, that one is required in which *W* is a maximum or minimum. <note>This is the principle of reciprocity: for example, the shape that encloses the greatest area for a fixed perimeter (a circle) is also the shape that has the smallest perimeter for a fixed area.</note> Next, it is also understood that the question can be proposed in such a way that its solution pertains to the absolute method of maxima and minima; for the proposed problem agrees with this one: where, among all curves whatsoever related to the same abscissa *AZ*, that one is required in which the expression $a V + b W$ is a maximum or minimum. If a second-order <term>secundi gradus: a differential equation involving second-order derivatives, like acceleration.</term> differential equation is found, then the found curve will be determined by two points; it is, however, consistent and accepted practice that the endpoints of the curve itself, *a* and *z*, be prescribed, and in these cases the Problem will be determined if that condition is added: that the sought curve be contained between the given limits *a* and *z*. If, however, a fourth-order differential equation results, then the satisfying curve will be determined by four points assigned at will; it will therefore be appropriate to define these such that, besides the endpoints *a* and *z*, the position of the **tangents** at these endpoints is simultaneously prescribed. If one arrives at a sixth-order differential equation, then the curve will be determined by any six points: in their place, however, there can be prescribed first both endpoints *a* and *z*, then the position of the tangents at these endpoints, and thirdly the curvature <note>original: "curvedo"</note> at these very locations or the magnitude of the **radius of osculation** <term>radius osculi: the radius of a circle that perfectly touches and matches the curve's bend at a specific point.</term>. These things having been noted, it will be understood from the Solution itself what kind of condition ought to be added to the proposition of any Problem so that it may become fully determined: and this reminder has its place not only here, but also in the **Absolute Method** and the remaining **Relative Method**.

->SCHOLION III.<-

39. A distinction of the greatest importance is also especially to be noted here, from which we took the primary division of the treatment in the **Absolute Method**. It consists, moreover, in the manner in which the found curve satisfies the Question. For it can happen that any portion of it, referred to an indefinite **abscissa** <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or distance along the x-axis.</term>, may enjoy the required property; then there are also cases in which only that portion which corresponds to the defined abscissa *AZ* = *a* satisfies the condition of the Problem. This latter case happens if this quantity *a* either does not enter at all into the equation which the Solution provides, or can be absorbed into the arbitrary quantities $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

->EXAMPLE I.<-

40. *Among all curves related to the abscissa $AZ$, in which the formula $\int y x dx$ <note>This integral represents the moment of the area under the curve with respect to the y-axis.</note> holds the same value, find that one in which the value of the formula $\int yy dx$ <note>This integral is related to the moment of inertia or the volume of a solid of revolution.</note> is a minimum.*

Therefore, the common property will be $W = \int xy dx$, of which—since $d(xy) = y dx + x dy$—the differential value <term>valor differentialis: in Euler’s method, this refers to the expression derived from varying the integral to find its extremum.</term> is $= n\nu \cdot dx \cdot x$. The formula of the maximum or minimum is $V = \int yy dx$, of which—since $d(yy) = 2 y dy$—the differential value is $= n\nu \cdot dx \cdot 2y$. Therefore, having performed the division by $n\nu \cdot dx$, this equation will be obtained: $\alpha x + 2 \beta y = 0$; from which it is clear that a straight line passing through $A$ and forming any angle with the axis $AZ$ satisfies the Question. And because the length of the abscissa $AZ = a$ does not enter into the calculation, any portion of this straight line will satisfy it equally. But if it is required that for a given abscissa $AZ = a$, the formula $\int y x dx$ obtains a given value, say $B$; then, because $y = mx$ <note>Substituting the linear equation into the integral to find the slope.</note>, it becomes $\int y x dx = \frac{1}{3} mx^3$; and therefore $\frac{1}{3} ma^3 = B$; from which the position of the straight line

### EXAMPLE II.

41. *Among all curves of the same length connecting points $a$ and $z$, find that one which encloses the maximum or minimum area $aAZz$.*

Since the common property is the length of the arc $= \int dx \sqrt{1 + p^2}$ <note>Euler uses the variable $p$ to represent the slope of the curve, $dy/dx$.</note>; its differential value will be $= -\nu \cdot d \left( \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+pp}} \right)$. Then, the formula for the maximum or minimum is the area $\int y dx$, whose differential value is $\nu \cdot dx$. From this, for the sought curve, the following equation is obtained: $dx = b \cdot d \left( \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+pp}} \right)$, and by integrating, $x + c = \frac{bp}{\sqrt{1+pp}}$. Consequently, $p = \frac{x+c}{\sqrt{b^2 - (x+c)^2}} = \frac{dy}{dx}$. From here, by integrating once more, it becomes $y = f \pm \sqrt{b^2 - (x+c)^2}$, or $b^2 = (y - f)^2 + (x + c)^2$; which is the general equation for a **Circle**. For this reason, any arc of a Circle drawn through the points $a$ and $z$ will, among all other curved lines of the same length, enclose either the maximum or minimum area $aAZz$. However, a circular arc of a given length can be positioned between the boundaries $a$ and $z$ in two ways: one in which it turns its concavity toward the axis $AZ$, and the other in which it turns its convexity. In the first case, it is manifest that the area will be a maximum, while in the latter it will be a minimum. And hence, if the boundaries $a$ and $z$ are given, along with the length of the curve established between these boundaries—which must certainly be greater than the straight line connecting these boundaries—the solution will be fully determined: for a single arc of a Circle of this length can be described through these boundaries,

45. *Among all curves $az$ containing equal areas $aAZz$, determine that which, when rotated about the axis $AZ$, generates a solid of minimum surface area.*

Since the common property is established in the area = $\int y \, dx$; its differential value will be = $nv \cdot dx$. <note>In the calculus of variations used here, $v$ represents an infinitesimal change in the vertical position ($y$), and $n$ is a constant multiplier used to balance the constraints of the problem.</note> Next, the formula which must be a minimum is $\int y \, dx \sqrt{1 + p^2}$, whose differential value is = $nv \cdot (dx \sqrt{1 + p^2} - d \cdot \frac{yp}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}})$; <note>The formula $\int y ds$ (where $ds = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}$) relates to the surface area of a solid of revolution, omitting the constant $2\pi$. The term $p$ represents the slope $\frac{dy}{dx}$.</note> from which there arises, for the sought curve, this equation $n \, dx = dx \sqrt{1 + p^2} - d \cdot \frac{yp}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$, which, multiplied by $p$ and integrated, yields $ny + b = \frac{y}{\sqrt{1 + p^2}}$, or $\sqrt{1 + p^2} = \frac{y}{ny + b}$; from which results $p = \frac{\sqrt{y^2 - (ny + b)^2}}{ny + b} = \frac{dy}{dx}$; and $dx = \frac{(ny + b) dy}{\sqrt{(1 - n^2) y^2 - 2bn y - b^2}}$. From this it is evident that if $b = 0$, then the curve would result in a straight line joining the points $a$ and $z$. Next, if $n = 0$, because $dx = \frac{b \, dy}{\sqrt{y^2 - b^2}}$, the curve will be a <term>Catenary</term><note>A catenary is the curve a hanging chain assumes under its own weight. Here, it describes the profile of a "catenoid," which is a minimal surface.</note> turning its concavity toward the axis $AZ$. But if $n = 1$, it becomes $dx = \frac{(b - y) dy}{\sqrt{2by - b^2}}$; from which, by integrating, there arises $x = c + \frac{2b - y}{3b} \sqrt{2by - b^2}$; which is for an algebraic curve, and in rational terms yields $9b(x - c)^2 = (2b - y)^2 (2y - b)$. It is therefore a line of the third order and belongs to the 68th species of **NEWTON**. <note>original: "ſpeciem 68 **NEWTONI**"</note> <note>Sir Isaac Newton classified cubic equations (curves of the third order) into 72 distinct species in his 1704 work "Enumeratio Linearum Tertii Ordinis."</note>

### EXAMPLE VI.

46. *Among all curves $az$ of the same length, define that which, rotated about the axis $AZ$, produces a maximum solid.* <note>In this context, a "maximum solid" refers to the maximum volume of the shape generated by the rotation.</note>

Among all curves, therefore, that share the common property $\int dx \sqrt{1+p^2}$ <note>This integral represents the arc length of the curve, where $p$ is the slope $dy/dx$.</note>, that curve is sought in which $\int y^2 dx$ is a maximum. <note>This integral is related to the volume of a solid of revolution or the moment of inertia about the axis.</note> Since the differential value of the formula $\int dx \sqrt{1 + p^2}$ is:

$x = \int \frac{\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad}{\sqrt{b^4 - (y^2 + bc)^2}}$.
This curve possesses the property that its radius of curvature <note>original: *radius osculi*, the "kissing circle" radius that measures the sharpness of a curve's bend.</note>, which is generally $= dx : d \frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^2}}$, becomes $= \frac{b^2}{2y}$; that is, it is proportional to the inverse of the ordinate $y$ <note>The ordinate is the vertical $y$ distance from the axis.</note>; from which it is clear that the sought curve is the **Elastica** <note>The *Elastica* or Elastic Curve describes the shape of a thin flexible rod under tension. Not only can the arbitrary constants $b$ and $c$ be used to ensure the curve passes through the given endpoints $a$ and $z$, but they also allow the arc intercepted between these points to be of a specified size. If $c = 0$, the **Rectangular Elastica** is produced. Furthermore, in no case can the construction be completed by the quadrature <note>The process of finding area or "solving" the integral.</note> of either a Circle or a Hyperbola, unless $b$ and $c$ are infinite (in which case the line $az$ becomes a straight line) or $b = c$. $x = \int - \sqrt{2b^2 - y^2} + b \log \frac{\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad}{y}$.
